title: Olive groves of locals seized in Afrin
content:
According to local sources, the Rajo Economic Office seized an olive grove belonging to an 80-year-old woman named Fidan Bilal.




On October 22, the Rajo Economic Office reportedly disregarded the law by bringing workers to Fidan Bilal’s grove and having them harvest the olives for its own benefit.




In the Bilbil district, the Bilbil Economic Office seized resident Ahmed Mamo’s olive grove in the village of Qestel and harvested 28 sacks of olives.




The Bilbil Economic Office stated that the regional director had ordered the seizure of Ahmed Mamo’s grove and prohibited him from harvesting his own olives.




Ahmed Mamo still has 140 olive trees that have yet to be harvested.

title: Journalists march against repression in 10 cities: Without free press, there can be no free society
content:
Numerous press organizations, including the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG), the Journalists’ Union of Turkey (TGS), DİSK Basın-İş, and the Journalists Association, took to the streets in 10 cities under the slogan “No to censorship! Freedom for news reporting.” A joint press statement was read out in all 10 cities.




The joint statement, titled “Journalism in Turkey means standing with the people, not with those in power, politicians, or capital!”, was read out during the marches and protests, which includes the following:




“As press organizations representing journalists who defend the public’s right to information and pursue the truth, we declare: Enough is enough! We cannot breathe!




We will not remain silent in the face of a system in which journalism is treated as a crime, news reporting as a threat, and the truth as something dangerous; a system in which not only journalists but everyone who raises objections is subjected to censorship, repression, and punishment. There can be no talk of press freedom in a country where trustees are appointed to television channels, news websites are blocked, reporters are arrested, social media accounts are shut down, and journalists are forced to work under conditions resembling slavery while their social rights are stripped away.




Nor can there be any talk of democracy in a country where a media outlet or journalist is targeted almost every day, journalists are arrested over stories they have or have not reported, social media accounts are shut down, and journalists struggle with hunger.




Journalism stands with the people. When workers are deprived of their rights, when laborers’ resistance is suppressed, when women face violence, when young people are condemned to a future without prospects, when poverty deepens, and when public resources are transferred to capital, it is journalism’s public responsibility to bring these realities to light. Journalists have a duty to reveal what the public needs to know, not to conceal what those in power do not want known.




Journalism cannot be the voice of political power or capital! An approach that presents the interests of those in power or political authorities as the interests of the people, places employers’ economic power above the truth, and regards proximity to the political establishment as a guarantee of professional security is not journalism. It merely perpetuates existing power relations. Those who rely on the political “principles” of the day rather than universal principles should know that those political “principles” will inevitably disappear one day.




Journalists who are paying the price today are being targeted because they ask questions that displease those in power, investigate how public resources are spent, report on allegations of corruption, and amplify the voices of workers resisting injustice, women fighting for their rights, LGBTI+ people struggling for equality, young people raising objections, and the oppressed. Some are detained, some are imprisoned, and others are placed under house arrest. Some lose their jobs, their income, and the ability to continue practicing their profession. Others are forced into silence by the insecurity created by censorship and repression.




They are not paying the price merely for reporting a story. They are paying the price for the public’s right to know the truth, for holding public authorities accountable, and for society’s ability to make free decisions about its own future. Therefore, repression targeting journalists is also an attack on society’s right to access the truth. It must not be forgotten that when a journalist’s pen is broken, society is condemned to darkness. And that is precisely what is intended: journalists must not write, and society must not learn the truth.




Censorship, self-censorship, shutdowns, and arrests are not problems that concern journalists alone. They constitute an obstruction of society’s most fundamental democratic rights and a blow to the public’s right to information. The message of our dozens of colleagues who cry out, “Journalism is not a crime,” is directed at those in power, but our fellow citizens must hear it too. It is your rights that are being silenced. It is your right to access the truth that is being obstructed. It is your right to learn the facts and form your own political will that is being denied. They do not want workers, farmers, tradespeople, civil servants, women, young people—in short, this society, all of you—to learn the truth or stay informed about developments. It is not only journalists who are being silenced. You are being silenced too!




Over the past two years, government-appointed trustees have taken control of Flash Haber TV, Ekotürk TV, the Habertürk Group, TELE1, and most recently Halk TV, bringing an end to broadcasts on these channels that were critical of those in power. Access to the news websites JINNEWS, Mezopotamya Agency, and KAOS GL has been blocked, with T24, one of Turkey’s most widely followed news websites, becoming the latest target of this process. In addition, access restrictions have been imposed on the social media accounts of major news outlets such as Evrensel, Kısa Dalga, SolHaber, Yeni Yaşam newspaper, Ajansa Welat (AW), and Bianet, while separate access-blocking orders have been issued against many of their news reports. The accounts of dozens of journalists and organizations such as MLSA and İFÖD have also been blocked. Furthermore, media outlets such as Gazete Duvar and TELE2, which have been deprived of public advertising revenue and have struggled to survive, along with hundreds of local news websites, newspapers, and television stations, have been forced to cease operations. All of these are examples of how society’s lifelines are being cut off.




Democracy, freedom of expression, and freedom of the press are vital to society as a whole. We call on all our fellow citizens to stand in solidarity with journalists and defend journalism and the right to information. Break the silence! Strengthen solidarity! Stand together against censorship!




Today, we must question not only the government’s censorship policies but also the silence, indifference, and reluctance to show solidarity in the face of such repression.




Those who remain silent while Kurdish journalists are silenced, opposition journalists are arrested, independent media outlets are targeted, and public broadcasting is transformed into a mouthpiece for those in power, as well as those who ignore the repression faced by their colleagues, are harming the shared future of journalism.




Journalism is not merely about protesting injustice when it affects oneself. It is also about defending the right of journalists with different views to report the news. Normalizing self-censorship and choosing whom to support based on the identity, language, political views, or employer of those subjected to censorship means confining professional solidarity within the boundaries of narrow interests. Remaining silent when a journalist is silenced means forgetting that one day it could be your turn.




As press organizations and journalists, our only demand is to be able to practice our profession freely. We do not want to stand alone in this struggle. We call on all our colleagues to join us.




It must be emphasized once again that press freedom is not merely a concern for journalists but an issue affecting every segment of society. Without a free press, society cannot access the news.




Without a free press, there can be no free society!




Release our imprisoned colleagues. End the use of the judiciary as a weapon against news reporting. Put an end to the appointment of government trustees to media outlets. End unlawful access restrictions.




Distribute public advertising and official announcements fairly and equally. Stop the attacks that undermine press freedom, which is guaranteed by our Constitution.”




Amed




In Amed, representatives of the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG), the Mesopotamia Women Journalists Association (MKG), the Southeastern Journalists Association (GGC), the Journalists’ Union of Turkey (TGS), and DİSK Basın-İş gathered outside the Diyarbakır Courthouse. Carrying a banner reading “No to censorship, freedom for news reporting,” the journalists marched to the building of the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (BTK). During the march, they chanted slogans including “The free press cannot be silenced,” “No to censorship,” “Bijî çapemeniya azad” (Long live the free press), and “Don’t remain silent; if you do, you’ll be next.” They also carried placards bearing the logos of Mezopotamya Agency, Ajansa Welat, JINNEWS, Evrensel, Yeni Yaşam, Kısa Dalga, T24, and numerous other media outlets that have repeatedly been shut down or subjected to access restrictions.




The joint statement was read in Turkish by DFG Co-Chair Selman Çiçek and in Kurdish by MKG President Roza Metina.




Antalya




In Antalya, press organizations marched from the Attalos Statue to Republic Square under the slogan “No to censorship, freedom for news reporting,” protesting repression, censorship, and the appointment of government trustees to media outlets. During the march, participants carried banners reading “Journalism is not a crime” and “No to censorship, freedom for news reporting,” while frequently chanting slogans such as “The free press cannot be silenced,” “No to censorship, freedom for news reporting,” and “We will not surrender to darkness.”




Istanbul




Numerous press organizations, including the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG), the Journalists’ Union of Turkey (TGS), DİSK Basın-İş, and the Journalists Association, organized a march from the Bull Statue to the ferry terminal in Kadıköy, Istanbul, to protest censorship and repression targeting journalists. The march was attended by numerous journalists and citizens, as well as Tülay Hatimoğulları, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party).




Participants chanted slogans including “The free press cannot be silenced” and “Bijî çapemenîya azad” (Long live the free press), while carrying a banner reading “No to censorship, freedom for news reporting.” They also held placards displaying the logos of news agencies subjected to censorship. The names of journalists who had been killed were read aloud, with participants responding, “Present!”




The protest concluded with chants of slogans.

title: Saturday Mothers commemorate Hüseyin Toraman
content:
For 35 years, Hüseyin Toraman’s family has been searching for answers about his disappearance in state custody. The then 24-year-old teacher was abducted by armed men in plain clothes outside his apartment in Istanbul 35 years ago. Despite witness statements and an audio recording confirming his detention by the political branch of the Turkish police, his fate remains unknown. At their 1,126th vigil in Istanbul’s Galatasaray Square, the Saturday Mothers commemorated Toraman and demanded that his disappearance be investigated and those responsible be brought to justice.




As they do every Saturday, relatives of the disappeared gathered in Galatasaray Square in the Beyoğlu district, carrying photographs of their abducted and murdered family members and red carnations. The initiative’s statement was read out by Oya Ersoy, Co-Chair of the Human Rights Association (IHD).




Police confirmed detention – investigations yielded no results




On October 27, 1991, Toraman was taken away outside his home in Istanbul’s Kocamustafapaşa district by armed plainclothes men equipped with radios. His wife and several local residents witnessed Toraman being dragged into a white Toros—a reference to the notorious Renault station wagons used by Turkish security forces to abduct, torture, kill, and frequently forcibly disappear numerous opposition figures, particularly in Kurdistan.




Followin

title: Communalist students discuss new forms of organizing in Amed
content:
Under the slogan “It is time to unite through communally organized universities,” hundreds of students and young people from Kurdistan and Turkey gathered for a conference in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) on Saturday. At the ÇandAmed Congress Center, they discussed the political and social role of youth in the peace and democratic society process, self-organized university structures, and the struggle against social exploitation, environmental destruction, and state repression.




Large portraits of Abdullah Öcalan were displayed in the conference hall, alongside banners bearing slogans such as “The women’s path is the path of life” and “We started young, we will triumph young.” Participants welcomed arriving members of the Peace Mothers Council with a standing ovation. Following a minute of silence, the Kurdish anthem “Çerxa Şoreşê” was sung.




“Youth are the fundamental force in building society”




Hasan Karsu, speaking on behalf of the students, focused his speech on social and ecological crises. In light of the ongoing destruction of nature, particularly in Kurdistan, and growing social insecurity, he called upon young people to take responsibility for creating an alternative way of life. “We must not underestimate the social power that students can generate. We must recognize that young people who develop their own independent will can achieve things beyond our imagination. Youth are the fundamental force in building society,” he stated.







Karsu pointed out that the current conditions are characterized by oppression, exploitation, bullying, and violence. “Young people are deprived of their autonomy and reduced to passive objects within society. However, these policies will not break the resistance of the youth. Those who impose all of this on us should know: You will not be able to take our youth away from us. You will come to realize that we are the voice of millions.” Karsu called for strengthening political organizing at universities and schools and intensifying the struggle for equal, free education in the mother tongue.




“Combining our historical role with practical work”




Referring to the new phase of the Kurdish freedom struggle, Karsu explained that while the means and methods of political struggle are changing, its fundamental objectives remain the same. “We have deviated neither from our spirit nor from our goals. We are simply in a phase in which our means and methods are changing. In this new era, we must combine our historical mission with our practical work.”




Karsu remarked that the students are part of a revolutionary tradition that transcends social boundaries and embraces far-reaching solidarity. He said their task is to build a democratic alternative to the existing system within universities. At the same time, he warned of social problems such as drug trafficking, organized crime, and violence against young people. He argued that these developments could not be viewed independently of state strategies aimed at weakening social organizing.







TJA activist Akgül: Dogmatism makes us grow old




Nesrin Akgül of the Kurdish women’s movement TJA devoted her speech to the question of how revolutionary openness and the capacity for social renewal can be preserved. She referred to Abdullah Öcalan’s political approach and his call of February 27, 2025. “With February 27, Abdullah Öcalan once again rejuvenated society and the movement,” Akgül said. She underlined that the Kurdish leader has maintained his capacity for intellectual and political renewal despite his many years of imprisonment.




“What exhausts young people the most and makes them grow old is dogmatism. It damages relationships and imposes limits on them. When we overcome rigid patterns of thought, we remain young. Living together with differences, with people who are different from us, keeps us young.”




Ahmet Emre Taştan spoke on behalf of the Free University Movement, linking his speech to the words, “The sun will belong to those who struggle at dawn.” The conference then continued with a film screening.







Rojava University calls for protection of autonomous university structures




One of the main focuses of the conference was messages of solidarity from various youth and student organizations. Alongside YUNA – Democratic Youth from Germany, messages of solidarity were also sent by the World Youth Strike Movement, the youth wing of the Party of the Oppressed (EHP), youth communes, the Revolutionary Students Union, Libertarian Youth, and the Revolutionary Youth Forces (Dev-Güç), among others.




A Kurdish-language message from Rojava University received particular attention. It emphasized the importance of the conference for organizing young people and warned of attempts to alienate youth from their cultural and political identity through drugs, social estrangement, and other methods of state influence. At the same time, the students criticized the slow progress of the peace process. They said Öcalan remains in isolation, and his physical freedom is an essential prerequisite for advancing the process and resolving existing problems.




Regarding the ongoing integration process in Rojava, the university emphasized that democratic integration must not be equated with abandoning social self-governance. “We want our universities and institutions to remain autonomous. We will give up neither our educational rights nor our linguistic rights. Only in this way can we preserve our identity and culture. You should know that you are not alone!”




Solidarity from Kobanê and Maxmur




Kobanê University also sent a video message describing the conference as a new step toward organizing young people. It urged students from all four parts of Kurdistan to support the initiative and strengthen their joint political efforts. “This conference is a new step, and young people must take further steps. Students from all four parts of Kurdistan should embrace this conference and its motivation and support this struggle. We are ready to do everything in our power.”




A message of solidarity was also received from the Maxmur refugee camp. It referred to the peace and democratic society process and criticized the failure to take the necessary political steps so far. “If the state had taken the necessary steps, we would also be in this hall today.”




The conference will continue with further discussions on student organizing and the establishment of communalist university structures.

title: YJA Star: We are the inheritors of Bêrîtan’s legacy
content:
The Central Headquarters Command of the Free Women’s Troops (YJA Star) commemorated guerrilla commander Gülnaz Karataş, known by her nom de guerre Bêrîtan Hêvî, highlighting her significance for the Kurdish women’s freedom movement on the 34th anniversary of her death. In a statement on Saturday, YJA Star Command paid tribute to Bêrîtan Hêvî’s resistance against surrender during the Southern War of 1992, describing her political and military legacy as one of the foundations of Kurdish women’s autonomous organization.




Bêrîtan Hêvî was born in 1971 in Bingöl, North Kurdistan, and died on October 25, 1992, in the Xakurke region of South Kurdistan. During clashes between PKK guerrillas and Peshmerga forces allied with the Turkish army, she was surrounded by members of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP). She refused to surrender, fought until her last bullet, destroyed her weapon, and jumped from a cliff to avoid capture.




Her death became an important reference point in the development of autonomous women’s structures within the guerrilla movement. On November 1, 1993, the establishment of a women’s army was announced. YJA Star sees itself as continuing this development and the tradition of resistance among Kurdish women, which it traces from Dersim to the present day.




The full statement by the YJA Star Central Headquarters Command reads as follows:




“Bêrîtan embodies the reality of women who organize and liberate themselves, establish their own identity, and express it through their lives. She represents women’s struggle for their existence within the Kurdish freedom movement, the lived and realized reality of women who lead a people’s struggle for freedom, and their stance against subjugation.




The fact that the spirit of resistance of the women who defied subjugation during the Dersim massacre and threw themselves from cliffs took shape once again in Bêrîtan represents the continuity of a tradition of resistance. The spirit of Besê and the women of Dersim found its expression in Bêrîtan and came to life anew in the struggle of the present day.




Bêrîtan represents the fighting woman who resisted surrender in the 1992 war against reactionary Kurdish collaborationism and whose resistance unfolded at the edge of a precipice. Through her determined stance against collaboration and betrayal, she also laid a foundation, as a woman, for the unity and collective action of the Kurdish people.




“Fight, my rose, fight with determination”




Through her ideological awareness, Bêrîtan developed a strong stance. She acquired strategic and tactical skills, advanced as a commander, and put her convictions into practice. In doing so, she embodied the standards, principles, and political line of the fighting woman.




With the words, 

“Fight, my rose, fight with determination. By fighting, we liberate ourselves; by liberating ourselves, we become beautiful; and the more beautiful we become, the more we are loved,”

she expressed the holistic development of the individual and the path of struggle. Through her stance and actions, she became a guiding figure in the women’s freedom movement. She demonstrated once again that the establishment of a women’s army and the struggle cannot be reduced to armed resistance alone, but require a conscious stance and a profound understanding of one’s own reality.




Through her life, she transformed the aesthetics of struggle, the ethics of resistance, and the standards and principles of love into a manifesto. Bêrîtan inscribed her life and struggle into history, verse by verse. She gave voice once again, at the very edge of the precipices, to the existence of women who were meant to be buried in history and condemned to silence in the depths of the abyss. From there, she carried the cry of women’s resistance to all women. With the words, 

“The revolution demands a stormy personality,”

 she continually recreated herself through resistance against backward traditions and collaborationism. With every bullet she fired and every chain of enslavement she shattered, she unleashed new storms. Like a poem, she inscribed the truth of women’s resistance into history and gave it a distinct identity.




A legacy for the women’s freedom movement




Through her struggle, Bêrîtan not only wrote the manifesto of her own time. She also gave new meaning to the legacy of the women whose heritage she had inherited—the Besês. She left future generations the consciousness of a commander and a vision of resistance intended to give them the courage to rewrite the as-yet-unwritten history of women’s liberation. As YJA Star, we are today the organized successors of the line of struggle and the understanding of leadership embodied by martyr Bêrîtan. Every fighter in the women’s freedom movement who takes her manifesto as a guiding principle is committed to carrying forward this legacy and putting it into practice.




Throughout the course of the struggle, this culture of struggle and resistance has given rise to hundreds more Bêrîtans. Her legacy has multiplied and been passed down to future generations. The legacy embodied by Bêrîtan has grown through years of struggle in the mountains and cities, finding renewed expression in martyr Axîn Cûdî, martyr Sema, and hundreds of other women and men of the freedom movement.




We are the inheritors of Bêrîtan’s legacy




Chairman Rêber Apo [Abdullah Öcalan] stated that the greatest response to the legacy of the martyrs is to expand the struggle and recreate oneself in the awareness of their stance. On this basis, and with the aim of further developing the tradition of resistance embodied by martyr Bêrîtan and honoring the legacy of the martyrs, he announced the establishment of an autonomous women’s army on November 1, 1993. As YJA Star forces who follow Bêrîtan’s path and inherit her legacy, we declare that we will connect the women’s liberation movement with the truth she embodied in every moment of life and struggle.”

title: Democratic Integration Conference in Zurich discusses democratic transformation, equal coexistence
content:
The Kurdish Social Research Association (Akademî Kurd) is holding a conference titled “Democratic Integration” in Zurich, Switzerland. The conference, taking place at the Kirchgemeindehaus, is examining the concept of democratic integration from various perspectives within the framework of LAbdullah Öcalan’s Manifesto for a Democratic Communal Society.




The conference, attended by academics, politicians, legal experts, and researchers, focuses on the theoretical foundations of democratic integration as well as its social, political, and cultural dimensions. Legal reforms necessary for a democratic resolution of the Kurdish question, equal citizenship, the democratic republic, and the democratic communal economy are also among the main topics of discussion.




Dilan Çetinkaya: The process places significant responsibilities on all of us




The conference began with a minute of silence in memory of the martyrs of the revolutionary struggle, followed by an opening speech delivered by Dilan Çetinkaya, Co-Chair of the Democratic Kurdish Council of Switzerland (CDK-S).




Dilan Çetinkaya began her speech by commemorating the martyrs of the Kurdish Freedom Struggle and drew attention to the Kurdish people’s struggle for freedom spanning more than half a century. Stating that this struggle has brought significant gains to the Kurdish people, Çetinkaya emphasized the historical importance of the peace and democratic society process initiated under the leadership of Abdullah Öcalan.




Çetinkaya stated that the ongoing process places significant responsibilities not only on political actors but also on all segments of society, stressing that democratic transformation must be reflected in every aspect of life. “Change must not remain merely in words; it must take place in every sphere. We must thoroughly understand Leader Öcalan’s concept of democratic integration and carry out our reconstruction accordingly,” she said.




Veysi Aktaş: Democratic integration is based on the democratic transformation of all peoples




Following the opening speech, the conference proceeded to its first session, titled “The conceptual and theoretical framework of democratic integration.” Moderated by Gülistan Arslan, the session featured Kurdish politician Veysi Aktaş and sociologist, academic, and author Nazan Üstündağ as speakers.




Veysi Aktaş began by thanking Akademî Kurd for organizing the conference. Stating that democratic integration is one of the fundamental concepts of the peace and democratic society process, Aktaş said that the concept points not only to the resolution of existing problems but also to the building of a democratic future in which peoples can live together in equality and freedom.




Aktaş explained that democratic integration is based on different identities and social groups creating a shared democratic life while preserving their distinct identities. “Democratic integration is a concept based on the democratic transformation of all peoples, not just the Kurds. It is founded on coexistence with differences, equality, equal negotiation as a method, and democratic participation,” he said.




Emphasizing that democratic integration does not mean assimilation or the elimination of differences, Aktaş stated that the concept is fundamentally based on the recognition of different identities, social pluralism, and democratic participation. In this respect, he explained that democratic integration entails not only the recognition of the political and social rights of Kurds but also the restructuring of society as a whole on a democratic basis.




‘The fundamental principle is equal citizenship’




Remarking that democratic integration rests on several fundamental principles, Aktaş said that equal citizenship is foremost among them. He emphasized that equal citizenship cannot be understood merely as formal equality before the law, highlighting the importance of enabling different identities and social groups to participate in political and social life while preserving their distinct characteristics.




Aktaş stated that democratic integration is directly linked to the perspective of a democratic republic and stressed the need to establish legal guarantees to ensure that democratic transformation becomes lasting.




“Democratic integration is also based on the Democratic Republic. Achieving this is possible through the implementation of a legal process. Certain legal reforms are necessary for it to become a reality in everyday life,” he said.




Stating that discussing democratic integration solely at the theoretical level would not be sufficient, Aktaş emphasized the importance of safeguarding principles such as equal citizenship, democratic participation, and the recognition of different identities through concrete legal and political arrangements.




‘The process is not limited to laying down arms’




Aktaş also addressed the question of why the concept of democratic integration was chosen, stating that this approach is important for understanding the scope of the peace and democratic society process.




Emphasizing that the process cannot be viewed as limited to laying down arms or ending armed conflicts, Veysi Aktaş explained that democratic integration also encompasses the participation of Kurds in political life with their own identity, language, and social existence.




In this context, Aktaş stated that democratic integration aims to create the conditions for Kurds to pursue their democratic struggle within the existing political and social system without abandoning their identities, adding that this also requires the democratic transformation of both the state and society.




Nazan Üstündağ: Kurds were forced to live as ‘smugglers’ in every sphere of life




Following Veysi Aktaş, sociologist, academic, and author Nazan Üstündağ took the floor, examining the concept of democratic integration through the historical experiences of the Kurdish people, their relationship with the state, and the discrimination they have faced in social life.




Üstündağ stated that the Kurdish people have historically faced various prohibitions, policies of denial, and discrimination in political, cultural, and social spheres, emphasizing that this situation has directly affected their daily lives and their relationship with the state.




Explaining that Kurds have often been forced to live outside the boundaries of the official system in order to exist with their own identities, Üstündağ described this historical condition using the term “smuggler.”




Nazan Üstündağ pointed out that the Kurdish people have faced various obstacles not only when crossing borders but also when speaking their language, preserving their culture, and expressing their political identity. The Kurds, she added, have been forced to live almost like “smugglers” in many spheres of life.




Üstündağ stated that one of the most important aspects of democratic integration is the creation of a social and political order in which Kurds no longer face such constraints simply to exist with their own identity. In this regard, she emphasized that democratic integration cannot be understood as the unconditional adaptation of Kurds to the existing order. Rather, she said, the essential issue is to create democratic conditions in which Kurds can live freely and equally while preserving their identities.




‘I understand democratic integration as a struggle against the state’




Nazan Üstündağ stated that democratic integration has become more important today than ever before, emphasizing that the concept should not be approached solely through legal reforms or political compromises.




She pointed out that democratic integration also entails redefining the relationship between the state and society, and cannot be considered independently of the democratic struggle. “I understand democratic integration as a struggle against the state,” Üstündağ said, adding that democratic integration should be viewed as a process involving the questioning of existing power relations and the expansion of society’s democratic rights. Highlighting the importance of democratic integration in overcoming the exclusion and discrimination historically experienced by Kurds, Üstündağ said, “In this context, democratic integration is linked not only to enabling Kurds to participate in public and political life with their own identity but also to the transformation of state-society relations on a democratic basis.”




The conference will continue with sessions featuring Syrian Presidential Advisor Mazlum Abdi, sociologist Engin Sustam from Paris 8 University, TJK-E (Kurdish Women’s Movement in Europe) member Zîlan Diyar, DEM Party Central Executive Board member Derya Arslan, İmralı Delegation member and lawyer Özgür Erol, lawyer Hüsnü Yılmaz, researcher and economist Ahmet Pelda, and sociologist and anthropologist Neşe Özgen. The sessions will address the political, sociological, cultural, legal, and economic dimensions of democratic integration, as well as the democratic resolution of the Kurdish question.

title: KOMAW calls for international action against death sentence for Varisheh Moradi
content:
The Association of Families of Martyrs and the Disappeared (KOMAW) called on international institutions to intervene against the renewed death sentence imposed on Kurdish activist Varisheh Moradi. In a statement, the organization condemned the Iranian regime’s execution policy and the ongoing repression of women, political activists, and opposition groups. KOMAW has submitted a dossier on Moradi’s case and other human rights violations in Iran to international institutions.




In November 2024, Branch 15 of the Revolutionary Court in Tehran sentenced Moradi to death on charges of “rebellion against the state.” The Supreme Court overturned the ruling in December 2025 due to serious deficiencies in the investigation. Instead of conducting the additional investigations ordered by the Supreme Court, the same court branch once again imposed the death penalty in mid-October. The defense has described the proceedings as unlawful and rejected the accusations against Moradi. The new verdict is not yet final.




KOMAW views the proceedings as another manifestation of the systematic oppression of the Kurdish population in particular, as well as other communities in Iran. “Women who fight for freedom, equality, and democratic rights are particularly vulnerable to persecution and severe punishment. title: PKK prisoners: We accept neither forced expressions of remorse nor delays in our release
content:
PKK prisoners in Turkish prisons have strongly criticized the continued obstruction of prisoner releases, the practice of forcing prisoners to express remorse, and the lack of political steps in the peace and democratic society process. In a statement signed by Deniz Kaya, they called on the Turkish government to fulfill its responsibility for a democratic resolution of the Kurdish question, remove legal and political obstacles, and create the conditions for the freedom of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan.




The statement focuses on the decisions of prison Administrative and Observation Boards, which prevent prisoners from being released even after they have served their regular prison sentences. The prisoners particularly reject demands that they renounce their political beliefs or express remorse in order to regain their freedom. They also recall the history of resistance among Kurdish prisoners, particularly in Diyarbakır (Kurdish: Amed) Prison following the military coup of September 12, 1980.




The full statement on Saturday reads as follows:




Delays in the peace process weaken the will to find a solution




“The current peace and democratic society process has opened the door to a historic phase in which our peoples’ hopes for a free, equal, and democratic life are growing. The determination Abdullah Öcalan has demonstrated to advance this process, end armed confrontations, and develop a democratic political solution, as well as the steps he has taken toward these goals, are evident.




Restricting the fundamental issues of a democratic solution to the framework of security measures, postponing legal reforms, and prolonging the process by making it conditional on certain requirements do not strengthen the will to find a solution but instead undermine it. Such an approach risks deepening existing deadlocks rather than paving the way for a solution.




It is clear that peace cannot be achieved through statements alone but requires concrete steps, mutual responsibility, and an approach that places democratic transformation at its core. If this new phase is truly intended to mark the beginning of democratic change, the benchmark must not be a redefinition of security policy. Rather, what matters is that the state demonstrates its willingness to democratize itself through concrete, practical steps.




Arbitrary obstruction of prisoner releases 




The current stance of the state and government, which involves prolonging the process and delaying concrete steps under various pretexts, is incompatible with the peace and democratic society process. This is particularly evident in the violations of rights in prisons, the continued delays in prisoner releases, the unresolved situation of sick prisoners, and the forced declarations of remorse imposed through decisions by the Administrative and Observation Boards.




It is unacceptable that the situation of our comrades who have been imprisoned for decades and have already served their legally prescribed sentences is subjected to arbitrary assessments and political conditions. When subjective judgments replace legal guarantees, prisoners’ rights are restricted through administrative mechanisms, and their releases are postponed indefinitely, serious concerns arise regarding the principles of law and justice.




The situation of all our comrades whose release is being obstructed, particularly sick prisoners, must be addressed on the basis of human rights and the guarantees of the rule of law.




We reject the policy of forced expressions of remorse




As imprisoned members of the PKK movement, we explicitly declare that we will not accept any approach aimed at breaking our will. We reject both the policy of forced declarations of remorse imposed by the Administrative and Observation Boards and measures intended to pressure us into abandoning our convictions. For us, freedom is not a right that can be made dependent on the approval of a committee, a declaration of remorse, or the expectations of those in political power. Freedom is inseparably linked to human dignity, democratic life, and fundamental human rights.




The tradition of resistance from Amed to the present day




Our history of struggle is a history of resistance against subjugation and of the determination to achieve freedom in the face of policies of denial and annihilation. The experience of fifty years of struggle represents a tradition of resistance forged through great sacrifices and our people’s pursuit of freedom. This history is also one of ideological, political, and organized resistance carried out in prisons under the harshest conditions.




Under the dark conditions of fascism following the military coup of September 12, 1980, the resistance in Amed Prison, in particular, became etched into collective memory as a historic stand against the denial of the Kurdish people, the suppression of their identity, and attempts to break their will. The tradition of resistance that emerged in the prisons demonstrated that oppression and violence cannot break the human will.




The preservation of the ideal of freedom despite severe torture, isolation, deprivation of rights, and all forms of oppression remain one of the fundamental pillars of our struggle today. As bearers of this historical legacy, we know that no mechanism of oppression can destroy our convictions or our claim to freedom.




As in the past, we remain steadfast today in the face of all attempts to break our will. Our tradition of resistance in the prisons, which has never bowed to policies of oppression and subjugation, remains determined to continue the struggle for freedom and a dignified life. This determination is not merely an individual stance. It is an expression of our responsibility toward the collective memory of our people, their history of struggle, and a democratic future.




Abdullah Öcalan’s physical freedom must not be postponed




The freedom of Abdullah Öcalan is one of the fundamental and urgent issues in the peace and democratic society process. A democratic resolution of the Kurdish question and the establishment of lasting peace require the creation of conditions under which Abdullah Öcalan can live and work freely. The obstacles preventing him from expressing his ideas freely and playing an active role in the process must be removed.




The failure to establish the conditions for his physical freedom and a life in freedom, and the refusal to recognize his political and legal status, contradict the expectations of a democratic solution. For the peace and democratic society process to move forward, concrete steps toward freedom and democracy must be taken on a legal basis. These include creating the conditions for Öcalan’s freedom, ending violations of rights in prisons, ensuring the immediate release of sick prisoners, and abolishing arbitrary practices that restrict the right to freedom.




A democratic solution requires mutual responsibility




We emphasize that peace and a political solution cannot be advanced through unilateral efforts alone. The state must also assume responsibility and remove legal and political obstacles. Peace and a solution cannot be sustainable if one side continuously takes steps while the other keeps delaying the process. A democratic solution requires mutual responsibility and concrete political will.




As those resisting in the prisons, we will continue to defend our convictions, our identity, and our determination to achieve freedom wherever we may be. Drawing strength from our history of struggle, we will continue to support our people’s aspirations for freedom and democracy. We will maintain our stance against oppression, isolation, threats, and policies aimed at breaking our will, and we will continue to raise our voices for peace, a democratic solution, and the development of a life in freedom.




Call to the people and the public




We address the following appeal to our people and the public:




For peace to become more than just a word, for a democratic solution to bring about genuine social transformation, and for violations of rights to come to an end, concrete steps must be taken. Violations of rights in prisons must be eliminated, the freedom of sick prisoners must be guaranteed, and arbitrary obstacles to prisoner releases must be removed. Conditions must be established under which Abdullah Öcalan can live and work freely, and his physical freedom must be guaranteed.




As bearers of a fifty-year history of struggle and the tradition of resistance in prisons, we remain committed to our demands for freedom and democracy. We reaffirm that our will cannot be broken, our convictions cannot be extinguished through oppression, and our tradition of resistance cannot be erased from memory.




We accept neither forced declarations of remorse nor policies aimed at breaking our will or delaying our freedom. We will continue our struggle for the physical freedom of Abdullah Öcalan and the democratic future of our peoples. Drawing strength from our tradition of resistance in prisons, we will continue to advance our demands for freedom, democracy, and a dignified peace through the building of a democratic society.”

title: Construction Workers' Union, an model for independent unionism
content:
The idea of independent trade unions operating outside the established confederations has long been debated in Turkey. Criticism of existing unions has also led to the establishment of independent organisations in particular sectors.




The debate has been driven by accusations that unions fail to defend workers' rights, cooperate with employers and pay their officials high salaries. Against this backdrop, one union has attracted attention for adopting a different approach.




Founding members killed in massacres




The Construction Workers' Union (Insaat-Is) has distinguished itself through its organising efforts in a sector where trade union activity has historically been limited in Turkey. Operating in the construction industry, which has largely been neglected by trade union confederations, Insaat-Is works in a sector where working conditions make collective bargaining negotiations difficult and maintaining a stable membership has never been possible. Since its official establishment in 2014, the union has become known not only for its trade union struggles but also for its activities in other areas.




The union emerged from discussions and organising efforts prompted by a question raised during a workers' resistance at the Sapphire Tower construction site in 2010: “Why don't construction workers have a union?” The union has also attracted attention for its stance on wider social and political developments. One of its founding members, Ethem Sarısülük, was shot and killed by police in Ankara during the Gezi Resistance.




Six other founding members, Serdar Ben, Tekin Arslan, Erol Ekici, Tayfun Benol, Ismail Kızılçay and Gökmen Dalmaç, were killed in the ISIS attack on a peace rally outside Ankara Train Station on 10 October 2015. The union's history includes several significant workers' struggles in recent years, including the Emaar resistance, the Third Airport resistance and the Financial Centre protests. Insaat-Is has also drawn attention through its solidarity efforts in earthquake-affected regions, as well as statements and campaigns organised during the resistance in Kobanê and Sur.




The union's activities intensified following the Ankara Train Station Massacre. Insaat-Is continued its work with an approach that differed from conventional forms of trade union struggle.




The Construction Workers' Union organising coordinators Anıl Deniz Gider and Yunus Özgür, together with union executive Ekrem Ekşi, spoke to ANF about the union's history, its experiences of struggle and its approach to trade union organising.







 







‘We lost six comrades in Ankara, but we knew we could carry on their work’




Yunus Özgür pointed out that the idea of independent trade unionism emerged at a time when conventional trade union structures had reached their limits. He continued: “The idea of independent trade unionism emerged at a time when the traditional trade union movement in Turkey was no longer sufficient and could no longer respond to the problems and organising needs of the working class.




Why the construction sector? Following the organising efforts of figures such as İsmet Demir in the construction industry during the 1970s and 1980s, neither the Turkish revolutionary movement nor the trade union confederations undertook any significant organising work in this sector. For the confederations, construction is an extremely difficult sector to organise, and the chances of securing a collective bargaining agreement are less than one in a thousand. In other words, there are virtually no membership dues to be collected.”




Özgür explained that the founding idea behind Insaat-Is emerged during the resistance at the Sapphire construction site. He also highlighted the importance of Serdar Ben, one of the union's founding members, who was widely known as Maviş: “The process essentially began with Mustafa's resistance at the Sapphire construction site in 4th Levent. Maviş had a profound influence on both the trade union movement and the revolutionary movement in Turkey. Our comrade Serdar, in particular, pioneered a new path despite the trade union confederations.




Our union representatives who attended the 10 October rally were there not primarily to support a particular peace policy, but to stand alongside the oppressed Kurdish people. We lost six of our representatives there, although calling them representatives feels rather strange. We lost six comrades who had built this union from nothing, who had created it from the ground up and who carried all its accumulated experience.




10 October was a traumatic event for the entire revolutionary opposition and society. For us, the trauma was particularly profound because we lost six of our founding members.”




Yunus Özgür recalled that the union organised its first major resistance following the Ankara Train Station Massacre at the Emaar construction site.




He said, “The trauma continued to affect us afterwards, but we threw ourselves into the struggle without hesitation. We told ourselves, ‘We are going to carry this work forward. A banner has been left in our hands.’ The organising work that Maviş and our other comrades had begun at the first Emaar construction site had remained unfinished.




At Emaar, we both found a way to ease our grief and gained confidence in our ability to carry on the struggle. We told ourselves, ‘We lost six comrades, but we can carry their legacy forward.’ Despite all our shortcomings and weaknesses, we came to believe that we could do justice to the work they had begun.”




‘The union was built through immense sacrifices and hard work’




Anıl Deniz Gider, an organising specialist with Insaat-Is, recalled that another founding member of the union was Ethem Sarısülük, who was killed by police during the Gezi Resistance.







 







Gider said, “The establishment of the Construction Workers' Union  was never simply about setting up a table and a few chairs and organising workers within a narrow framework. From the outset, the union pursued an approach that directly addressed wider social issues. The foundations of this union were laid through immense sacrifices and tremendous effort. Ethem Sarısülük, who fought on the barricades in Ankara and lost his life during the Gezi Resistance; Duran Baysal, one of our founders who was working on the construction of a mosque in Diyarbakır (Amed) in 2014; and Hasan Oğuz, the European coordinator of the Revolutionary Construction Workers' Union (Dev Yapı-Iş), who contracted Covid-19 while working at a construction site during the pandemic and died following a heart attack, are among the symbolic figures of this struggle. We continue this struggle as a generation carrying forward the banner left to us by the comrades who made these sacrifices.”




‘The interests of the working class took priority through joint struggle’




One of the union's most significant struggles was the resistance at Istanbul's Third Airport construction site. Tens of thousands of construction workers participated in the protests, which attracted attention in Turkey and internationally. Workers also faced police detentions and arrests during the resistance.




Anıl Deniz Gider described the events: “The Third Airport construction site, which had been designated as a pilot area, was an enormous project employing between 30,000 and 40,000 workers. Around 300 to 350 workers had lost their lives in workplace killings, while companies operating under the IGA consortium were responsible for serious violations of workers' rights. On the morning of 14 September, adverse weather conditions, delays to shuttle buses and workers being transported in severely overcrowded vehicles became the final straw, triggering a mass uprising.




Union officials at the construction site were singled out as targets. Nearly 2,700 workers were detained in a single night. Helicopters and riot-control vehicles (TOMAs) were deployed during the operations, which resulted in the arrest and imprisonment of union officials. Although those imprisoned were released after approximately two and a half to three months, convictions were subsequently handed down in the cases brought against them. The resistance received extensive coverage in the Turkish and international press, bringing the exploitation of construction workers into the public spotlight.”




Gider also discussed the resistance at the Istanbul Financial Centre, which represented a different approach to trade union struggle. He explained that Insaat-Is had achieved significant gains by joining forces with the Revolutionary Construction Workers' Union, another union operating in the same sector, in a form of cooperation rarely seen among trade unions.




Gider said, “The Istanbul Financial Centre project involved a rotating workforce of more than 30,000 workers and received investment from institutions such as the Turkish Wealth Fund and Emlak Konut. Insaat-Is joined forces with Dev Yapı-Is, setting aside concerns about institutional influence and membership numbers to prioritise the interests of the working class. The two unions launched a joint campaign under a shared banner with the slogan ‘Enough Is Enough’. This united approach to struggle continued in the reconstruction efforts carried out in earthquake-affected regions following the earthquakes of 6 February.”




Anıl Deniz Gider stressed that the union rejected the prevailing model of trade unionism and continued: “We maintain an uncompromising stance against yellow unionism, bureaucratic management within trade union confederations, exorbitant salaries and excessive spending of membership dues. Given the nature of construction sites, we have adopted an approach based on direct, legitimate and militant struggle rather than allowing ourselves to become trapped in bureaucracy. We have fought for workers' rights through protests, occupations and, when necessary, radical actions such as blocking traffic on the Bosphorus Bridge.”




‘We went beyond workers’ rights to put social solidarity into practice’







 







Anıl Deniz Gider stressed that the Construction Workers' Union carried out activities extending far beyond conventional trade unionism and challenged that traditional approach. He explained that the union had organised a solidarity campaign following the Kobanê Resistance.




Gider said, “Insaat-Is did not limit its activities to defending workers' rights but also developed significant forms of solidarity across society. Through the ‘Lay a Brick’ campaign, we contributed to the construction of a health centre in Kobanê and sent a delegation to the region. During the Sur Resistance, we called on our members not to work at construction sites involved in the destruction of the area. During the pandemic, we organised food parcel distributions. This solidarity initiative later developed into a Workers' Cooperative in cooperation with local farmers.




Following the earthquakes of 6 February, the Solidarity Search and Rescue Team was formally established with the participation of construction workers, students, women and teachers. Through training programmes and practical exercises, the team began carrying out activities across Turkey.”




Ekrem Ekşi, one of the union's executives, explained that the concept of independent trade unionism represented a rejection of trade union bureaucracy and yellow unionism.




Ekşi said, “Insaat-Is has a trade union approach that serves no interests other than those of the working class. It opposes approaches that divide the struggle into separate sectors and reduce the demands of the working class to localised and partial issues. In this sense, independent trade unionism means pursuing a path independent of the dominant political approach. The union's practices, its response to social developments and its activities within the construction sector clearly demonstrate this.




The bourgeoisie's approach is based on dividing the struggle of the working class and undermining collective resistance whenever workers come together and their struggles gain strength. By dividing workers into sectors and creating distinctions between permanent and temporary workers, it places various obstacles in the way of working-class mobilisation. Independent trade unionism maintains that developing a line of struggle free from this political approach is the principal means through which the working class can achieve its fundamental interests. Through its activities, Insaat-Is has consistently sought to carry forward this tradition.”




‘We showed that workers hold the power to liberate themselves’




Ekrem Ekşi stressed that the union's organising efforts were not confined to workplace struggles but extended into wider society. He continued: “One of the fundamental principles on which we cannot compromise is that our struggle must not be limited to the construction sector. Today, working-class struggles are emerging in many different areas, and joining forces with these struggles is entirely consistent with the union's fundamental approach. This understanding is also why we participate in militant trade union networks and have transformed our union premises into a centre of solidarity with working people.




Our union premises are not simply a place where construction workers gather or where issues concerning the sector are discussed. On the contrary, they are a space where people come together in solidarity to confront problems affecting their neighbourhoods, local communities and working people across Turkey. They are a practical expression of the understanding that working people can achieve liberation only through their own collective efforts. As part of this approach, we organise cinema days for children at the union premises. University students and people from various grassroots organisations also participate in these activities, sharing responsibilities on an equal footing and working together to make them possible. Our primary goal in the coming period is to expand this struggle based on solidarity and strengthen the bonds that bring people together.”

title: Biçer: Humanitarian and legal steps needed for ill prisoners
content:
Rights violations against sick prisoners continue to increase in prisons. Obstacles to accessing healthcare, delays in hospital transfers and the failure to release seriously ill prisoners are threatening prisoners' right to life.




Sebahat Biçer, an executive of the Federation of Associations for Solidarity with Prisoners' Families (MED TUHAD-FED), spoke to ANF about the rights violations faced by ill prisoners.




‘Urgent steps must be taken regardless of discussions on the peace process’




Sebahat Biçer pointed out that despite ongoing political discussions about the peace process, no concrete progress had been made in prisons. She stressed that releasing sick prisoners was a humanitarian necessity that should not be subject to political bargaining.




Biçer described the lack of progress in prisons and the deep anxiety experienced by prisoners' families: “Yes, that is correct. This peace process has been discussed for more than two years, but so far there has been no progress whatsoever regarding prisons. In fact, regardless of the process, sick prisoners should be released as soon as possible. This is a humanitarian necessity. Yet we have sick prisoners whose coffins could be carried out of prison at any moment. We have prisoners with stage-four cancer. We have sick prisoners who cannot meet their basic needs or sustain their lives independently. Unfortunately, no solution has been found for any of them. Families are deeply worried, and the condition of our friends in prison is deteriorating with each passing day.”







 







‘Even those who have completed their sentences are held hostage and threatened’




Sebahat Biçer said prisoners whose health was deteriorating were being subjected to pressure by prison administrations, including those who had completed their sentences but had not been released.




Biçer said: “Take Önder Poyraz, for example. He uses a wheelchair and cannot meet any of his basic needs, including bathing. His fellow prisoners take care of his needs, yet he is still being held in prison. Similarly, nothing is being done even for seriously ill prisoners who have completed 30 years in prison and should have been released. Although they have served their sentences, they are not being released.




We have prisoners with stage-four cancer who are approaching the end of their lives. They should be spending their final days with their families, but instead they are being held hostage in prison. Looking at the current process, unfortunately, no measures have been taken to address either their situation or that of prisoners whose releases have been postponed. They are being held entirely at the discretion of prison administrations. They are now being threatened with statements such as, ‘We will keep you here until the very end. You will leave in a coffin.’ Our friends are being held hostage under increasingly severe conditions of isolation, accompanied by such threats.”




‘They are beaten on their way to treatment, and violations are covered up’




Biçer described the conduct of prison officials and incidents of physical violence against prisoners being taken for medical treatment.




She said: “As I mentioned, prison administrations and even guards make threats, saying things like, ‘We will always prevent your release.’ One of these sick prisoners is Devrim Ayık. He has a colon condition and is completely blind in one eye. Even with glasses, he can only see up to one metre ahead with his other eye. He is beaten while being taken for medical treatment and severely beaten again on his return to prison. Attempts are being made to cover up what happened. His family noticed his condition during a prison visit and began pursuing the matter. Many others are being subjected to similar treatment.




Recently, our friend Celal Yıldırım in Urfa also suffered a heart attack, and his condition is deteriorating with each passing day. Yet they are deliberately keeping these prisoners behind bars. They are not being released for political reasons. Our friends are being detained even though they have completed their sentences.




We will not abandon this struggle. We will stand by our friends until the very end and be their voice outside prison. We will also continue to stand alongside their families.”




‘There are nearly 400 ill prisoners, 180 of them seriously ill’




Sebahat Biçer provided figures on the overall situation in prisons, criticised the authorities' indifference and called on the state to take concrete action. Biçer said: “There are currently nearly 400 ill prisoners, 180 of whom are seriously ill. These are people whose conditions are so severe that they cannot sustain their lives independently. Unfortunately, the authorities have turned a deaf ear and are taking no action whatsoever. Humanitarian steps must be taken regardless of the peace process.




There is a process underway, but the steps are always being taken by one side. The state must now take a step as well, beginning with sick prisoners. If a seriously ill prisoner with stage-four cancer or another terminal illness were released, they would simply be lying in bed beside their family. These are people who are no longer capable of carrying out any activities. The state is acting on political considerations. It continues its policy of intimidation and repression by keeping sick prisoners behind bars, which is why it refuses to release them.”




‘Transfers far from families and inadequate treatment are policies of intimidation’




Biçer criticised the continued detention of seriously ill prisoners in facilities far from their families and the restrictions imposed on their access to healthcare.




Biçer concluded: “Similarly, requests to transfer sick prisoners are not being granted. There are seriously ill prisoners being held far away from their families. One of them is Botan Kars. He is being held in Van (Wan) Prison, while his family lives in Diyarbakır (Amed). Despite repeatedly requesting a transfer closer to his family, the authorities have refused. His mother has stage-four cancer and cannot travel to visit him. This is also a policy of intimidation and repression.




The medical treatment provided to prisoners is seriously inadequate. There are major shortages of medication. They are either not taken to hospital at all or are beaten while being taken there. They are subjected to demands for searches inside their mouths. Families also face severe pressure when they visit prisons, while sick prisoners receive only partial and inadequate treatment, often limited to painkillers and other medication intended merely to relieve symptoms. Neither seriously ill prisoners nor other sick prisoners are being provided with comprehensive medical treatment.”

title: Mihemed: We will continue our struggle for constitutional recognition of Kurdish in Syria
content:
Reactions continue in Rojava Kurdistan to the Damascus transitional government's decision concerning the Kurdish language. On 17 October 2026, the Initiative for the Constitutional Recognition of Kurdish and Its Adoption as an Official Language in Syria was announced in Qamishlo. Hesen Mihemed, a member of the initiative, spoke about its activities, aims and objectives.




Hesen Mihemed said there was an urgent need for such an initiative today. He said, “We worked to establish this initiative because our aim was to secure official status for our language. For the past 15 years, students in Rojava have generally been reading, writing and receiving their education in Kurdish, their mother tongue. Unfortunately, under the latest decision, the Syrian Minister of Education has allocated only a few hours, three hours in total, to Kurdish. Even if some other subjects, such as philosophy, mathematics and history, can also be taught in Kurdish, this is unfortunately not enough.




The Kurdish people are an indigenous people, as stated in Article 13 of the Syrian presidential decree. Kurds have rights as Syrian citizens. They must be able to speak, read and receive education in their own language. Unfortunately, however, there has recently been a retreat from these rights. That is why our initiative seeks recognition of Kurdish as an indigenous language alongside Arabic and aims to secure its official status. Just as Arabs can study and receive education in their own language, Kurds must also be able to receive education in theirs. This is why we considered it important to establish such an initiative.”




‘Efforts to secure official status for Kurdish will continue’




Hesen Mihemed stressed that efforts to secure official recognition of Kurdish would continue. Mihemed said: “Kurdish must be permanently recognised as an official language in Syria's future constitution. We will carry out our work towards this goal. They acknowledge that Kurdish is an indigenous language and that Kurds are Syrian citizens. But if the rights verbally acknowledged for Kurds are not reflected in practice and enshrined in the constitution, it cannot truly be said that those rights have been recognised. In such circumstances, there can be no genuine justice regarding Kurdish rights. That is why we are making these efforts. There are human rights organisations, civil society organisations and institutions such as the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). There are organisations that defend the right of every people to speak and receive education in their own language, particularly when it comes to children's education.




We believe that if we continue our efforts, maintain our activities and pursue our work with determination, we can secure our rights. We will establish relations with legal organisations, international institutions and all organisations working on children's rights and issues concerning children. We will also maintain contact with national institutions working in education and language teaching, as well as civil society organisations, intellectuals and individuals concerned with the rights of peoples. Our aim is to establish relations with every organisation working on language rights. We have already established contacts with international and civil society organisations both inside and outside Syria. We contacted and visited them before formally establishing and launching the initiative. We met with representatives of Assyrians, Armenians, Chaldeans and other communities. We developed relations with individuals and institutions representing different peoples.




We explained that we are a civil initiative, that we are not affiliated with any political party and that our work is peaceful. Our objective is to ensure that Kurdish is permanently recognised as an official language in Syria's future constitution. We do not want division. Demanding official status for one language does not mean diminishing or eliminating another language, nor does it mean dividing the country. On the contrary, it represents richness and diversity. In many countries around the world, education is provided in two, three, four or even five languages. We want this to be possible in our own country as well. We are asking for support in this regard. The people we met told us that they supported us, that they could join the initiative and that Kurds were entitled to this right. They also expressed their willingness to become part of the initiative.”




‘Multilingual education does not divide a country; it enriches it’




Hesen Mihemed stressed that multilingualism did not mean dividing a country but, on the contrary, represented a source of richness and diversity. Mihemed continued: “There will be no division in Syria over language or education. What we are demanding is constitutional protection for Kurdish. This would enrich both education and the country's culture. We want to carry out activities towards this goal and raise awareness among all the peoples around us. Allowing people to receive education in their mother tongue and recognising their languages as official languages in the constitution does not mean dividing the country. Nor does it mean weakening another language or diminishing the position of the language spoken by the majority in Syria. Take Arabic, for example. Granting Kurdish official status would not represent a loss for Arabic. On the contrary, it would enrich the country.




This would improve education, mutual understanding and linguistic diversity. One of our objectives is to make our voices heard by all relevant institutions and individuals. We are trying to reach organisations concerned with children's rights and education in the mother tongue. So far, we have managed to reach some individuals and organisations, particularly those outside Syria. Unfortunately, we have not yet been able to reach everyone or every organisation because our initiative was established only recently. Nevertheless, we are continuing our efforts to make our voices heard as widely as possible. The countries and organisations concerned have signed conventions recognising that children should be able to speak, learn and receive education in their mother tongue. Every child should be able to speak, learn and receive education in their own language. Speaking and receiving education in one's mother tongue is a right belonging to all citizens and peoples.




Syria signed a convention in 1993 concerning children's right to speak their mother tongue and the right of all peoples to receive education in their own languages. That is why we will work to reach the relevant institutions. They should also support us. We hope our efforts will succeed. I want to ask a question: Education is provided in five languages in Switzerland, two in Canada and four or five in South Africa. Have these countries been divided? Has multilingual education posed a threat to them? On the contrary, it has helped foster solidarity and equality in these countries. It has encouraged meaningful dialogue and mutual understanding between different communities and peoples. This is a form of richness. It helps develop cultural understanding between people.




Our demands are being misinterpreted. Our call for Kurdish to be constitutionally protected and recognised as an official language certainly does not mean that we want separation or to break away part of the country. Nor do we want to diminish the importance of Arabic as an official language of the state. Quite the opposite. We want Kurdish people to be able to speak, read and receive education in their own language, just as Arab people can speak, read and receive education in theirs. This creates richness and strengthens solidarity between peoples. As an initiative, we want to make one thing clear: Nobody should be afraid. We do not want separation or division, and we do not want to diminish the importance of any other language. We are simply demanding the right of a people to receive education in their own language.”




‘The Kurdish people must protect their language’




Mihemed said the establishment of the initiative had attracted considerable attention. He also said: “Everyone believes that the time has come for the Kurdish people to receive education in their mother tongue. Martyrs, students and teachers have made tremendous efforts towards this goal. Significant work has been carried out through activities organised in support of Kurdish, initiatives both inside and outside the country, and the many relationships established over the years. All these efforts have received support, and people have openly expressed their solidarity. We now want to carry out this work on an institutional basis and strive to secure official status for Kurdish. As an initiative, we have also visited Kurdish political parties. We met with all parties without discrimination because we are a neutral, civil, independent and peaceful initiative. Everyone should join this initiative, support it and contribute to our work. That is why we visited different political parties in Syria individually and invited them to participate. Kurdish is not the language of any particular group. It is the common language of the entire Kurdish people.




That is why we want to set politics aside and carry out this work as independent individuals. Our aim is for the initiative to achieve meaningful results and for Kurdish to be recognised as the language of the entire Kurdish people. We have therefore tried to bring everyone together. We hope that Kurdish parties will unite around the language issue through this initiative and that they will also be able to act together on other matters. We have worked to involve everyone in the initiative and secure their support. The vast majority of parties have expressed their support. They told us that our work and struggle were valuable and that they would join us. As an initiative, we call on the Kurdish people to take responsibility for their own future. Before turning to other institutions, we want the Kurdish people themselves, together with all sections of society, including political groups, intellectuals and academics, to fulfil their responsibilities. We expect everyone, including students, teachers and families, to take responsibility in this regard. Our hope is that the Kurdish people will protect their language. Today is a day of struggle to secure constitutional guarantees for Kurdish and ensure that it becomes a permanent official language in Syria's future constitution. This requires effort, hard work, resistance and struggle.




We hope that all families will send their children to school to receive education in their mother tongue. We also call on existing relevant institutions and those responsible for children and education to support us Together, we can make Kurdish an official language in the Syria of the future. We want a diverse, multilingual Syria founded on equality. Our hope is that, by working together, we can ensure that the Kurdish people also secure their rights.”
