title: Sevda Karaca: War policies undermine unity and labour struggles - Part One
content:
Sevda Karaca, Deputy Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP) and MP for Antep, answered ANF's questions about labour struggles and the struggle for peace.




Karaca said, “War permeates every aspect of social life. Workers' demands for higher wages, the right to strike, women's struggle for equality and people's democratic demands can suddenly be pushed into the background by debates over 'national security', 'the survival of the state' or the 'domestic front'. The racism, nationalism and chauvinism being fuelled also prevent people, women and young people from coming together around shared demands.”




Karaca stressed that Turkish workers also had a responsibility to oppose the policies of their own ruling classes and support the Kurdish people's demands for peace, equality and democracy. She added, “This is necessary not only as an act of solidarity but also to defend the independent interests of their own class. Because in an environment where peoples are turned against one another, it becomes harder to develop a common struggle against capital.”




How do you assess the current state of the labour struggle in Turkey? Is it sufficient, and where does it fall short?




One of the greatest contradictions in Turkey's labour struggle is this: workers' anger is growing, working and living conditions are deteriorating, and individual pockets of resistance are continuing and spreading. Yet this accumulation of struggle has not developed into an effective nationwide class movement or an independent political force representing the working class.




Workers in textiles, metalworking, logistics, mining and the service sector are engaged in fierce struggles over wages, working conditions and trade union rights across industrial regions with very different characteristics throughout the country. They continue to resist despite the threat of dismissal, pressure from employers, obstacles to trade union organising and the corruption of the trade union bureaucracy.




These struggles show us that the working class has not surrendered. However, the experience gained in one factory or one struggle is not being carried over sufficiently to other workplaces, sectors and cities. Resistance often remains confined to individual workplaces and struggles to develop into a collective class consciousness and political force.




What do you attribute these difficulties to?




We cannot attribute these shortcomings to a lack of willingness among workers to struggle. The limitations imposed by trade union bureaucracy, the lack of organisation, fear of unemployment, increasingly precarious employment and political repression are significant obstacles. But socialists and labour organisations must also confront their own responsibilities. Exposing workers' problems and voicing their legitimate demands is not enough. We must establish connections between these problems, bring struggles together, help workers develop confidence in their own strength and link economic demands to a political programme.




The connection between economic and political struggle does not emerge automatically. What we need today is to unite the fragmented experiences of the working class around a common struggle. We must ensure that workers have a say not only in confronting the employers in their own factories, but also in challenging the economic and political system that determines their working and living conditions. The working class needs to organise itself as a force capable of shaping society as a whole. We need to develop a strategy of struggle that transforms workers' scattered anger into collective strength, builds political action out of everyday experiences and enables the working class to shape society according to its own demands and objectives.




Are socialists sufficiently self-critical? Is enough thought being given to why poorer sections of society turn to ruling parties?




The government does not merely control economic resources and the institutions of the state. It also intervenes in people's everyday lives, their sense of belonging, their expectations and their relationships of trust. It creates the everyday, consistent and long-term mechanisms needed to sustain this influence. We cannot explain the political choices of a worker or a poor family solely in terms of economic interests.




People also make political choices based on belonging, trust, identity, solidarity and expectations for the future. Through the networks of everyday relationships it has established among working people, the government controls not only material resources but also the power to shape what society regards as a problem and whom people trust. Confronted with this hegemonic relationship, correctly identifying the problem is not enough. We must also question how we reach workers and working people in their everyday lives and which of their experiences we are able to transform into a common struggle.




‘

We must return to the old principles of organising’




Which of the everyday, consistent and long-term mechanisms of engagement established by the government do we possess? Socialists do not have these material resources at their disposal. For socialist organisations that lack the power, money and resources available to the government, there is ultimately no substitute for consistent work rooted directly in workers' living and working environments, work that does not lose its direction regardless of circumstances, together with perseverance and determination. This is how we can build lasting foundations within everyday life that respond to people's sense of belonging and their expectations. Perhaps I can give an example from Antep. This is essentially what we are trying to do there. We insist on working in working-class neighbourhoods, at the grassroots, where such efforts often remain unseen and unrecognised. This work has taken concrete shape in the workers' resistance struggles in Başpınar. Our efforts are fundamentally aimed at giving working people's struggles an organised foundation. This is not work that attracts attention on social media or is loudly advertised. It requires accepting the demanding task of long-term organising rather than seeking short-term results.




This is the only way to become an organised force rooted in the everyday lives of working people in industrial areas that are regarded as government strongholds, where every mechanism of its hegemony is deployed.




We must become part of people's everyday lives, learn alongside them, develop shared solutions rather than arrive with ready-made answers to their problems, and build political consciousness out of these experiences. For the Labour Party, one of our central challenges is to go beyond being a party that says the right things. We must become a political force that workers trust through struggle, where they make decisions collectively and recognise their own strength.




But something else is even more important to us. Socialists know that the fundamental task is to strengthen the organised power of the working class. The growth of socialist organisations and the growth of the working class's political power are not the same thing. That is why I sometimes disagree with assessments on social media that measure socialist parties by their membership numbers and similar indicators. An organisation's membership may increase. Its visibility on social media may grow. It may win more votes in elections. But none of these, on their own, can measure whether the working class is becoming a historical political subject.




In periods of severe repression, discussions about turning workers and working people into an organised force tend to focus largely on finding new methods and approaches. I disagree with this. In periods such as these, when fear and political and economic repression become increasingly ruthless, we need to return to the old, time-tested methods of organising. Rather than searching for some magical 'new' form of organisation, we need to return to much older principles of organising.




Working-class organising is not glamorous. Spending years building an organisation in a workplace or a working-class neighbourhood is no easy task in a country where the aggression of the one-man regime constantly forces us to respond immediately to one attack after another. Winning a worker's trust or spending years building a lasting organisation in a neighbourhood is not highly visible work. In this climate of repression, it cannot be. Unfortunately, in an atmosphere of left-wing populism where visibility is sometimes valued more highly than becoming deeply rooted in workers' lives, discussions can proceed on entirely the wrong basis. It seems almost characteristic of our times to shy away from the long and demanding nature of organising working people, and to regard forceful rhetoric as more important than devoting time and effort to a street, a factory or three politically conscious workers in that factory. What I mean by time-tested knowledge is precisely this: revolutionary politics is built not so much on these visible displays, but on the often unseen labour of organising.




No matter how high poverty and hunger rates rise, how much anger repression generates, or how clearly the nature of the government becomes apparent to broad sections of society, social struggles will not develop automatically unless we become deeply involved in them as an organising force. Nor will it be possible to transform spontaneous eruptions of anger into purposeful political struggles. Those spontaneous outbursts will eventually subside. The conditions that gave rise to them will either be addressed by the system to some extent or, more often, become normalised in the minds of millions as circumstances that simply have to be accepted. The existing order will find a way to preserve itself.




We have seen numerous examples of this at different moments, from the Gezi resistance to the events surrounding 19 March. Transforming social energy from immediate reactions into lasting organisation requires time, effort and patience. Rather than constantly trying to respond to every new issue the government places on the agenda, our priority must be to build the foundations for sustained struggle. If we are to respond to attacks, our response must emerge from those organised foundations. We must concentrate our efforts in the vital centres of working-class life. Working-class neighbourhoods and industrial areas must be our priority. Only in this way can 'working people' cease to be an abstract expression and become a concrete political subject, conscious of their class position and shared interests. This requires persistence.




‘We must strengthen people's capacity to act collectively’




At the stage we have reached, repression and oppression may be presented as the only reality, and each new wave of attacks may leave people feeling overwhelmed, wondering how they can possibly respond to everything. Yet the issues at stake, and the foundations for resisting them, have actually become clearer. Whatever the government does, it cannot completely exclude people from politics in Turkey.




We can see how essential organisation is if people are to play a decisive role in political life. In recent years, we have repeatedly been told that everything depends on a leader, a saviour, the ballot box or electoral campaigns. Politics has increasingly been discussed as though it were simply a matter of the performance of professional politicians, party leaders and MPs. Yet these approaches have repeatedly proved ineffective. We must strengthen what really matters: people's capacity to act collectively through organisation. Political organisation is one of our most fundamental challenges. It is not simply about expanding political parties. It also means building women's associations deeply rooted in neighbourhoods, initiatives established by residents against local drug gangs, parents' groups fighting for free school meals, villagers coming together to protect their living environments, and students organising dormitory committees, corridor by corridor, because there is no hot water in their accommodation. We need to devote time and effort to strengthening these forms of organisation.




One of the most decisive factors in this period is ideological clarity and understanding. For nearly 50 years, not only in our country but across the world, we have repeatedly heard claims that ideologies are dead, that they destroy freedoms, and that politics is essentially a matter of pragmatism. The Justice and Development Party's (AKP) attempts to co-opt opposition politicians in order to divide and weaken the opposition, the lack of a political programme that may appear left-wing but is essentially rooted in liberalism, and the tendency to regard positions that remain within the existing system and fundamentally serve capital as preferable under conditions of repression all demonstrate how important ideological clarity and consistency become when political struggles intensify.




Professor Cangül Örnek made an observation recently that I agree with: for the first time in many years, the political situation in Turkey has become remarkably clear. There is no longer any political force that people can rely on other than their own capacity to organise and act. Perhaps for the first time since the military coup of 12 September 1980, we are living through a historical period that offers considerable opportunities to strengthen opposition to capital. Today, people are experiencing enormous anger towards capital, but that anger has not yet become fully politicised. We must give it a political direction and prevent it from being absorbed back into the existing system. This is also what we are seeing internationally, from France to Albania.




We are confronted with a brutal labour regime that condemns the working class to ruthless working conditions and extremely low wages, attempts to discipline workers through the fear of unemployment, and traps people in lives stripped of dignity. The scale, consequences and cruelty of poverty are frequently discussed, but there is very little discussion of the means of struggle. There is only diagnosis! It is not enough to define injustice, lawlessness and inequality solely through the government's most prominent attacks. General statements about justice and the rule of law are ineffective unless they are grounded in clear, fundamental demands that working people can embrace.




The subjects of opposition politics are not merely those who are politically active in some way and face repression because of it. The real subjects of opposition politics are the exploited and the oppressed. Politics that neglects this reality has no prospect of expanding its influence or bringing about change.

author: Unknown
title: Hawari: Syria could lose a century without guaranteed rights
content:
The transitional administration established in Syria following the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad's government faces fundamental challenges, including political legitimacy, economic recovery and the protection of the rights of the country's diverse communities. Journalist and writer Nidal Hawari spoke to ANF about a range of issues, from tensions in Hasakah (Hesekê) and the situation of Alawites and Druze to regional power struggles and strategic straits. He warned that the administration's failure to develop lasting solutions to these problems was increasing uncertainty and deepening social tensions.




Hawari stressed that developments in Syria could not be considered in isolation from one another.




‘The legitimacy of the transitional administration is disputed’




Hawari pointed to the structure of Syria's transitional administration, saying that the current political order had not been established by a government directly elected by the people. He said the way the administration had been formed, from the presidency to the transitional institutions, had raised questions about its legitimacy. He added that the structure established under the leadership of Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) was not based on a consensus encompassing all communities in the country.




Hawari said that the forces which had gained influence in Syria following the overthrow of the Assad government were attempting to reorganise their political and regional interests, but had failed to establish a common political position even among themselves. He pointed out that the administration had been unable to stabilise the country politically, economically or legally, placing the process of rebuilding state institutions at risk. Hawari stressed that a transition to a democratic system required the establishment of accountable institutions based on the will of the people and subject to public oversight.




‘The economic crisis is deepening and artificial crises are being created’




Hawari warned that Syria was facing a severe economic crisis, pointing to difficulties in paying public employees' salaries and the administration's dependence on external resources, which restricted its ability to act independently. He said uncertainty surrounding future support from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and other countries was increasing the pressure on the administration. Any reduction or suspension of foreign assistance would make it even more difficult for the authorities to maintain public services.




Hawari stressed that the economic crisis could not be separated from the political crisis. He said the administration's failure to resolve economic problems was intensifying social tensions and creating conditions conducive to new political crises and security problems.




He also expressed the view that artificial crises and hostilities were being created between different sections of society to conceal economic problems. Hawari said this was placing additional pressure on communities outside the central administration or those demanding recognition of their identities and rights.




‘Tensions in Hasakah and the provocation of tribes are not independent of external factors’




Hawari addressed attacks against Kurds in Hasakah and the positions adopted by Arab tribes. He said these developments could not be reduced solely to relations between the transitional administration and the Kurds, stressing the need to examine the political positions of the tribes and the regional influences shaping them. He pointed out that Arab tribes held differing positions among themselves. Some had previously issued statements supporting the agreement between the Kurds and the transitional government within the framework of integration, but had subsequently retreated from those positions.




Hawari stressed that this shift was significant in the context of regional power struggles. He suggested that the conflict of interests between Turkey and Israel could also influence the positions of local actors, pointing to the incitement of certain Arab tribes against the Kurds. He linked the continuation of attacks and tensions, despite the flexibility shown and concessions made by the Kurds on certain issues during the integration process, to the absence of a lasting legal framework in Syria and interference by certain states. Hawari stressed that lasting peace in Syria could not be achieved solely through temporary agreements between local actors.




Hawari also discussed the historical and social characteristics of the tribes, describing certain tribal structures around Raqqa and Deir ez-Zor as communities that had historically positioned themselves according to regional balances of power. Referring to the work of historian and orientalist René Dussaud, he recalled that these structures had been shaped by migration movements and had played important roles in military service and animal husbandry during the Byzantine and Sasanian periods. Hawari said power relations continued to determine their positions today. He pointed out that Turkey exercised influence over certain tribes and that local structures could act under its direction.




The future of the Druze and Israel's policy towards Syria




Hawari discussed the situation of the Druze community in southern Syria, saying that developments concerning its future could not be considered separately from regional power struggles. He pointed to Israel's influence in the region, saying that Druze areas were moving towards more independent military and administrative structures, with local forces preparing to establish autonomous administrative and military institutions with Israeli support. Hawari also addressed Israeli military activity around Damascus, noting that the regional objectives of Turkey and Israel did not always coincide and that tensions between the two countries could influence the positions of local forces.




He pointed to the potential impact of elections in Israel and the US midterm elections on regional policies, while stressing that states would continue to pursue their long-term strategic objectives. Hawari said the implications of any new political arrangement emerging in Druze areas for Syria's territorial integrity would depend on how the central administration responded to the demands of different communities. He added that efforts to secure local autonomy could gain momentum in an environment where rights were not guaranteed.




‘The problems facing Alawites are worsening’




Hawari warned that the problems facing Alawites in Syria were becoming increasingly severe. He said security concerns persisted, particularly in coastal areas, while allegations of attacks against Alawites and hate speech were intensifying social tensions. He said Alawites were being targeted during periods of crisis for the transitional administration, with employees and workers facing attacks. Hawari added that Alawites were also encountering difficulties in accessing public-sector employment. Hawari pointed out that past massacres were being brought back into public debate through allegations involving individuals associated with the former government, while responsibility for certain attacks was being attributed to Alawites.




He discussed accusations surrounding the Baniyas and Reyhanlı incidents, which have recently been debated in the media, in this context. Hawari stressed that claims concerning responsibility for these incidents needed to be verified through independent investigations. He also reported that an Alawite religious figure who had reportedly crossed into Syria through Hatay had disappeared, stressing that the person's fate needed to be established.




Hawari said protecting cultural rights would become increasingly difficult when even the right to work was not guaranteed. He stressed that independent investigations and legal accountability should take precedence over sectarian accusations.




The integration process of the Kurds




Hawari returned to the issue of integrating the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into central state institutions, saying that the Kurds had demonstrated flexibility and adopted a constructive approach throughout the process, but that their rights had not been permanently guaranteed. He stressed that Syria lacked a functioning state governed by the rule of law and pointed to the absence of the institutional framework needed to ensure the implementation of integration agreements.




Hawari warned that leaving recognised rights dependent on decisions made by the transitional administration posed serious risks. Hawari asked, “Can we really regard these rights as rights?” and stressing that they must be founded on social consensus, constitutional guarantees and independent judicial mechanisms. Hawari said the Kurdish people continued to face attacks against their flag and symbols expressing their identity. He stressed that integration must be accompanied by arrangements that protect education, security, political representation and cultural freedoms.




‘New balances of power are emerging along the Lebanon front’




Hawari discussed the relationship between Iran and Hezbollah and developments in Syria, noting that Syria had long occupied an important position in Iran's regional connections and the logistical routes extending to Hezbollah.




He said Iran had been forced to adapt to new circumstances following the overthrow of the Assad government. Hawari explained that Tehran was seeking to maintain contact with different political actors, viewing its longstanding relations with Muslim Brotherhood circles and the possibility of establishing contact with HTS within this framework.




Hawari said there were concerns that a possible military operation by HTS against Lebanon could alter the balance of power, adding that the Lebanese authorities were taking this scenario into account. He also addressed the conflict of interests between Turkey and Israel, saying that Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem's statements concerning relations with Turkey could not be considered separately from regional strategic calculations. Hawari pointed out that forces reaching agreements in Syria could find themselves confronting one another elsewhere.




Developments in Yemen




Hawari said developments in Yemen needed to be assessed alongside the changing balance of power in Syria and Lebanon. He drew attention to allegations concerning Turkey's military cooperation with Saudi Arabia and possible measures against the Houthis in Yemen. He also referred to reports that Egypt had sent military shipments towards Yemen, suggesting that these developments could indicate the emergence of a regional military alliance.




Hawari stressed the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, saying that Iran's power was not limited to its nuclear programme. He pointed out that control over energy transportation and maritime trade routes provided a major strategic advantage. He warned that any disruption in the Strait of Hormuz would affect the global economy. Hawari also highlighted the critical importance of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait because of its position between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Hawari said the establishment of a broader military front against the Houthis in Yemen, combined with Iran's involvement in the conflict, could draw the region into a much wider war.




‘Peoples could lose a century if they fail to protect their rights’




Hawari warned that Syria's transitional process would also shape the lives of future generations and said: “The region is preparing for the next hundred years. If peoples lose their rights today, fail to protect them and cannot secure their future, they may have to live with the consequences for perhaps a century.”




Nidal Hawari stressed that rights must be protected through concrete and lasting guarantees rather than temporary decisions. He said uncertainty about the future could not be overcome without establishing a system that safeguarded the rights of Kurds, Alawites, Druze and other communities, ensured political participation and resolved disputes through the rule of law.

title: YJA Star guerrillas: Martyr Beritan is the embodiment of a free life
content:
Throughout the history of the Kurdish people, there have been many heroic epics that live on in the people’s memory and are never forgotten. Martyr Beritan (Gülnaz Karataş), who shouted in the face of traitors and became a symbol of resistance and the free woman’s stance, represented the essence of the Kurdish woman.




Hesret Dilgeş Amed, one of the YJA Star commanders, spoke about martyr Beritan’s actions and resistance. Beginning her remarks by commemorating martyr Beritan and the martyrs of October.

At that time, there were also liquidationists within our movement who wanted to dismantle it. Martyr Beritan put Öcalan’s ideas into practice in her own life. For this reason, no force could intimidate her or break her resolve.

title: Slovenian philosopher Slavoj Žižek writes letter to Öcalan
content:
Slavoj Žižek, a Slovenian philosopher and one of the leading figures in Marxist thought, wrote a letter to Abdullah Öcalan. The letter, which Žižek sent to the Imralı delegation, reads as follows:




“Dear Abdullah Öcalan,




Today, there are leaders whom we feel compelled to support only because they represent the least bad option among two or three bad choices. However, choosing between bad options never brings a solution; it merely produces a compromise that carries within itself the seeds of its own failure.




You are one of the very few leaders who can and should be supported unconditionally. This is because you combine a principled stance and a profound, theory-based approach with sound pragmatism and a willingness to make difficult decisions.




You are fully aware that the struggle you are waging for the Kurds is not a struggle against the Turks. If you succeed, it will not be only the Kurds who benefit; both sides will win. All citizens of Turkey will enjoy greater freedom, peace, and prosperity.”

title: Öcalan’s book ‘Manifesto of the Democratic Communal Society’ banned in prison
content:
The administration of Siverek No. 1 T-Type Closed Prison in Urfa has prohibited political prisoner Tacittin Kalgı from receiving the book 

Manifesto of the Democratic Communal Society

. The decision was justified on the grounds that the book allegedly contains material posing a threat to security. DEM Party MP Newroz Uysal Aslan has therefore appealed to the Human Rights Commission of the Turkish Parliament, calling for an investigation into the ban.




The measure is based on a decision issued by the prison administration on October 8, under file number 2026/390. The decision specifically objects to passages addressing the historical and political dimensions of the Kurdish question, Abdullah Öcalan’s ideas, the history of the Kurdish movement, and the paradigm of a democratic society.




The prison’s Education Board maintains that the book damages the reputation of the state, contains terrorist propaganda, and could incite hatred and hostility.




Even Öcalan’s call for peace is deemed objectionable




In her petition, Uysal Aslan pointed out that even passages concerning Öcalan’s February 27, 2025, Call for Peace and Democratic Society were deemed objectionable. The book addresses, among other issues, the transition from armed struggle to democratic politics and perspectives on coexistence within society.

title: Three dead and two missing after flooding in Urmia
content:
At least three people have died in severe flooding in Urmia province in Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan). Two others remain missing, while six people have been injured. Heavy rainfall and hailstorms triggered flash floods, particularly in the northern part of the province. The districts of Selmas and Maku have been hardest hit.




According to the provincial Red Crescent Directorate in Urmia, the fatalities occurred in the village of Kaniyan near Selmas, where flooding intensified significantly overnight. Following an extensive search, rescue teams recovered three bodies, including those of a ten-year-old girl and a 63-year-old man. The search for two other missing people is ongoing.




Severe damage to homes and infrastructure




The floodwaters caused extensive damage to homes, roads, and utility infrastructure, particularly in rural areas. According to preliminary assessments, at least 25 houses were flooded and partially destroyed. Eleven vehicles became stranded in floodwaters on connecting roads and near villages.




Search and rescue teams were dispatched to the affected areas. Residents of several flooded villages had to evacuate their homes and were moved to safety.

title: More than 70 Kurdish families face displacement in Kirkuk
content:
Demolition work for a planned housing development began on Thursday in the Kurdish village of Aliawa in Kirkuk province. More than 70 families face the destruction of their homes and the threat of displacement once again. Residents are protesting the authorities’ actions, pointing out that the land was officially allocated to them years ago.




The village is located on the main road between Kirkuk and Dibis, northwest of the provincial capital. According to local media reports, construction machinery arrived on Thursday and began demolishing shops and commercial premises. More than 70 residential buildings are expected to be demolished in a subsequent phase. Residents say that between 70 and 80 Kurdish families are affected.




‘Now they want to displace us again’




The residents are internally displaced people from Kirkuk who were officially resettled in Aliawa in 2011 and 2012 under Article 140 of the Iraqi Constitution. The constitutional provision calls for the normalization of conditions in disputed territories and the resolution of their political status.




“These plots of land were officially allocated to us by the Commission for Displaced Persons. Now they want to drive us out without any regard for our rights, through political interference. This means we are being displaced once again,” a villager said.

title: Shengal delegation holds talks at the European Parliament
content:
A diplomatic delegation from Shengal visited the European Parliament in Strasbourg to raise awareness of the situation facing the Yazidi population and the threats to the region. The discussions focused on conditions in Şengal and the challenges confronting its people.




The delegation included Azad Hisên, co-chair of the Shengal People’s Council; Sara Şengalî, a member of the Jineolojî Committee; and Kurdish politician and former Member of the European Parliament Feleknas Uca.




During their visit, the delegation members met with representatives of various political groups and parties in the European Parliament. Those they met included Swedish MEP Jonas Sjöstedt of The Left group, Austrian MEP Andreas Schieder (SPÖ), Galician MEP Ana Miranda Paz, and German MEPs Katrin Langensiepen (Greens), Martin Schirdewan (Die Linke), and Özlem Alev Demirel, also of Die Linke.

title: “Democratic Integration Conference” to be held in Zurich
content:
The Kurdish Association for Social Research (Akademî Kurd) will hold a conference titled “Democratic Integration” tomorrow, Saturday 24 October, in Zurich. The conference will examine the concept of democratic integration from various perspectives within the framework of the Manifesto for a Democratic Communal Society put forward by Abdullah Öcalan.




The conference will bring together academics, politicians, lawyers, and researchers to discuss the theoretical foundations of democratic integration, as well as its social, political, and cultural dimensions. Legal reforms and a democratic communal economy will also be among the main topics of discussion, particularly in relation to a democratic solution to the Kurdish question.




The conference will begin at 9:15 a.m. with the first session, titled “The Conceptual and Theoretical Framework of Democratic Integration.” Running until 10:45 a.m., the session will feature Kurdish politician Çetin Arkaş and sociologist, academic, and author Nazan Üstündağ.




Political, sociological and cultural dimensions to be discussed




The conference’s second session, scheduled for 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., will focus on “The Political, Sociological, and Cultural Dimensions of Democratic Integration.”

title: Imprisoned PKK members commemorate martyrs and reaffirm commitment to peace
content:
PKK prisoners incarcerated in Turkey issued a joint statement commemorating those who lost their lives in the Kurdish freedom struggle and reaffirming their determination to carry forward their legacy through the Peace and Democratic Society Process. In the statement released by Deniz Kaya, they emphasized that remembering the martyrs is inseparably linked to the pursuit of a democratic resolution to the Kurdish question.




The statement followed the publication of the identities of members of the Kurdish freedom movement who lost their lives at different times and in various areas of resistance. The prisoners paid tribute to their fallen comrades and all those who lost their lives in the struggle for freedom and democracy.




“The martyrs embody the historical memory of our struggle, its ideological core, and the deepest truth of our pursuit of freedom,” the statement said.




It added that each individual’s life and struggle formed part of the collective aspiration for a free life, the determination to resist, and the hope for a democratic future.




Embedding peace in society




The statement underlined that: "Commemoration means not only keeping the past alive in collective memory but also taking responsibility for the future. Honoring the martyrs must be reflected in political attitudes, the assumption of social responsibility, and organizational renewal."

title: Özbingöl: Government politicians must act responsibly for peace
content:
The recognition of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan's political status as the chief negotiator and the provision of conditions enabling him to work freely are among the key demands for advancing the Peace and Democratic Society Process. However, successive statements on the issue by Mehmet Uçum, Chief Adviser to the President and Deputy Chair of the Presidential Legal Policies Board, have sparked criticism.




Uçum, who has reduced the question of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan's status to the issue of disarmament, claimed that raising demands such as Öcalan's release was obstructing the process. His remarks have drawn criticism for disregarding the historical and political dimensions of the problems arising from the denial of Kurdish identity. 




Uçum also made the following remarks on discussions surrounding a new constitution: “The advancement of democracy and the adoption of a new constitution will only become matters for the entire nation to address and implement once the transition to a Terror-Free Turkey has been completed, ethnic and identity politics have been left behind, and the issues associated with them have been resolved not only in practice but also in people's minds. No one should expect the new constitution to be negotiated on the basis of ethnic and identity politics. Nor should anyone entertain the notion that the new constitution will include approaches based on ethnic and identity politics.”




Sevda Çelik Özbingöl, Co-Spokesperson of the Law and Human Rights Commission of the Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), spoke to ANF about Uçum's remarks. She stressed that such statements did not contribute to the peace process. Özbingöl said, “These are not words or approaches that contribute to the peace process,” and emphasising that representatives of the government must act with a sense of responsibility that helps advance the process.




‘Peaceful language and attitudes are crucial’




Sevda Çelik Özbingöl said that they had consistently stressed the importance of the language of peace since the beginning of the Peace and Democratic Society Process. She underlined that the language and attitudes adopted by politicians play a significant role in determining how the process develops.




Özbingöl said, “We have always maintained that the level of responsibility demonstrated by those conducting this process, including politicians, is also reflected in their use of peaceful language and their attitudes. We have approached this issue with that understanding from the very beginning. One of the most important aspects of peace is achieving social peace and reconciliation. That is why we believe politicians bear responsibility for this process. Their language, the words they choose and the comments they make are extremely important to its progress. We believe that those who hold positions of considerable responsibility, particularly politicians within the current government, must act with a sense of responsibility that contributes to the process and helps build social peace.”




‘Mr. Öcalan's role, mission and status must be legally guaranteed’




Sevda Özbingöl stressed that the position of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan should be considered from two perspectives. The first concerns rulings by international judicial bodies establishing violations of rights and the implementation of the Right to Hope. The second relates to Abdullah Öcalan's role in the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




Özbingöl continued: “First of all, the issue must be considered in terms of the rulings on human rights violations issued by international judicial bodies and the exercise of the Right to Hope. There are many prisoners serving aggravated life sentences who are affected by this situation. This is entirely a matter concerning the law governing the execution of sentences and the prison sentence enforcement system.




The second issue, which we consider the most important, is ensuring that Mr. Öcalan has the conditions to work freely, given his role in leading the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Particularly after the law is passed by Parliament, the conditions for freedom must be established for all members and leaders of the organisation, above all Mr. Öcalan, without any discrimination, even if this is achieved gradually.




Even before that, the necessary conditions must be established for Mr. Öcalan to conduct this process directly. Mr. Öcalan's role, mission and status must be properly and clearly defined to institutionalise the process and carry it forward, and to establish the conditions for political struggle and peaceful social life following the end of the armed struggle.”




‘The security-oriented approach to the Kurdish question must change’




Sevda Özbingöl pointed out that Presidential Chief Adviser Mehmet Uçum's characterisation of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan was political rather than legal. She stressed that the process must be secured through social and legal guarantees, legislation and regulations adopted by Parliament. 




Özbingöl emphasised the need to change the security-oriented approach to the Kurdish question and continued: “The peace process requires resolving the Kurdish question through democratic and political means, moving beyond the security-oriented approach, and healing a century-old wound in society. That is what laws are for. There may be different stages to this. In the first stage, one of the priority steps towards negative peace is the initial law adopted by Parliament to regulate disarmament. However, this must be followed by legislation that establishes positive peace, in other words, the legal arrangements necessary to make peace a reality in everyday life.




This process must, of course, involve discussions about a social contract based on equal citizenship. We must also discuss local government, truth and accountability, and the situation of sick prisoners. In other words, legal arrangements are needed to address the consequences of the conflict.




However, ensuring that the process is properly conducted and implemented by defining, recognising and legally guaranteeing Mr. Öcalan's role and mission is also one of the state's primary and fundamental responsibilities as a party to the peace process.




The attitudes and approaches of those conducting the process, as well as their use of peaceful language, are therefore extremely important. Just as a mentality of conflict is constructed, peace must also be built. The divisions created by othering, hostility and security-oriented policies must be overcome through peaceful language, and the wounds must be healed through a peaceful approach.




I do not believe it is right to draw a general conclusion from an isolated attitude. At this stage, I would remind politicians within the government of their responsibility to act accordingly. As the Law and Human Rights Commission of the DEM Party, we consider the peaceful language of those conducting the current process just as important and valuable as the legislation to be introduced.




I believe that Mr. Öcalan must be able to conduct this process and that ensuring the conditions for him to work and live freely is the duty and responsibility of everyone who seeks to advance and build peace in our country. Statements to the contrary do not contribute to the peace process; they undermine it. I believe everyone must act with an awareness of this responsibility.”




‘Equal citizenship must be discussed unconditionally for a democratic peace process’




Sevda Özbingöl also criticised Uçum's remarks about abandoning ethnic and identity politics, stressing that the concept of equal citizenship should not be approached within a narrow framework.




Özbingöl said: “Of course, the Kurdish question cannot be reduced to ethnic and cultural debates. We must recognise that the Kurdish question is also a question of democracy. Everyone needs to understand that if a democratic peace process is to be pursued, equal citizenship must be discussed unconditionally. We must recognise that this is not simply an ethnic or cultural issue. The definition of equal citizenship is an important, fundamental and vital human issue that is also debated within international legal discourse. It cannot be confined to narrow ethnic discussions.




Equal citizenship naturally encompasses the right to live in one's mother tongue, freedom of belief, women, nature and everyone in society. We need to approach the issue more comprehensively. Universal principles of law and peace also require a much broader and more detailed discussion. 




If these discussions are conducted according to immediate or short-term political interests, they will not produce meaningful results. Equal citizenship is an issue that must be discussed with the participation of academics, legal professionals, human rights defenders and all sections of society. In this respect, I find the current debate rather narrow. I do not believe it adequately addresses the needs of the process.




If we are genuinely discussing a constitution-making process, I believe these political interpretations are incompatible with a process based on constitutional equality and social participation. A constitution must encompass the whole of society and must be approached from a perspective that moves beyond the security-oriented, exclusionary and monolithic mentality that has prevailed until now.




I believe we need some time to achieve this. The participation of all sections of society in the peace process, and in every subsequent stage, including the development of future legislation, will be an essential building block. This is not a process that politicians can conduct on their own. Nor is it merely a political debate confined to a particular period or stage. Politicians will, of course, play a leading role in the parliamentary dimension of the process. However, social peace directly concerns all of us.




I therefore do not believe that statements and attitudes driven by political reflexes are sufficient to build this peace. To build social peace, all those who support peace, everyone who longs for peace and fraternity, and all sections of society that have suffered as a result of the conflict must take ownership of the peace process.”

title: Resistance against solar power plant project kicks off in Amed
content:
Resistance against the planned “Zenkar 2 Solar Power Plant and Energy Storage Facility” project in Amed’s Arzoxlî neighborhood entered its second day. While legal proceedings against the project’s “Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Positive” decision are ongoing, company employees entered the construction site accompanied by the gendarmerie and riot police.




In response, neighborhood residents, representatives of political parties and civil society organizations, and environmental activists marched to the project site. A banner reading “Our ancient city of Ğırap and our village must not be sacrificed to capital” was unfurled, while protesters chanted, “Our land, our water, our existence.”




Prevented from accessing fields




Residents encountered a gendarmerie blockade near the project site and demanded an explanation of the legal basis for the work being carried out in the area. Lawyer Ahmet İnan, chair of the Environment and Urban Affairs Commission of the Amed Bar Association, said the restrictions were not limited to the project site and that access to fields outside the construction area was also being blocked.




Berdan Öztürk, a DEM Party member of parliament for Amed, said they opposed the project, stating that villagers were being deprived of their right to life and that people were being forced to leave the places where they lived.

title: Aydın: Peace process cannot be reduced to disarmament
content:
As discussions over the peace process continue in Turkey, Cihan Aydın, Co-Chair of the Human Rights Association (IHD), assessed the current stage of the process and the shortcomings of the legal measures introduced so far. Aydın said the state must take responsibility for democratisation if lasting peace is to be achieved.




Aydın warned that the process would remain fragile unless steps towards disarmament were accompanied by measures to strengthen fundamental rights and freedoms. He stressed that the steps taken since the beginning of the process were important, but that the legal framework still contained significant shortcomings.




Aydın said the process had been under way for more than two years. He pointed to statements by the government and Devlet Bahçeli, followed by the Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan's declaration on 27 February. He described the subsequent mutual expressions of goodwill and the steps taken by the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) towards laying down its arms and dissolving itself as important milestones.




Aydın said the law adopted at the current stage contained significant shortcomings. He noted that it focused primarily on disarmament and offered no guarantees or commitments concerning democratisation or the fundamental rights and freedoms of Kurds. He added that they had previously raised these criticisms, but the legislation had been adopted in its existing form despite all objections.




Aydın explained that the next stage of the process would involve awaiting a determination and confirmation by the National Security Council (MGK), with the publication of its decision in the Official Gazette also under consideration. He also referred to recent statements by the movement's leadership, which announced that some armed elements had withdrawn from Turkey and that camps close to forces in Turkey and the Kurdistan Region had been evacuated.




Aydın said these statements indicated that the commitments made had been fulfilled, while the government had yet to issue a comprehensive statement on the developments. He noted that government officials had largely confined their remarks to saying that the process was being monitored and observed. Nevertheless, he described the stage reached as significant.




‘Categorical distinctions are an obstacle to the peace process’




Aydın criticised the introduction of categories based on types of offences and historical distinctions in the new law, describing the approach as a serious mistake. He explained that, on the one hand, there was an organisation seeking to lay down its arms and pursue its demands for rights and freedoms through active political participation. On the other hand, the legislation divided individuals and groups within that organisation into different categories. Aydın said this was not an appropriate approach.




Aydın stressed that the law not only lacked provisions concerning fundamental rights and freedoms but also contained shortcomings regarding disarmament itself. Excluding some members of the organisation from its scope could make it more difficult for the process to move forward. He emphasised the importance of legislation that would cover all armed forces without discrimination if the disarmament process was to achieve its objectives. Such an approach, he said, would allow the process to advance more effectively and develop more quickly into a genuine peace process.




He recalled that they had expressed these concerns while the legislation was being drafted. Once the draft was made public, they had argued against introducing categorical distinctions. Aydın stressed that the state should introduce legal measures to facilitate the process when dealing with an organisation that had declared its willingness to disarm.




Aydın said the existing legislation was regarded as an obstacle to the proper development of the process and should not be treated as something that could never be amended. He argued that the law could be reconsidered in light of the process's needs and any obstacles that emerged, pointing out that certain problems had already become apparent even before implementation began.




‘The peace process must be addressed as a whole’




Cihan Aydın also discussed how universal human rights principles, confronting the truth and combating impunity should be addressed in conflict resolution processes. He said they had listened to United Nations experts who had participated in conflict resolution processes in different countries. International experience, he explained, demonstrated that such processes needed to be approached comprehensively, as an integrated package, rather than being limited to disarmament.




Aydın stressed that strengthening fundamental rights and freedoms, implementing democratic reforms, introducing legal and constitutional changes, and establishing mechanisms for confronting the past must also form part of the resolution process. He pointed out that the law adopted in Turkey contained no democratic reforms or guarantees concerning fundamental rights and freedoms. Nor did it include provisions addressing the past, truth-seeking or reparations. Aydın said these issues therefore had no place within the existing framework for a resolution. He explained that disarmament had been identified as the first stage of the process, but subsequent stages needed to include legal and constitutional measures addressing Kurds' demands for rights, freedoms and equality. 




Aydın noted that no timetable had been established for these measures. Aydın also recalled statements by some figures within the ruling circles who had dismissed Kurds' demands for rights and freedoms as unrealistic, or even described them as a fantasy. He said the content of the law, political statements and the government's failure to take confidence-building measures had created a situation that undermined hopes for social peace. Aydın stressed that disarmament and democratisation did not have to wait for one another, adding that there was no obstacle to taking steps in both areas simultaneously.




‘The trustee policy and the plight of sick prisoners remain unresolved’




Aydın highlighted the steps needed towards democratisation, pointing out that the practice of appointing trustees to municipalities continued and that those appointed to replace elected municipal administrations remained in office. He stressed that the situation of sick prisoners also needed to be addressed urgently. Aydın said the IHD regularly monitored the issue through its Prison Commission and received numerous applications concerning prisoners' health conditions.




Aydın said prisoners suffering from serious illnesses, including those unable to care for themselves, continued to be held in prison. He noted that the association had documented cases of prisoners dying in custody, as well as others who died shortly after their release. He recalled that the issue of sick prisoners had also been raised during the 2013–2015 peace process. Aydın stressed that making human life a subject of political bargaining was morally unacceptable and that seriously ill prisoners should be released.




Aydın also addressed the situation of prisoners whose release had been postponed. He said that under practices commonly known as infaz yakma (the arbitrary extension of imprisonment), prisoners who had completed 30 years of their sentences were having their release delayed on various grounds. He pointed out that some prisoners had now spent 32 or 33 years behind bars, describing this as a separate and serious problem.




Aydın also criticised the failure to implement rulings by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and the Constitutional Court (AYM). He said resistance to the release of Selahattin Demirtaş and his colleagues continued, stressing that all these issues needed to be considered alongside the broader shortcomings in democratisation.




‘Repressive policies are a major obstacle to peace’




Aydın said judicial and political operations against civil society organisations, opposition parties and human rights groups were continuing. He also pointed to severe restrictions on the media, saying that the social media accounts of civil society organisations, rights groups, journalists and news agencies were repeatedly being shut down.




Aydın linked these developments to the erosion of the rule of law and the shrinking of democratic space. He stressed that without steps towards democratisation, a free and equal life could not be guaranteed for any section of society in Turkey. He said the government's increasingly authoritarian and inward-looking policies posed a significant obstacle to the peace process and undermined hopes for social peace. Aydın emphasised that peace could not be achieved solely through statements by political actors, but required concrete measures to strengthen democratisation and the rule of law.




‘Civil society must be an active participant in the process’




Aydın also assessed the role of civil society in the current process, saying that organisations had been significantly weakened by repression. Nevertheless, he noted that organisations continuing their work were preparing periodic reports, sharing their observations and recommendations with the public, and putting forward proposals on the steps that needed to be taken.




Aydın said civil society had not yet become a genuine actor in the process. He pointed out that the government had failed to give sufficient consideration to the statements, proposals and recommendations of civil society organisations, stressing that it needed to listen to these proposals and put them into practice. He emphasised the importance of establishing mechanisms that would ensure the active participation of civil society organisations if the process was to advance effectively.




Aydın recalled that the IHD and various civil society organisations had been heard by the parliamentary commission and had presented their views. He noted that numerous organisations and academics had submitted proposals, particularly concerning fundamental rights and freedoms and a lasting resolution of the Kurdish question. He said some of these proposals had been reflected in the parliamentary report, but the same could not be said of their implementation. Aydın argued that although the government had listened to civil society, it had not demonstrated sufficient political will to act on its recommendations. Aydın stressed that the parliamentary commission and its subcommittees to be established in the coming period should have a participatory structure. He said women's and youth organisations, as well as civil society groups, must be represented in these mechanisms. He warned that unless different sections of society were able to participate directly, the process would remain an initiative conducted solely between the actors on the two sides, making it more fragile.




Aydın also stressed that statements about building broad public support for peace needed to be backed by concrete policies. He highlighted the importance of ensuring that different sections of society participated not merely as observers, but as active participants in decision-making and implementation. He said civil society had an important role to play in explaining peace to different sections of society and creating opportunities to discuss the process with them. Aydın added that civil society participation would give the process both momentum and resilience.




‘Lasting peace is impossible without democratisation’




Cihan Aydın also assessed the future of the process, stressing that guaranteeing political activity and ensuring the participation of all sections of society as equal citizens were essential to achieving lasting peace. He said establishing lasting peace would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, unless these conditions were met. Aydın stressed that the government needed to abandon its repressive policies and rapidly change its approach to democratisation. He also highlighted the importance of implementing the measures and legal reforms outlined under the democratisation provisions in Article 7 of the parliamentary report.




Aydın emphasised that lasting peace could not be achieved simply by laying down arms. He said concrete guarantees were needed in the areas of fundamental rights and freedoms, equal citizenship, the rule of law, democratic politics and public participation. He concluded that taking these steps would strengthen public support for the peace process and enable it to advance more quickly, effectively and with greater resilience.

title: SGDF member Usta: I was abducted, tortured and forced to become an informant
content:
Hasan Basri Usta, a member of the Federation of Socialist Youth Associations (SGDF), said he was forced into a vehicle by individuals who identified themselves as police officers while returning home in Ankara's Dikimevi neighbourhood on the evening of 15 October. Usta said he was beaten inside the vehicle, that his abductors attempted to unlock his phone using his fingerprint and that he was pressured to provide information about people he was involved in political activism with.




Usta told 

Bianet

 that he was subjected to violence and threats for approximately three hours before being taken out of the vehicle blindfolded in an isolated, mountainous area of Ankara's Mamak district. He said his abductors threatened that they would not let him go unless he agreed to their demands and warned that they would find him again.




Usta described the incident as an attempt to intimidate him over his political activities and force him to become an informant. He recalled that he had previously been arrested ahead of the NATO summit and released after spending three months in prison, adding that his previous imprisonment had also been used to threaten him.

title: Fırat: Cem Foundation seeks to appoint trustee to Kıraç Cemevi
content:
A vigil launched in protest against the eviction order to transfer Kıraç Cemevi, which was built through the collective efforts of local people in Esenyurt and has served the community for nearly 20 years, to the Cem Foundation has achieved its first result. The eviction has been postponed for one month. Those demanding the complete cancellation of the transfer decision are determined to continue their vigil outside the cemevi until their demand is met. Celal Fırat, Istanbul MP for the Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), spoke to ANF and said, “The Cem Foundation, which operates according to the government's mentality, is seeking the support of the government-appointed trustee who took control of Esenyurt Municipality to effectively impose a trustee on Kıraç Cemevi as well.”




‘The walls of this cemevi were built through the people's labour!’




Celal Fırat, MP for the DEM Party, brought the decision to transfer Kıraç Cemevi to the Cem Foundation on the grounds that it stands on Treasury-owned land before parliament and met with the Interior Minister to seek its cancellation. Fırat stressed that the cemevi had been built over the years through the collective efforts of the Alevi community.




Fırat explained that Alevis from Yozgat and Ordu, as well as Turkmen and Çepni Alevis, live in the area surrounding Kıraç Cemevi. He said, “Around 20 years ago, Turkmen Alevis from Yozgat and Ordu, together with our Çepni community members, came together in Kıraç, Esenyurt, and established a place of worship using their own resources. Some contributed their labour, others their earnings, and some donated an entire day's wages. The walls of that cemevi contain more than stone and concrete. They hold the memory of a neighbourhood, the sweat of its people, the prayers of mothers, the breath of pirs and the collective labour of generations. In the 1990s, when Alevi institutions had limited opportunities to obtain legal status and organise, many cemevis began operating under foundations recognised as serving the public interest. Kıraç Cemevi also began providing services under the Cem Foundation during this period. However, this did not change the fact that Kıraç Cemevi is a place of worship built and managed through the collective efforts of local people, where cem ceremonies have been held, lokma offerings shared and funeral services carried out for years. The Kıraç Cemevi Cultural Association, made up of local residents, has been responsible for running the cemevi for years. There had been no problems until now. However, problems have continued for the past year because the Cem Foundation has attempted to remove the existing local management and replace it with its own appointees, relying on the authority to make appointments granted by its statutes. Alevis are standing up against this imposition by the Cem Foundation, which refuses to recognise the will of the people. The community does not accept this system of appointed management.”




‘The Cem Foundation sought control of the cemevi from the trustee who seized Esenyurt Municipality’




Fırat pointed out that the Cem Foundation had claimed the land on which Kıraç Cemevi stands belongs to the Treasury and had requested its allocation from the Ministry of Environment and Urbanisation and Esenyurt Municipality, which is under the control of a government-appointed trustee.




Fırat said that the dispute had led to legal proceedings between the parties. Although the Kıraç Cem Cultural Association filed a lawsuit seeking to suspend the eviction decision issued by Esenyurt Municipality, Istanbul's 3rd Administrative Court rejected the request for a stay of execution. He explained that Esenyurt Municipality's Municipal Police Directorate served an eviction notice on the Kıraç Cem Cultural Association on 6 October 2026, ordering it to vacate the cemevi. Fırat said, “Citing the decision of Istanbul's 3rd Administrative Court dated 10 September 2026, which rejected the request for a stay of execution, Esenyurt Municipality's Municipal Police Directorate claimed that the Kıraç Cem Cultural Association was occupying the premises unlawfully. The directorate notified the association that it must vacate the building and hand over the keys to the Istanbul Provincial Directorate of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change under the Istanbul Governor's Office. The Municipal Police Directorate gave the association 15 days from the date of notification to vacate the premises and explicitly threatened that the institutions would otherwise be forcibly evicted.”




‘Alevis resolve their disputes through cem ceremonies, before pirs and the community, not in court!’




Fırat recalled that residents of Kıraç neighbourhood had been holding a vigil for a week in protest against the decision. He stressed, “The eviction has been postponed for one month, but this does not resolve the problem. The people want their will to be respected and the decision to be cancelled entirely.”




Fırat recalled that Alevi tradition requires disputes to be resolved through cem ceremonies, in the presence of pirs and the community, and called on the parties to come together and reach a mutual agreement. Fırat said, “Alevism has its principles of conduct and religious practices. It teaches people to control their hands, tongues and desires. If there is a dispute, those involved are called to account through the power of the cem and the guidance of the pir. The community reaches a decision there. Councils are convened, and the problem is discussed and resolved before the people. Throughout the Republican era, Alevis have always tried to resolve their disputes within their own communities, in the presence of their pirs and ana spiritual leaders, rather than through the courts. But now, for the first time, an institution, the Cem Foundation, is attempting to impose an appointed administration on a cemevi through Esenyurt Municipality. They are probably drawing inspiration from the current atmosphere of chaos in the country. Eighty per cent of the Cem Foundation's management consists of Alevi businesspeople. Their involvement is valuable and meaningful. But they must respect the will of the people.”




The Cem Foundation leadership sought to establish an Alevi Imam Hatip high school in 2018




Fırat pointed out that the Cem Foundation leadership now seeking to take control of Kıraç Cemevi was the same leadership that had attempted to establish an Alevi Imam Hatip religious vocational high school in Halkalı, Istanbul, in 2018.




Fırat responded: “At the time, I was President of the Federation of Alevi Associations, and I fought hard against this initiative. As a result of that struggle, I managed to have the school closed. The Ministry of National Education was also forced to back down. That was one of the good things I accomplished. Why? What does an Alevi Imam Hatip high school even mean When establishing these schools, this leadership shamelessly declared, ‘We established these high schools to save Alevi children from drugs and terrorist organisations.’ Yet Alevi children are here today, struggling to prevent Kıraç Cemevi from being taken over by a leadership with precisely this mentality. But those people are not here to witness it. I have two daughters, and my neighbour is from Trabzon. How could I say to my neighbour, ‘Your child should attend a Sunni school, and mine should attend an Alevi school’? How would we live together then? We have defended scientific, secular education in the mother tongue for years. Unfortunately, this mentality is now trying to impose the same approach on cemevis. They have money and resources, and they are trying to use them to demonstrate their power.”




‘Do not interfere in Alevi affairs. The decision must be cancelled, not postponed!’




Fırat said he had contacted the Presidency of Alevi-Bektashi Culture and Cemevis to prevent the eviction of Kıraç Cemevi. He said, “I called Esma Ersin, head of the Presidency of Alevi-Bektashi Culture and Cemevis. I told her that we might have different views, but what was being done was unethical. She then spoke to the Interior Minister. As a result, the eviction was postponed for one month. But that is not enough. This decision must be cancelled. Look at Istanbul today. There is widespread corruption and poverty. Flooding has claimed eight lives and left thousands of people affected because homes were built along streambeds. Instead of taking action against those responsible, they are effectively trying to impose a trustee on a place where people come together to share their lokma offerings. And they want to do this in cooperation with Esenyurt Municipality, where the people's will has been usurped through the appointment of a trustee. This approach is unacceptable. The Interior Ministry's decision to postpone the eviction was important in preventing tensions here. But the issue is not simply postponing the eviction for one month. They must not interfere in the internal affairs of Alevis.




They say the land belongs to the Treasury. But how many buildings in Istanbul are not built on Treasury-owned land? That is the question we should be asking. They have made investments worth billions of dollars on Treasury-owned properties. They have built villas and enormous residential complexes, places ordinary people cannot afford to live in. They leave those developments untouched, yet issue demolition orders for four- or five-storey buildings constructed through people's own labour and hard work. The Interior Minister should devote some attention to these issues. He should send the police after those involved in corruption and the misappropriation of funds. He should direct the authorities towards the doors of those businesspeople, not towards our cemevis.”




Fırat calls on the Cem Foundation to ‘come before the community and account for its actions’




Fırat continued: “Our religious tradition includes the practice of dara çıkmak, standing before the community to account for one's actions. As I said earlier, if there is a problem, those involved come before the pirs and the community. Any dispute can be resolved there. If we Alevis cannot resolve a matter within our own community through this practice, it means we have lost Alevi thought, our faith, our culture and the truth at the heart of our beliefs. When I raised these issues in parliament, the Cem Foundation issued a statement attacking me.




They accused me of lying and misleading the public. Let them come here themselves. Why can't they come? They use hostile and divisive language. It is unacceptable. Alevis must not use language that divides or hurts people. What kind of mentality says trustees should be appointed everywhere, even to cemevis? We say our path is founded on love, yet the voice of love can no longer be heard. You adopt the government's mentality and seek support from Esenyurt Municipality, which has been seized through the appointment of a trustee. Have cemevis become the next targets for trustees? How can such a thing be possible? Our path is founded on love, dialogue and mutual consent. Everything begins with dialogue. We need to come together, talk and stand before the community to resolve our differences. I am renewing this call to the Cem Foundation.”

title: Political prisoner Ali Adıman’s release postponed by six years for using the phrase ‘Mr. Öcalan’
content:
Newroz Uysal Aslan, an MP of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) for Şırnak province, submitted a parliamentary question to Justice Minister Akın Gürlek, stating that political prisoners’ rights to freedom of expression and to submit petitions are being violated through disciplinary sanctions in prisons.




The parliamentary question stated that solitary confinement penalties imposed on Ali Adıman, who is held in Bolu F-Type Prison, for using the phrase “Mr. Öcalan” in a petition sent to the Ministry of Justice had been used as grounds to postpone his release by six years.




In her parliamentary question, Newroz Uysal Aslan asked what legal basis justified imposing disciplinary sanctions on prisoners and postponing their release for using a form of address that, she argued, does not constitute a criminal offense. She also raised the question of whether decisions made by prison administrations could take precedence over the constitution, laws, and rulings of higher courts.




The MP demanded information on how many prisoners had received solitary confinement penalties for using the phrase “Mr. Öcalan,” how many had been prevented from being released, and how many appeals against these decisions had been resolved.

title: DEM Party criticizes the government over the process: Why are steps toward peace being delayed?
content:
The Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) spokesperson Ayşegül Doğan assessed the progress of the Peace and Democratic Society Process at a press conference following her party’s Central Executive Committee (MYK) meeting. Stating that the process was being delayed, Doğan said uncertainties surrounding democratization and legal reforms persisted despite statements from the government.







 










When will Abdullah Öcalan’s conditions be changed?




Recalling the call made by Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahçeli in parliament on October 22, 2024, Ayşegül Doğan stated that no significant changes had been made to Öcalan’s conditions since then, apart from visits by the DEM Party’s Imrali delegation.




Doğan noted that family visits had not been placed on a regular schedule either.




“Since the call made on October 22, 2024, changes to Mr. Öcalan’s conditions have been limited to visits by the DEM Party’s Imrali delegation. Family visits are taking place, but there is no regular schedule for them. So, as a political party that frequently seeks answers to this question, we ask: When will these conditions change?”




Who is delaying the process?

title: Altun: We must dedicate 24 hours a day to Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom
content:
Kenan Altun, who had been imprisoned for 30 years, was released from Maltepe No. 1 L-Type Prison. Welcomed outside the prison, Altun said, “We have been released after 30 years, but Abdullah Öcalan is still inside. If we do not dedicate our 24 hours to Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom, we will not achieve results.”







 







Altun also delivered the following message: “All our friends send their greetings. On their behalf and my own, I thank you for welcoming me. Many of our friends inside are ill. I have just left behind a friend who is 84 years old and still in prison. Nevertheless, both I and all our friends are in very high spirits. They all send you their warmest greetings.




All our people must work together and dedicate our 24 hours to peace. We know that the burden we carry is very heavy. This is not a time to sit back; on the contrary, it is a time to intensify the struggle. For all the sacrifices we have made, for our future, and for our children, we must dedicate our 24 hours to the struggle.”
