title: DBP engages with the public on peace: ‘We will develop a roadmap’
content:
The Democratic Regions Party (DBP) is holding public meetings in various cities under the slogan “Building the language of peace together with the people” to promote broader public participation in the peace and resolution process. The meetings, attended by party leaders, co-chairs, members of the Central Executive Committee (MYK), and Party Council members, are continuing across numerous cities in Kurdistan.




Aiming to reach a broad cross-section of society, from workers and civil society organizations to different faith communities and political groups, the DBP seeks to listen to the public’s expectations and proposals during these meetings and develop new policies concerning the process.




‘We aim to reach all segments of society through these meetings’




Speaking to ANF on the scope of the initiative, DBP Party Council member Bünyamin Şeker emphasized that the public meetings go beyond simply organizing gatherings. The activities are not limited to a single day, but involve extensive programs held across different parts of each city. Through these programs, the party aims to reach all segments of society and shape the discourse on peace together with the people.




Şeker pointed out that the primary objective of the public meetings is to help society understand the process, adding that the party has been working toward this goal since the February 27 declaration.




Şeker said: “We are engaged in continuous efforts, mobilizing to ensure that people understand this process. The state is not making sufficient efforts to encourage broader public participation in the process. Claims that society is not ready for the process are also incorrect. Through these meetings, we are trying to reach even those who remain skeptical of the process. At these public meetings, we are shaping the discourse on peace together with the people. We are receiving tremendous support from our people. There is strong public participation, with people openly expressing their views and expectations.”










https://1649452211.rsc.cdn77.org/20261020092554_2026-10-21-amed-bunyamin-seker-dbp-parti-meclisi-uyesi-baris-ve-demokratik-toplum-sureci-1.mp4













‘We are developing new policies’




Şeker stated that the views expressed during public meetings play a decisive role in shaping new policies. The meetings are not merely intended to provide information but also to identify the needs and expectations of the people, he added.




“The people themselves express what they expect and how they believe the process should proceed. As their representatives, we develop new policies based on the conclusions drawn from these discussions. We assess the debates and outcomes concerning what needs to be done to move the process forward and seek to formulate new policies accordingly,” Şeker said.




‘The lack of concrete steps is increasing concerns’




Şeker emphasized that distrust of the state is among the main concerns raised during the meetings, linking this distrust to existing policies and the failure to take concrete steps.




“We can see that the people have a clear understanding of the process. The fact that the state has taken no action has left them waiting with growing conern. When we look at the government’s policies and the way it is managing the process, it becomes clear that the people’s concerns are justified,” he said.




‘We will develop a roadmap based on the people’s demands and criticisms’




Bünyamin Şeker stated that the lack of concrete steps and the perception that the process is being conducted unilaterally are among the main concerns expressed by the public. He added that another important issue discussed during the meetings is the potential gains that could emerge if the process succeeds.




Emphasizing that the public has particularly strong expectations regarding identity and language rights, Şeker said: “This struggle has been going on for many years. For more than a century, the state has pursued policies of denial and rejection. At various times, policies of annihilation were also implemented. Will all of this come to an end through this process or if the process succeeds? Will we be able to freely express our identity and use our language? These are the questions people are asking. Their demands and criticisms will be collected and analyzed, and a roadmap will be developed accordingly.”




‘We aim to increase support for the process’




Bünyamin Şeker stated that the public meetings are not limited to a fixed timetable and the initiative will continue according to the needs of the process. Meetings are ongoing in areas where the DBP is organized, with activities also being carried out in Dersim, Elazığ, and Ağrı.




Şeker explained that, alongside the party’s two co-chairs, members of the Central Executive Committee (MYK) and Party Council are also conducting activities in different cities.




He concluded: “We have no predetermined timetable or expected completion date. We are not taking a technical approach of saying, ‘We will start on this date and finish on that date.’ Our aim is to hold public meetings in as many cities as possible, leaving none out. Through these meetings, we want to increase public support for the process and help overcome the lack of trust. We will seek to explain how sincere and committed our party and political movement are, and how much effort we are making to ensure the success of the process. This is the strategy we have adopted, and we will continue working accordingly.”

title: Ruşen Yakut: Policies of impunity in femicide cases must end
content:
According to Ruşen Yakut of the Rosa Women’s Association, the growing number of femicides in Turkey and Kurdistan reflects a systematic, patriarchal structure of violence. Militarization, state repression, and impunity for perpetrators are exacerbating the situation, while state protection mechanisms frequently fail. In an interview with ANF, Yakut calls for a fundamental shift in policies concerning women, Turkey’s return to the Istanbul Convention, and the consistent criminal prosecution of violence against women.




“We are living through a period in which femicides are increasing dramatically. This violence has now reached the scale of systematic femicide,” Yakut said.




She identifies the patriarchal system itself as the root cause: “Militarism, which underpins nation-state structures, the growing emphasis on security, and the strengthening of sexist policies worldwide are further fueling violence against women.”




Yakut argues that the Turkish government’s policies are shaped by an authoritarian, nationalist, and sexist vision of society that undermines fundamental freedoms and social diversity. At the same time, the economic crisis, the growing prevalence of privately owned firearms, and the political climate are exacerbating violence.




“We are facing a reality in which women are murdered almost every day, either in their homes or on the streets, while children are subjected to attacks even in schools.”










https://1649452211.rsc.cdn77.org/20261017133358_2026-10-17-amed-rusen-yakut-rosa-kadin-dernegi-uyesi-kadin-katliamlari-ve-cezasizlik-politikasi-1.mp4













‘We do not want to be reduced to mere statistics or objects in news reports’




In response to the escalating violence and the lack of criminal prosecution, women’s organizations in Amed have come together to launch the “Women, Justice and Memory Vigil”. The ten-week campaign protests patriarchal government policies, impunity in femicide cases, and the concealment of suspicious deaths of women.




“We do not want to be reduced to mere statistics or objects in news reports,” Yakut emphasized. “Every murdered woman had dreams, children, plans for the future, and her own struggle for a life free from violence. We want to remember not only how they were murdered, but also the lives they fought to live.”




The vigil also aims to exert public pressure on the judiciary. Women’s organizations are demanding that perpetrators be identified, investigations be conducted effectively, and unexplained deaths be thoroughly investigated. According to Yakut, the initiative has already gained support beyond the participating organizations in its first few weeks. Men have also expressed solidarity without being specifically called upon to do so.




Visitors to the vigil frequently commemorate Rojin Kabaiş, Gülistan Doku, and Narin Güran. However, the initiative seeks to ensure that individual cases do not overshadow others. Instead, it aims to highlight the lives of women who have been murdered most recently each week.




“We wish we did not have to report a single femicide. Yet in the very first week, we had to commemorate eight murdered women, and in the second week, there were another eight,” Yakut said.




State protection mechanisms are failing




The women’s rights activist is particularly critical of the practices of judicial and security authorities. She stressed that existing protective measures are not consistently enforced, warning signs are ignored, and acts of violence are not prevented even when victims have previously sought help from state institutions.




“Even when a woman is murdered, we see that the system puts the woman, rather than the perpetrator, on trial,” Yakut said. She added that even in cases where the perpetrator’s identity is clear, sentence reductions for supposedly good behavior or penalties imposed at the lower end of the statutory range effectively create impunity.




“In cases of suspicious deaths, investigations are often inadequate. Case files are immediately closed with the designation ‘suicide’ or ‘accident.’ The cycle of violence behind these deaths and the failure of state institutions are not investigated,” she underlined.




Yakut pointed out that many murdered women had previously filed complaints, obtained protection orders, or submitted medical reports documenting the abuse they had suffered.




“We are talking about murders that unfolded in plain sight and could have been prevented,” Yakut said. Nevertheless, because authorities and public institutions fail to fulfill their obligations, the violence ultimately results in death.




Call for Turkey to rejoin the Istanbul Convention




As an urgent priority, Yakut calls for Turkey to rejoin the Istanbul Convention on preventing and combating violence against women. In her assessment, the cycle of violence has intensified since Turkey’s withdrawal. She also emphasized the need to consistently implement the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) and the Turkish Constitutional Court, and to require all state institutions to adopt gender-equal practices.




Yakut pointed out that effective preventive measures against threats, stalking, and the proliferation of privately owned firearms are also necessary, along with independent oversight of state protection measures by women’s organizations.




“Failures by public officials must be vigorously investigated, and the policy of impunity must be brought to an immediate end,” Yakut demanded.




She stressed that state institutions must also take responsibility for overcoming patriarchal attitudes.




“We need policies that do not blame women but instead seek to understand and protect them,” Yakut added.

title: DBP: Kurdish unity is critical in the face of multidimensional warfare
content:
The Democratic Regions Party (DBP) released the final declaration of its Party Council (PM) meeting held in Amed (tr: Diyarbakır) on October 18.




Published under the title “Kurdish Unity Is Critical in the Face of Multidimensional Warfare,” the declaration assessed global and regional developments, including those in the Middle East and Kurdistan, and outlined the party’s plans for the coming period.




“Mr. Öcalan’s vision of a democratic society has created an important historical foundation for ending conflicts and strengthening democratic politics, both in the Middle East and in Turkey,” the declaration said.




Call to intensify the struggle for freedom, equality, and peace




Emphasizing that the Middle East does not need new wars, new borders, or new hegemonic relationships, the final declaration stated:




“What the peoples of the Middle East need most is a new social paradigm that strengthens grassroots organization, prioritizes women’s freedom, defends ecological living, reinforces democratic politics, and builds a shared future for all peoples. Democratic local organizations and the collective will of the peoples represent the strongest democratic alternative to both imperialist interventions and authoritarian regimes. For this reason, we invite all peoples to become active participants in building a democratic society and call on them to intensify the struggle for freedom, equality, and peace.”




‘Failure to secure free conditions for Öcalan is a shortcoming’




Emphasizing that unity among the Kurdish people is of critical importance in the face of multidimensional warfare, the DBP statement continued:




“The Kurdish people, who have faced policies of denial and annihilation for centuries, have reached a stage where they can play an active role in building peace and a democratic society thanks to their efforts, struggle, and sacrifices. Today, too, the Kurdish people and their friends, regardless of borders, will undoubtedly honor these sacrifices and further strengthen their efforts and struggle.




The Peace and Democratic Society Process has progressed to this point thanks to the historic initiative, determined stance, and calls made by Mr. Abdullah Öcalan. He has been playing a one-sided game of chess, making tremendous efforts to build a Democratic Republic in which all parties and oppressed groups can live as equal citizens. Advancing this vision and democratizing the Republic are fundamental responsibilities of ours and of all democratic forces.




The fact that Mr. Öcalan, the Coordinator of Peace and Political Participation, has still not been provided with the conditions necessary to work freely and that his legal status has not been established constitutes a historic shortcoming.”




‘The path of women’s freedom’




The statement emphasized that the process provides a foundation on which all segments of society can live freely with their own identities. It continued:




“Freedom of identity, one of Turkey’s greatest needs today, is key to addressing interconnected issues such as justice, equality, women’s freedom, ecological destruction, and poverty. With this understanding, the process represents a historic opportunity that must be embraced and advanced by all those who wish to transform Turkey into a country in which they want to live.




Embedding peace in society, securing broad public support for the process, and establishing legal and legislative guarantees are not steps that should be postponed or made conditional. Social transformation can only become lasting when it is founded on a strategy of women’s freedom. We can build peace by fostering a culture that upholds the right to a life free from violence.




We reaffirm our commitment to continuing our struggle to ensure that women’s leadership and the principles of women’s freedom become decisive in every sphere of life, as essential foundations for embedding peace in society and building a democratic society.”




Process of democratic unity




The Peace and Democratic Society Process initially generated great excitement and hope among the people. The primary aim of those opposing the process, both in their thinking and their actions, is to undermine society’s expectations of it.




Undoubtedly, the greatest harm that could be done to this historic opportunity would be to confine the process to a narrow framework or vested interests through narratives portraying it merely as ‘disarmament’ or a ‘transition process.’ The significance attributed to this process goes far beyond simply ending armed conflict.




It is a process of democratic unity in which all identities marginalized by the nation-state mentality can contribute as equal participants. Continuing to view it as a transitional process means overlooking the social dynamics it seeks to create and delaying its progress.




Special warfare policies




Special warfare policies intensified in Kurdistan are becoming increasingly pervasive, targeting society as a whole, particularly women and young people, with the aim of fragmenting the social fabric, undermining the collective conscience and judgment of the people, and preventing them from organizing.




These attacks, which seek to deprive people of their identity, future, hope, and sense of security, attempt to exploit every vulnerability.




We will not remain silent in the face of these attacks directed against society’s moral and political values.




We will strengthen solidarity and grassroots participation




Our response to the wars and attacks we face is a multifaceted democratic struggle aimed at rebuilding an organized society across all sectors of social life.




We regard young people as a driving force in shaping society and women as the leading and founding agents of a democratic society. We consider it essential to the struggle for a democratic society that young people organize in the fields of free thought, production, culture, art, sports, and democratic politics, and that women participate equally, freely, and decisively in every sphere of life.




Together, we will build a process through which we grow stronger by expanding solidarity and collective social engagement, empowering marginalized groups and ensuring that their needs and voices become active forces in shaping society.




Training programs to be expanded and intensified




In light of these assessments, plans have been drawn up for the coming period, with the aim of deepening training programs, completing party congresses, organizing training for leadership bodies in locations where congresses have been held, and continuing the public meetings launched under the slogan ‘We Build the Language of Peace Together with the People.’




The aim is also to expand these public meetings with the participation of members of the Party Council (PM), the Central Executive Committee (MYK), and elected representatives.




Our Party Council, fully aware of the historic duties and responsibilities ahead, has emphasized that all our organizational structures will participate more actively in the process, demonstrating responsibility and initiative in keeping with its spirit.




It has also reaffirmed its commitment to undertaking the necessary work to strengthen democratic politics, develop women’s and youth organizations, democratize the Republic, and turn this effort into a collective struggle involving all segments of society.”

title: Where are the Zapatistas 30 years later?
content:
The Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN – Ejército Zapatista de Liberación Nacional), which emerged in Chiapas in the first days of 1994, came to the world's attention through an armed uprising in a region of Mexico marked by widespread poverty and inequality, where Indigenous people make up a significant proportion of the population. However, it was not only the uprising that made the Zapatista experience distinctive.




In the years that followed, the movement moved away from the goal of seizing state power and developed a practice of autonomy centred on the right of Indigenous communities to govern themselves. In this direction, it established autonomous governance, education, healthcare and production structures based on local communities. Over more than thirty years, as demands for Indigenous rights and political autonomy were not sufficiently realised, the Zapatistas declared their own autonomous governance structures and reorganised them several times. Having established autonomous municipalities and regional administrative centres for a period, the movement dissolved these structures in 2023, shifting decision-making processes to a model based on smaller, local communities.




During this process, it developed its own mechanisms for education, healthcare, justice and community governance outside the official structures of the state, and prioritised the collective use of land and natural resources. We spoke with Professor Neil Harvey of New Mexico State University about the Zapatistas.




Who is Neil Harvey?




Dr Neil Harvey is Professor and Head of the Department of Government at New Mexico State University, specialising in Political Science, Public Law and Administration. Harvey, who studies social movements and struggles for democracy in Mexico and Latin America, has conducted field research in Chiapas. He is the author of The Chiapas Rebellion: The Struggle for Land and Democracy (Duke University Press, 1998) and has published numerous articles on the Zapatista movement and autonomy.




More than thirty years have passed since the 1994 Zapatista uprising. How would you describe the most significant transformation the movement has undergone in the process of moving from an armed uprising to the construction of autonomous political and social structures?




This transformation involved several important changes over time. First, there was a shift from armed uprising to a peaceful strategy based on effective communication, which gained broad support within Mexican society and internationally. Second, there was a transition from the highly centralised position of military commanders to a structure in which civilian Zapatista members in hundreds of local communities assumed stronger leadership. Finally, the language used by the movement changed. The more traditional revolutionary discourse of the Latin American left was replaced by an approach in which different goals and cultural elements, both specific to the Indigenous peoples of Chiapas and appealing to humanity as a whole in a broader sense, were continuously expressed.




Rather than seizing state power, the Zapatistas developed autonomous structures in areas such as local governance, education, healthcare and justice. Why did this path emerge, and what has enabled these structures to survive for so long?




Shortly after their uprising in 1994, the Zapatistas clearly stated that their aim was to "change the world without taking power". By this, they meant that they refused to engage in a struggle to seize state power in Mexico, preferring instead to create their own forms of self-government and autonomous decision-making mechanisms. This approach represents a different understanding of revolution, aimed at avoiding the pitfalls of centralised leadership, a single ideology and the associated pyramid-shaped organisational structure that can emerge when attempting to seize state power. It is a call to change the world by starting from the specific conditions of each place and period in which struggles for justice emerge, while doing so in alliance with one another.




The goal of autonomy initially emerged as an extremely urgent need in the rural Indigenous communities of Chiapas. In these areas, the presence of teachers, doctors and other services provided by central or local governments was very limited. In the 1970s and 1980s, while the EZLN was undergoing its own process of independent formation, community members were also working with the Catholic Church and some left-wing social movements to meet basic needs and improve living conditions. Given the persistent poverty and deaths from treatable diseases, these initiatives were of great importance. Over the past thirty years, the Zapatistas have built new structures upon these efforts by expanding education, healthcare and agroecology projects. At the same time, they rejected government programmes that they believed were tied to political conditions.




In 2023, the Zapatistas undertook a major restructuring of their autonomous structures, placing greater emphasis on Local Autonomous Governments (GAL). Why was this change necessary?




The transition to the more decentralised GAL structure emerged as a result of self-criticism of the model that had been in place for 20 years. The Zapatistas' regional Good Government Councils (Juntas de Buen Gobierno – JBG) were initially necessary for coordinating projects and collaborating with solidarity groups. However, over time, they became too centralised and were no longer sufficiently accountable to the local communities they were supposed to serve. Therefore, this change can be seen as an internal correction within the Zapatista model of autonomy. The aim is to give local communities a greater say and more participation in the decisions made by the movement.




The Zapatistas have also introduced the concepts of "the commons" and "non-ownership" in relation to some of the reclaimed lands. What do these mean in terms of autonomy, land and living together?




"The commons" and "non-ownership" are important in at least two interconnected ways. First, they offer a direct and practical way of reducing conflicts with non-Zapatista community members who, in the past, were mobilised by anti-Zapatismo political actors. Emphasising the shared use of some agricultural land by Zapatistas and non-Zapatistas helps build mutual trust, as the economic and social needs of these rural communities are largely similar, regardless of their political affiliations. Second, "the commons" and "non-ownership" are central to the Zapatistas' political goal of building relationships rather than fuelling divisions. The proposal to consider disputed lands as "ownerless" also challenges the widespread belief that the concept of property itself, whether in the form of private or state ownership, is closed to debate and to alternative understandings of our shared world.




In Turkey, discussions are taking place about ending the conflict between the Turkish state and the Kurdish movement, which has continued for more than forty years. Issues such as local democracy, women's participation, ecology and self-government are also important in Kurdish political thought. Without equating the two experiences, where do you think the meaningful common ground lies, and where should caution be exercised in making comparisons?




The Zapatistas' armed uprising defied even their own fears that the army would immediately suppress the rebellion. Although their methods did not receive the same level of support, their demands quickly gained support from broad sections of society. The armed conflict was relatively short-lived. After 12 days, both sides agreed to begin peace negotiations through a mediator accepted by both parties, the Catholic bishop of the region where the uprising took place. Compared with the conflict between the PKK and the Turkish army, this was a much shorter period. Furthermore, the Mexican government did not insist on the Zapatistas' disarmament, and disarmament has not become a major issue over the past thirty years. Throughout this period, the movement has continued to exist primarily through non-violent strategies, building autonomous healthcare, education and agroecology projects within its own communities.




The peace negotiations were also short-lived (1994–1996) and did not result in a lasting agreement. The agreements signed by the parties in 1996 concerning the recognition of Indigenous peoples' rights and cultures were not implemented by successive Mexican governments. As a result, the Zapatistas turned to putting their rights to autonomy into practice through their own methods. One of the government's arguments was that recognising the customs and traditions of Indigenous communities would threaten human rights law; another was that autonomous Indigenous governments would lead to the fragmentation and "Balkanisation" of the Mexican nation. Although none of these claims had any factual basis, they allowed the government to present itself as a defender of liberal tolerance and national unity. However, this was far removed from the understanding represented by the Zapatistas. The peace process in Turkey will need to avoid forms of exclusionary nationalism in order to enable the peaceful and democratic participation of all groups within a more inclusive country.




What is the most important lesson that more than thirty years of Zapatista autonomy offers to movements seeking to move beyond armed conflict while preserving their political identity and collective organisation?




The most important lesson is this: despite, or perhaps precisely because of, the counter-insurgency operations and paramilitary violence they have faced since 1994, the Zapatistas continue to embrace life and make it their priority. The movement remembers its past but looks towards the future. This can be seen both in the generational change among those involved in the movement and in its openness to art, theatre, music and dialogue. Their fundamental aims are based on building relationships and valuing them. The issue is not simply to achieve something for the Zapatistas, but to work towards ensuring that all humanity can live a dignified life in the future, at a time of global crises and wars.




The lesson offered by the Zapatistas is that we must stop the destruction of the conditions that make life possible in the future and refuse to accept the collapse these conditions are undergoing today. In this context, as part of the "Journey for Life" (La Gira por la Vida), the Zapatistas are planning for 1,111 people from their communities to travel from Chiapas to Mexico City in December 2026 to meet with and support families searching for their missing loved ones. This action can be seen as a stance that affirms the value of the lives of the missing and rejects the normalisation of the killing of thousands of people at the hands of criminal organisations, the militaristic policies that have been implemented since at least 2006 without success, as well as corruption among state officials and their collaboration with criminal organisations.




Armed conflicts leave behind deaths, trauma and collective memory. How have Zapatista communities related to those who lost their lives? What place does the memory of the dead hold in the movement's political and social life?




The most important point to emphasise here is that the Zapatistas embrace life and have always refused to create a cult around fallen heroes or martyrs. They have no interest in establishing museums about the armed period of the uprising or fuelling nostalgia. This period was extremely horrific: at least 145 people lost their lives, homes were destroyed and thousands of people were displaced by the Mexican army. Added to this were ongoing human rights violations caused by counter-insurgency operations and paramilitary groups, as well as events such as the massacre of 45 people by paramilitaries in the village of Acteal in 1997. The movement has always focused on celebrating life in all its beauty: the land, waters, youth, art, science, relationships with visitors from all over the world, and the joy of learning from one another on equal terms. This approach is also clearly expressed in the Zapatistas' "Declaration for Life", published in 2021. Nevertheless, those who lost their lives in the fighting in January 1994, or those who later died from illness, such as Comandanta Ramona, have not been forgotten. Their lives are remembered in murals, theatrical works and writings.




It is also important to remember that the uprising was carried out against forgetting. No one should have had to risk their life to gain access to clean water, housing, schools, health centres, freedom and peace. However, the Zapatistas felt they had to make this decision. During the decade before 1994, thousands of Indigenous people in Chiapas died from treatable diseases, and almost no one noticed. Faced with these preventable deaths, the Zapatistas chose life.




The Zapatista experience is often praised internationally. However, this experience also has its difficulties and contradictions. What do you think have been the main limitations of Zapatista autonomy?




One of the problems that emerged immediately after the uprising was that Subcomandante Marcos, who was non-Indigenous, of mestizo [a person of mixed European and Indigenous American ancestry] origin and educated in the city, became an overly central figure and almost the sole voice of the Zapatistas, despite his own efforts to explain that the movement was not about him. Much of the media focused heavily on Marcos, while saying very little about the movement's other Indigenous leaders and members. This created problems both in terms of how the movement was portrayed externally and highlighted the need to restructure its internal organisation by transferring decision-making authority from military commanders to the civilian support bases in the communities. This process was linked to the establishment of autonomous governance and became increasingly established after 2001. Another challenge was putting into practice the goal of ensuring broad participation by women and young people. Although positive steps were taken, this was not an easy process.

title: Ulus: Healthcare must be free and accessible to all
content:
Structural problems in public hospitals and shortcomings in healthcare services are making it increasingly difficult for citizens to access medical care. People struggling to secure appointments through the Central Physician Appointment System (MHRS) sometimes have to wait at least 15 days just to submit an appointment request. Patients who eventually manage to obtain appointments after considerable effort must then try to explain their health problems within limited consultation times due to overcrowding in hospitals.




Difficulties in securing appointments and restrictions on consultation times are further deepening problems concerning the quality and accessibility of healthcare services.




Mehmet Nuri Ulus, Co-Chair of the Diyarbakır (Amed) Branch of the Health and Social Service Workers’ Union (SES), spoke to ANF about the problems facing public hospitals.




‘Healthcare is not being transformed, it is going backwards’




Ulus recalled that the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government has introduced healthcare reform and transformation programmes since 2002. He said that the policies implemented in recent years have caused serious problems in healthcare services and continued: “The AKP government has announced numerous programmes under the names of healthcare reform and healthcare transformation. However, particularly over the past 10 to 15 years, what has been called healthcare transformation has, from our perspective, meant collapse and regression. We have experienced both the COVID-19 pandemic and the earthquake during this period. These major crises showed us just how inadequate the healthcare system was in responding to the problems that arose.




The healthcare system should have been prepared for these crises and should have had the capacity to meet society's healthcare needs. Healthcare is a service that must be provided within the framework of the social welfare state. Everyone must be able to receive healthcare services equally, accessibly and in their mother tongue.




However, in recent years, we have seen healthcare services increasingly turn into a system in which those who have money can access care more easily. The proliferation of private hospitals is one aspect of this. Another is the emergence of an approach in which even public hospitals link faster access to certain tests, radiological examinations, medical reports and surgical procedures to payment. This undermines the principle that healthcare services should be equal for everyone.”




‘Physical queues have been replaced by virtual queues’




Ulus addressed the appointment crisis in the healthcare system, pointing out that the queues once seen outside hospitals now continue through the Central Physician Appointment System. He said appointment systems should make healthcare more accessible, but many citizens are currently unable to secure appointments.




Ulus said: “The AKP government used to say that people had to go to hospitals early in the morning and wait in queues to see a doctor. Today, physical queues have been replaced by virtual queues. Instead of waiting for hours outside hospitals, people now try to book appointments on their phones or online. However, when you access the system, you cannot find an available appointment. The queues have therefore not disappeared; they have simply changed form. Citizens now find themselves waiting in front of digital systems to access healthcare.




People face serious difficulties securing appointments, particularly in departments such as ear, nose and throat, ophthalmology and dermatology. Citizens who cannot obtain appointments are then forced to turn to private hospitals. However, considering the economic crisis, the struggle to make ends meet and the housing problems in Turkey, not everyone has the financial means to seek treatment at private hospitals.




As a result, the inability to access healthcare has become another dimension of economic hardship. Healthcare should be free and accessible, yet citizens are forced to stretch their financial resources to obtain the medical care they need.”




‘The budget is not allocated to preventive healthcare services’




Ulus said that the problems facing the healthcare system are not limited to difficulties in securing appointments. He drew attention to the following issues: “When we look at the Ministry of Health's budget and healthcare policies, we see that preventive healthcare services are consistently pushed into the background. Yet healthcare is not simply about people going to hospital and receiving treatment after they become ill. Creating the conditions that prevent people from becoming ill is also a fundamental part of healthcare. Clean air, clean water, preventive vaccinations, and psychological and social support must all be considered within this framework.




However, the current system places greater emphasis on curative healthcare services. We see that a large proportion of the budget is directed towards hospitals, medical examinations and treatments, while preventive healthcare services do not receive sufficient support.




Preventive healthcare services involve measures aimed at preventing illness in society. Strengthening these services means taking the necessary precautions before people develop health problems. Healthcare policies must be restructured around this approach.”




‘The lack of healthcare services in Kurdish persists’




Mehmet Nuri Ulus highlighted the importance of the mother tongue in healthcare services and said: “To diagnose an illness correctly, you need to understand the patient's complaints and the problems they are experiencing. Language is one of the most important tools for this. Patients can explain themselves more comfortably when they are able to describe their condition in their mother tongue. Healthcare workers must also understand their patients correctly and obtain a complete medical history.




Although the Ministry of Health's systems provide opportunities to offer services in different languages, we do not see the same approach towards Kurdish. The necessary policies have not been developed to enable Kurdish-speaking citizens to receive healthcare services in their mother tongue. This is a significant shortcoming in terms of access to healthcare.




Language barriers can cause communication problems between patients and healthcare workers. Inadequate communication can lead to misunderstandings, patients being unable to fully explain their symptoms, and difficulties in the diagnostic process. For this reason, the mother tongue must be taken into account in healthcare services.




The necessary arrangements must be made to ensure that everyone can receive healthcare services in their mother tongue. The Ministry of Health must develop comprehensive policies on this issue without delay. Equality in healthcare cannot be achieved simply by keeping hospital doors open to everyone. A system must be established in which people can express themselves and communicate effectively with healthcare workers.”




‘Physical conditions in Diyarbakır hospitals are inadequate’




Ulus stressed that inadequate physical conditions in hospitals make it difficult to provide healthcare services. He said: “The adequacy of the buildings in which healthcare services are provided is also a major problem. We can see this clearly in Diyarbakır. There is talk of a new hospital under the name of a City Hospital. However, when we look at the condition of existing hospitals, we encounter serious shortcomings. 




It is reported that a demolition order was issued for Selahaddin Eyyubi Children's Hospital following the earthquakes of 6 February and that the building failed structural safety tests. Despite this, we are faced with a situation in which the necessary steps have not been taken, with austerity measures cited as the justification.




New hospital projects are being put forward on the one hand, while problems concerning the physical conditions of existing hospitals continue on the other. Buildings where healthcare services are provided must be safe and designed to meet the needs of patients and healthcare workers. Healthcare is not something that can be left to chance. The state has a responsibility to ensure that citizens receive healthcare in safe conditions.”




‘There can be no cuts to healthcare’




Mehmet Nuri Ulus said that resolving the problems in the healthcare sector requires a comprehensive change in policy. He added: “Our fundamental principle is that there can be no cuts to healthcare. The problems we are experiencing today show just how important this principle is. Cost-cutting measures may be discussed in every sector, but cuts to healthcare directly affect people's lives. The failure to employ the necessary healthcare personnel, improve the physical conditions of hospitals and allocate sufficient funding to preventive healthcare services makes it more difficult for citizens to access healthcare.




The healthcare system needs to be reassessed from beginning to end. First and foremost, healthcare services must be made equal, free and accessible to everyone. This requires employing sufficient numbers of healthcare workers, appointing healthcare professionals who are waiting for positions and improving the physical conditions of existing hospitals. Newly established units must also begin providing services only after the necessary infrastructure and staffing are in place.




In addition, more resources must be allocated to preventive healthcare services, and policies aimed at preventing people from becoming ill must be developed. The necessary arrangements must be made to provide healthcare services in people's mother tongues, and the barriers preventing patients from communicating effectively with healthcare workers must be removed.”

title: HANA: Iranian regime abducts and disappears Kurds
content:
The HANA Human Rights Organization has published a report on the arrest and abduction of Kurds by the Iranian regime.




According to the report, Diyako Bayezîdî and Mustafa Coşkar, both from Mahabad, were detained by the Iranian regime’s intelligence forces in the city and taken to an undisclosed location. The report also stated that 17-year-old Îlya Lutfî Tormakçî, who lives in the city of Baneh, was abducted by masked forces affiliated with the Iranian regime.




The report further noted that 19-year-old Ehed Meyhenxahî, from the Shino district of Urmia, was arrested on 19 October and transferred to Naghadeh Prison following a five-year prison sentence imposed on him.




Ehed Meyhenxahî had previously been detained by Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence (Ettelaat) on 24 January 2026, without a prosecutorial order, and was released on bail approximately one month later. He was subsequently sentenced to prison by the Shino Revolutionary Court on charges of “assisting anti-Iran opposition.”




The Hana Human Rights Organization’s report also stated that on 16 October, intelligence forces of the Iranian regime raided the home of Aram Eminî in Saqqez and abducted him without a written warrant or a prosecutorial order. The report said that, despite five days having passed, no information was yet available regarding Aram Eminî’s whereabouts.

title: Diyarbakır Bar Association: 568 rights violations against children recorded in six months
content:
The Diyarbakır Bar Association’s Children’s Rights Center compiled reports of children’s rights violations that came to public attention during the first six months of the year. According to the report, a total of 344 children lost their lives during this six-month period. Of these children, 326 died from preventable causes, while 18 died under suspicious circumstances.




A total of 224 children were involved in cases involving sexual offenses, violence, and grievous bodily harm, while the total number of children affected by violations of the right to life and other forms of victimization was recorded at 568.




Recommendations




The report outlined the following structural and legal recommendations:




- School Security, Public Safety in Surrounding Areas, and Disarmament: Physical inspections and X-ray barriers should be installed to prevent weapons such as smooth bore hunting rifles and knives from being brought into educational institutions. Criminal penalties for civilian gun ownership should be increased.




- MESEM Programs Should Be Suspended: MESEM programs, which place children in heavy and hazardous occupations, should be suspended. Industrial facilities and construction sites should be inspected by independent, multi-stakeholder monitoring boards.

title: Iran builds wall along border between South Kurdistan and Rojhilat
content:
According to RojNews, Iranian forces have built a 10-kilometer-long concrete wall stretching from the Seyranben Border Crossing on the border between Bashur (South Kurdistan) and Rojhilat (East Kurdistan) to an area behind the villages of Teymiz and Şêweguwêzan. Observation towers have also been constructed along the wall.




It was further reported that trenches measuring 3 meters wide and 4 meters deep have been dug along the borderline extending from the wall to the village of Mîşyawe, and that strict security measures have been imposed along the border.







 







Iran had previously sought to sever connections between Bashur and Rojhilat by laying barbed wire and landmines along the border. These efforts are now reportedly continuing through the construction of walls and trenches along the border between the two regions.




The construction of the wall and trenches is particularly noteworthy because it is taking place at a time when Iraqi Border Guard forces have been deployed along the borders and forces at border checkpoints belonging to both countries are engaged in dialogue.




Despite Iraqi and Iranian officials repeatedly emphasizing security coordination between Iran, Iraq, and the Kurdistan Region, the Iranian and Iraqi governments have chosen to remain silent about the reasons behind the construction of the wall and the digging of the trenches.

title: Second issue of Academy of Social Science Journal published
content:
The Academy of Social Science is an intellectual and political initiative devoted to the development of an integrative social science—“the sociology of freedom.” Inspired by the ideas of Abdullah Öcalan, the Academy explores human possibility, collective freedom, communality, and, in general, building of democratic modernity beyond domination and exploitation.




The journal of the Academy of Social Science, 

Democratic Modernity

, is a project to rethink social science as a means of human emancipation rather than simply an academic field of study. Its motto, 

Towards a Sociology of Freedom

, is strongly influenced by all struggles for freedom and equality, including Abdullah Öcalan’s paradigm of Democratic Civilization, the concept of democratic modernity, the revolutionary experience of Rojava, and the Kurdish women’s freedom movement. 




The journal critiques capitalism, hierarchical institutions, and conventional disciplinary boundaries, advocating instead for forms of social organization grounded in communal life, dignity, ecological awareness, and democratic participation.




The journal combines essays on political theory, sociology, art, food systems, jineolojî, knowledge, and community organizing. The journal will also be the address where the fruit of research communes such as

content:

title: Two women killed in Sulaymaniyah and Mardin
content:
Two women have died in Sulaymaniyah in South Kurdistan and in Mardin in North Kurdistan. Kîjan Bûrhan was shot by her father and succumbed to her severe injuries, while Remziye Damar was found dead in her home under unexplained circumstances.




Kîjan Bûrhan was shot by her father in Sulaymaniyah on Monday evening. The 30-year-old woman was struck by three bullets. She was taken for medical treatment in critical condition but died from her injuries on Tuesday afternoon.




Meanwhile, Remziye Damar was found lifeless in her home in the village of Boxazîyê in Kızıltepe district. Emergency services arrived following a call for assistance and confirmed her death. Her body was taken to the forensic medicine department of Kızıltepe State Hospital for an autopsy. Following the completion of the examinations, Damar was laid to rest in her home village of Boxazîyê.

title: South African women condemn death sentence against Varisheh Moradi, call for an end to executions
content:
Abahlali baseMjondolo (AbM), one of the largest grassroots movements to emerge in South Africa following the end of apartheid, issued a message of solidarity with Kurdish political prisoner Varisheh Moradi. Women members of the movement condemned the Iranian regime’s renewed death sentence against Moradi, issued on October 14, 2026, and called for the execution to be halted.




In a visual message featuring numerous AbM members, the movement called on the Iranian regime to end its policies of repression and executions targeting Kurds. The message demanded the immediate release of Varisheh Moradi and all other political prisoners, while expressing solidarity with the women’s freedom struggle in Kurdistan through the slogan “Jin Jiyan Azadî” (Woman, Life, Freedom).

content:

Gayatri Spivak stated that she was impressed by Öcalan’s resilience despite the conditions of his decades-long imprisonment and emphasized the importance of his call for gender equality. The letter reads as follows:

I have long been impressed by the resilience you have shown throughout your prolonged imprisonment, much of it spent in isolation. I have also been particularly moved by your call for gender equality. Now there is the Framework Law, which further strengthens the possibility of your release.




Your real challenges, however, are only now beginning. Because you have proposed the more complex and more productive path of democratic existence rather than a form of proto-nationalist self-preservation. title: Oil exploration expands across Kurdish regions
content:

Intensive drilling operations in Gabar, Cudî, Kato and Besta continue to displace local communities, devastate natural habitats, and deplete and pollute water resources. A similar situation is emerging in Batman (Êlih) and Diyarbakır (Amed), where shale oil drilling is expected to begin within the next one or two months. The Ecology Commission of the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD) Headquarters and the ÖHD Şırnak (Şirnex) Branch conducted a field investigation into the ongoing ecological destruction on Mount Gabar. The delegation announced that its findings would be compiled into a report and shared with the public. According to a report published by Mezopotamya Agency (MA), the ÖHD delegation examined tree felling and activities carried out under the pretext of oil exploration, drawing attention to pollution and environmental destruction.




The Tigris River is being poisoned




Hülya Yıldırım, a member of the ÖHD Headquarters Ecology Commission, spoke to

title: YRK: Our forces responded to attacks by Iranian Revolutionary Guards
content:
The Command of the East Kurdistan Defense Units (YRK) issued a written statement regarding the continued attacks carried out by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).




The YRK statement on Wednesday said:

We had previously issued the necessary warnings, making it clear that if the attacks continued, we would exercise our right to legitimate self-defense and respond accordingly. Despite all our warnings, the enemy continued its attacks.




On October 20, the enemy launched a mortar attack on the area surrounding the village of Degaga in the Kosalan region. The attack was carried out from military bases and outposts in the vicinity of Degaga, which had also served as the launch sites for previous attacks in the region. Our forces immediately responded to the attacks within the framework of legitimate self-defense. Our forces suffered no casualties or damage as a result of the attacks.”

title: Mechthild Exo: Jineolojî must become a lived foundation
content:
Twelve years after the first Jineolojî conference in Europe, Kurdish women’s science has established itself in numerous countries. However, its integration into society continues to face significant challenges. Peace and conflict researcher Dr. Mechthild Exo highlighted these issues on the sidelines of the latest Jineolojî conference. In an interview with ANF, she traces the development of academic and feminist work since 2014 and explains why research, political organizing, and social practice must become more closely interconnected in the future.




When the first European Jineolojî conference took place in Cologne in 2014, those involved were still at the very beginning of their work, Exo noted. There were no established structures, extensive educational programs, or sufficient translations of foundational literature. Jineolojî, which defines itself as the science of women and life and emerged from the Kurdish women’s freedom movement, first had to be introduced, explained, and made accessible, Exo stated.




“We didn’t really know what Jineolojî was. We only knew that a new science was being developed,” Exo said. "The first conference was largely characterized by a collective search for understanding. title: ÖHD: Peace cannot be built as human rights violations in prisons continue
content:
The Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD) drew attention to the continued extension of prison sentences and human rights violations despite the Peace and Democratic Society Process, and called for the release of political prisoners.




In a statement, the ÖHD said that the sentences of 90 prisoners had been extended over the past three months. The statement read: “While the Peace and Democratic Society Process is being discussed, penal policies incompatible with the spirit of peace continue in prisons. Over the past three months, the sentences of 90 prisoners have been extended. The eighth postponement of the release of Sermin Demirdağ, who has been imprisoned for 34 years, and the continued denial of freedom to sick prisoners such as Mehmet Sait Yıldırım demonstrate the systematic nature of this policy.”




The statement added: “Prisoners are being deprived of their freedom through arbitrary postponements of release, disciplinary punishments and human rights violations. Peace cannot be built in prisons where freedom is denied through arbitrary decisions. We make an unequivocal appeal to the Minister of Justice: Put an immediate end to the postponement of releases and arbitrary practices. title: Sermin Demirdağ’s release delayed for the eighth time
content:
The release of Sermin Demirdağ, who is being held at Kayseri Women’s Closed Prison, has been postponed for six months for the eighth time by the Prison Administration and Observation Board.




Sermin Demirdağ, who has been imprisoned since 13 April 1993, had previously had her release postponed seven times through board decisions at Sincan Women’s Closed Prison, where she was formerly held.




With this latest decision, the total time added to Sermin Demirdağ’s imprisonment has reached four years and three months, as her release has been blocked since 7 March 2023.

content:

Cumali Ararat said that October holds particular significance in the history of women's military organisation and the tradition of resistance.

content:

The article Uçum wrote is precisely the kind of article that opponents of the process, those seeking to sabotage it, would write. If that is the case, the government is attempting to lay the ideological groundwork for undermining the process. Tayyip Erdoğan has repeatedly said that the process is progressing well. title: Zübeyir Aydar: Kurds have the right to speak at the UN
content:
The Kurds' struggle for international recognition and representation is entering a new phase. Zübeyir Aydar, a member of the Executive Council of the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK), said that despite their population of approximately 60 million, Kurds are not represented internationally through their own political will. Aydar said, “We also want to be represented. Our demand is equality.”




Aydar spoke to ANF and emphasised that the initiative to secure representation at the United Nations (UN) is not merely a diplomatic demand but an important part of the Kurds' struggle for recognition as an equal people.




We spoke to Zübeyir Aydar, a member of the Executive Council of the KNK, about the demands raised and decisions taken at the conference organised by the KNK in Brussels on 3 October, as well as the importance of Kurdish national unity.




What challenges do Kurds face today in terms of international recognition and representation?




As a people and a nation, we are not officially recognised. Our struggle is for the Kurds to be recognised by everyone, just like other nations around the world. title: Commemoration in Kobanê for 68 martyrs
content:
A tent has been erected at Martyr Dicle Cemetery in Kobanê to commemorate 68 YJA Star/HPG guerrillas who fell as martyrs in different years while serving in the ranks of the Kurdistan Freedom Movement.




On Tuesday, a convoy of people from the cities and towns of Til Temir, Hesekê, Zirgan, Dirbêsiyê, Qamişlo, Dêrik, Girkê Legê, Til Koçer, Amûdê, Tirbespiyê and Çilaxa gathered at the Kandil Junction in Til Temir before setting off for Kobanê to attend the ceremony.




In observance of the commemoration, all shops and markets in the city of Kobanê were closed.




According to information provided by the Council of Martyrs’ Families, speeches will be delivered at the ceremony on behalf of the Council of Martyrs’ Families, the Kongra Star Coordination, political parties, the Democratic Islam Congress and numerous other organizations.




In addition, a video message from Murat Karayılan, central commander of the People's Defense Headquarter, will be shown. A video presentation documenting the lives, struggle and sacrifices of the fallen fighters will also be screened.

content:

The submission recalled the Committee of Ministers’ interim resolution of September 17, 2025, concerning the Gurban group of cases, which includes the “Öcalan No. 2” judgment.




It noted that the Committee had requested information from Turkey by the end of June 2026 on progress made in implementing the judgments, but that Turkey had failed to submit the required information or an action plan within that period.




The law office stated that Turkey had not established any legal mechanism allowing aggravated life sentences to be reviewed after a specified period.




Öcalan excluded from the scope of the legislation




The submission also addressed the bill on 

Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Cohesion

. Prepared as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the bill was submitted to the Parliamentary Speaker’s Office on 5 August and subsequently passed by Parliament’s Justice Commission. It was also debated in the General Assembly and adopted with 468 votes.

‘Knowledge is hidden in every aspect of life’




Meral Çiçek highlighted the methodological diversity of Jineology's educational activities in Europe, conducted through camps, seminars, workshops and conferences. She said these activities have encouraged women to develop new ways of questioning and examining the world around them.




Çiçek explained that education is not regarded merely as the transmission of knowledge, emphasising that Jineology encourages women to question existing knowledge while also transforming their understanding of where knowledge comes from.

title: Whereabouts of five people detained by Iranian forces unknown
content:
A report published by Kolbernews provided information about the disappearance of five mountaineers from Rojhilat (East Kurdistan) following their detention by Iranian state forces.




More than 30 armed Iranian intelligence agents reportedly raided the homes of seven members of the Helo and Sewz Mountain groups, independent mountaineering groups based in Saqqez. The mountaineers were detained following the home raids.




The report stated that the mountaineers Abdullah Amini and Rahim Haqparast were subsequently released. However, Mihemed Hekîmpûr, Mistefa Qadirî, Mihemedsalih Husênî, Husên Ebdulahî, and Xalid Rehemî remain in detention, and their whereabouts and fate are unknown.




It was reported that all the mountaineers had been subjected to torture while in detention. The report also stated that those whose fate remains unknown have been denied the right to meet with their families and lawyers.

author: Unknown
title: Rape case in Siverek highlighted at "Women, Justice and Memory" vigil
content:
Organised by the Amed Network Against Violence, the vigil continued for its third week outside Diyarbakır Courthouse. Participants carried photographs of women and chanted slogans including “Femicide is political,” “Protect, exonerate, prosecute” and “Jin, jiyan, azadî” (Woman, life, freedom).




Berfin Elçi, a member of the executive board of the Amed branch of the Human Rights Association (IHD), stated that femicides are not isolated incidents, but are the result of a male-dominated system, impunity and the mentality that seeks to control women’s lives.




Emphasising that women should not have to seek justice only after they have been killed, Berfin Elçi called for reports of violence to be taken seriously, suspicious deaths of women to be effectively investigated, and protection obligations to be fulfilled.




Drawing attention to the release of three defendants in the rape case in Siverek (Sêwereg), as well as the acquittal of the perpetrator tried on abuse charges despite Fatmanur Çelik’s pursuit of justice, Berfin Elçi stated that practices of impunity threaten women’s right to life.




Stories of murdered women were read aloud




During the vigil, the stories of Canan Yıldırım, Naz Aslan, Ebru Serep and Pınar Güneş, who died in different cities in October, were shared. It was reported that Canan Yıldırım was killed by the man she lived with in Antalya, while Naz As

title: Italian politicians call for Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom
content:
Politicians in Italy have stressed that the peace process between the Turkish government and the Kurdish people must advance through concrete steps, calling for Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom.




Speaking at a press conference on the peace process in Turkey, held on 20 October at Montecitorio in Rome, Movimento 5 Stelle MP Stefania Ascari said that the Kurdish people’s rights to preserve their language and culture, elect their representatives and determine their own future must be recognised.




Emphasising that these rights are universal for both Kurds and Palestinians, Ascari said that the peace process must not remain limited to statements alone.







 







Ascari: We support the process




Ascari said: “We support the peace process in Turkey and call for Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom. We want this both to ensure respect for his rights and to enable him to contribute to dialogue.”




Stating that the way must be opened for actors capable of conducting negotiations if a political solution is to be achieved, Ascari also called on the Italian government to act. She asked the government to explain what initiatives it would undertake to support the peace process and what demands it would raise regarding Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom and the rights of the Kurdish people in Turkey.

title: Bakırhan: There is no longer any justification for waiting, concrete steps must be taken
content:
Speaking at his party’s parliamentary group meeting, DEM Party Co-Chair Tuncer Bakırhan reflected on the meetings he held at the MERI Forum, organised in the Federated Kurdistan Region.




Bakırhan said they had met with Neçirvan Barzani, Bafil Talabani, Kubat Talabani, Mazlum Ebdî and İlham Ehmed at the forum, adding that Kurdish political actors attached importance to developing dialogue and to the ongoing process in Turkey.




A photograph is not enough




Bakırhan said: “Coming together and appearing side by side in a photograph is important. These meetings and photographs help close the distance that has emerged over the years, but a photograph is not enough; this rapprochement must also have political, social and diplomatic dimensions.”




The process is the hope of the entire region




Bakırhan drew attention to the ongoing political and social crises alongside wars in the Middle East, and said developments in the region were not confined to the countries directly involved, but also had economic and political consequences for other countries.




Bakırhan added that everyone in the region was seeking security, yet insufficient steps were being taken to establish genuine peace. He explained that the MERİ Forum had addressed the future of the Middle East, the position of the Kurds in the region, developments in Syria and the implications of the Peace and Democratic So

author: Unknown
title: The universal flow of our ancient culture
content:
We have spent the past several days attending the Jineolojî Conference alongside more than a hundred women comrades. It was exciting to see women from different regions and cultures come together through Jineolojî. Sharing Jineological experiences developed across every sphere of life was also enlightening, instructive and eye-opening.




I asked myself what this synergistic energy was that brought together women from different parts of the world. It was also heartening to see that many of them knew Kurdish and spoke it fluently. More than simply speaking the language, they regarded Kurdish as the language of free life, a language of relationships, consciousness and emotion. Perhaps this is the universal flow of our ancient culture: the archaic essence, the roots, flowing through different bodies, revealing the goodness and beauty of existence.




We live in an age in which meaning and feeling are increasingly eroding, or rather, being deliberately stripped of their value. Instead of the heartbeat, greenery, water and breath of life, we are trapped in an endless obsession with scrolling, wasting time with every swipe. This is turning individuals and society into robots day by day, destroying our ability to read, concentrate and create meaning, values and emotions. The virtual mindset of dominant masculinity encourages us not to write or think, making us participate in our own

title: KNK Women’s Commission: The Iranian regime will not be able to stop Kurdish women
content:
The Women’s Commission of the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) issued a written statement concerning the Iranian regime’s escalating repression of Kurds and its policy of executions.




Drawing attention to the growing threats and attacks against Kurds and opposition figures, as well as the ongoing repression of Kurdish women, the Commission stated that the death sentence imposed on Varisheh Moradi for a second time and the treatment of Zeynab Jalalian, who has been imprisoned for 18 years, demonstrate the regime’s fear of Kurdish women’s capacity to organise and mobilise.




Stating that the Iranian regime fears popular uprisings, the KNK Women’s Commission emphasised that the experience created by the “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” (Woman, Life, Freedom) movement has not yet been forgotten. The statement recalled that the death sentence imposed on Varisheh Moradi in November 2024 was overturned by a court in 2025, but that it was announced on 14 October 2026 that the death sentence had been reinstated.




The regime is targeting Kurdish women en particular




Stating that the Iranian regime’s actions demonstrate its hostility towards women, particularly Kurdish women, the KNK Women’s Commission noted that threats and repression would not force Kurdish women to abandon their struggle. title: Kobanê Museum becomes shelter for displaced residents
content:
Following the historic resistance in Kobanê, 70 percent of the city was completely destroyed. Part of Kobanê was left as it was, preserved as a museum for future generations: houses reduced to rubble and rooms without doors or windows.




Today, those ruins have become a shelter for many families. Displaced residents have been forced to move to Kobanê and settle there. Many of them come from Girê Spî, Raqqa and other areas from which people have been displaced. For years, these residents have been living among the ruins, holding on to the hope that one day they will return to their homes.







 







They have no choice but to live among the rubble in order to survive. Displaced residents living in the Kobanê Museum spoke to ANF about their hopes and desire to return.




A woman named Emîne Casim Qadir explained that they had been forced to leave Girê Spî eight years ago. She recounted their experience in the following words:




“When we left Girê Spî, we had to move to schools in the Xerabhişkê area. Later, we were told that there was a camp in the Til El Semin area, near Eyn Îsa, for people coming from Girê Spî, so we stayed in those tents. In summer, we lived in the scorching heat inside the tents; in winter, we endured the cold and rain.




“More recently, my husband, my children and I had to set out on the road once again, and we came to Kobanê. At first, we stayed

author: Unknown
title: YPJ remains an autonomous force in integration talks
content:
The Command of the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) issued a statement on recent developments and the new process, declaring that “in discussions and assessments regarding the integration process, the YPJ has secured its place as an autonomous and distinct force.”




The YPJ’s statement reads as follows:




“Having a significant history and a strong stance in the fight against terrorism and the protection of humanitarian values, the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) are informing the public, particularly our people, about recent developments and the new process. As part of efforts to establish regional stability and build a secure future, discussions and assessments regarding the integration process are ongoing. In this process, the YPJ is maintaining its place as an autonomous and distinct force.




The YPJ is not merely a military force; it is also a symbol of women’s will and labor. Therefore, comprehensive discussions are continuing regarding the details of participation and the YPJ’s role in the new structure, with the fundamental aim of preserving women’s identity, experience, and achievements. As the YPJ, we emphasize that our guiding principle at every step is to protect the achievements of our people and the legitimate rights of women. The outcomes of these discussions will be publicly announced in the coming period.”

title: Genç: The government tries to avoid the issue of Mr. Öcalan
content:
Two years after the launch of the Peace and Democratic Society Process and two months after the Framework Law was passed by parliament, the government's failure to take the necessary steps has caused discontent within the Kurdish Freedom Movement. In successive statements, the Co-Presidency of the Executive Council of the Kurdistan Communities Union (KCK) and the Movement's leadership once again emphasised that recognition of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan's political status as the chief negotiator in the process, and the establishment of conditions in which he can live and work freely, are their red lines. However, shortly after these statements, Mehmet Uçum, Chief Adviser to the President and Deputy Chair of the Presidential Legal Policies Board, told the press: “His status as a convicted prisoner will not change, nor will the serving of his sentence be suspended. Let us say Öcalan is appointed as a coordinator in the Subcommittee on Disarmament and Political Participation. Such an appointment would be nothing more than a working arrangement enabling him to fulfil his role in eliminating terrorism, in line with the perspective of integration with the state and society.” His remarks once again exposed the contradiction in the government's approach to the issue.

title: Iranian regime bombs Mêrîwan region
content:
The YRK (Rojhilatê Kurdistan Defense Units, Yekîneyên Parastina Rojhilatê Kurdistanê) Press Center issued a statement regarding attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).




The statement read: “On 18 October 2026, an attack was carried out in the Mêrîwan region using suicide drones and mortars. The attack was conducted by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Iranian regime. The area was first bombed with two suicide drones, followed by more than 30 mortar shells and heavy weapons. The attack damaged our people’s agricultural land and orchards, but our forces suffered no harm.”

title: Bakırhan: The framework law must now be implemented!
content:
Co-Chairs of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), Tülay Hatimoğulları and Tuncer Bakırhan, visited New Party Chair Özgür Özel. The delegation held a joint press statement at New Party headquarters following the meeting.




The visit reportedly focused on the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the 2027 budget and other current political developments.




Bakırhan said they had been visiting labour and professional organisations and trade unions for approximately a week. He said, “Today, we also began our visits to political parties, starting with New Party. New Party was the first to host us on this tour.”







Bakırhan added, “I recently attended a conference in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. Representatives of virtually all the different forces in the Middle East were there. I shared their views on the process underway in Turkey with the party chair and his delegation.”




The framework law must now be implemented




Bakırhan continued: “The framework law has been passed. It was one of the important stages of the process. This law has brought us into a new period. Society's expectations in this new period are now clear. Throughout the visits we have made and the meetings we have held with the people, everyone has expressed the same expectation: the framework law must now begin to be implemented. Society is waiting for the necessary legal arrangements.

title: Nihat Bertan released after 31 years in jail
content:
Nihat Bertan, who had been held for 31 years at Tekirdağ No. 1 Prison, was released. He was welcomed outside the prison by his family, members of the Association for Assistance and Solidarity with Families of Prisoners and Convicts in Marmara (MATUHAYDER), and representatives of political parties and civil society organizations. Those gathered chanted, “Bijî berxwêdana zindanan” (“Long live resistance in prisons”).




Speaking at the welcome, Cahit Direk, MATUHAYDER’s Tekirdağ provincial co-chair, referred to the Peace and Democratic Society Process and stated that all prisoners who had been held in prisons for more than 30 years must be freed.




Nihat Bertan said that he had left 12 doors behind him as he walked out of prison and conveyed greetings from his fellow prisoners. Noting that the prisoners’ greatest wish was to reunite with their people and continue the struggle, Bertan said: “Our happiness is incomplete, because half of our hearts are still in prison.”




Reminding those gathered that Leader Apo remains imprisoned on İmralı Island, Bertan stated that true happiness could not be spoken of until all prisoners, foremost among them Leader Apo, had regained their freedom.




Bertan said that public support was needed to ensure that the ongoing process was embraced by society, adding that the morale prisoners had today stemmed from the people’s struggle.

content:

Recalling that the names of 749 martyrs from North Kurdistan had previously been made public, Karayılan explained that identities had been announced late in previous years because of security conditions and delays in receiving information. He said: “I believe our esteemed families and our people will understand this, because the conditions at that time were truly difficult. Much of the information arrived late.”




Emphasizing that the struggle waged by Abdullah Öcalan and the martyrs had fostered a spirit of Kurdish national unity in all four parts of Kurdistan, Karayılan said that participation in the Apoist movement from every region had played a major role in developing national consciousness. He noted that no one could now deny that the Kurds are a nation and stated that the Kurdish people would liberate themselves under any circumstances.

content:
Kongra Star Coordination issued a statement concerning the death sentence handed down for a second time to Kurdish women's activist Varisheh Moradi by the Iranian judiciary.




The statement said that the decision to sentence Varisheh Moradi to death for a second time demonstrated Iran's determination to continue its policies of repression, intimidation and silencing of women. It stressed that a woman who had devoted her entire life to the Kurdish people's and women's struggle for freedom must not be left alone in the face of Iran's threats.




Kongra Star said that Moradi had resisted physical and psychological violence and the harsh conditions of the prison where she had been held for years.




The statement said, “Despite all this severe repression and these harsh conditions, Varisheh Moradi continues to resist, refusing to surrender her will for freedom. They want to silence Varisheh through the death sentence. However, no policy targeting a woman's life and struggle will succeed.”




The statement stressed that Iran's punishment of the Kurdish people, women and opposition groups within society went beyond security measures and penal policies.
