title: Call for investigation into boards blocking women prisoners’ release
content:
A protest was held outside the Ministry of Justice in Ankara over the repeated blocking of the release of women prisoners held in Sincan Women’s Closed Prison. Protesters called for an investigation into the Administrative and Observation Boards responsible for postponing release decisions.




The protest, organized by the Federation of Legal Solidarity Associations for Prisoners’ and Convicts’ Families (TUHAD-FED), was attended by representatives of political parties and legal organizations, as well as many others.




At least nine women prisoners at Sincan Women’s Closed Prison are currently being prevented from being released, including women who have been imprisoned for more than 30 years.




Nedime Yaklav, who has been in prison for 34 years, has had her release postponed seven times. Hicran Binici, imprisoned for 33 years, and sisters Nuriye and Devrim Adet, who have been in prison for 32 years, have each had their releases postponed five times. Zeliha Ustabaş’s release has been blocked four times, while Fatma Aslan and Melike Göksu have each had their releases postponed three times. Emine Abiş, who has been imprisoned since 2021, has also had her release postponed three times.

title: Soma’s deadly ‘fate’: 355 miners killed in 13 years
content:
Another mining accident occurred last Thursday in Soma, Manisa, a district known for the Soma Kömür Işletmeleri A.Ş. disaster in which 301 mine workers lost their lives 12 years ago. Workers had warned the company management about shortcomings in occupational health and safety, yet the accident occurred despite those warnings. This is why such preventable accidents are described as work-related killings. Companies seek to keep their profit margins as high as possible by failing to carry out regular maintenance or fully implement occupational health and safety measures, while facing no meaningful sanctions for these failures. Under such conditions, workers’ health and lives effectively become another cost to be cut.




In a feature article,

Manisa ranked first in mining-related worker deaths, followed by Zonguldak. The largest number of deaths occurred in lignite and hard-coal mines, followed by marble, chromium and copper mines. title: Özgür: Fund scandal is biggest fraud in Republic’s history
content:
Questions continue to surround the trillion-lira fund scandal that has shaken Turkey and left hundreds of thousands of citizens facing losses. The fact that the scandal has extended to the Justice and Development Party (AKP) ministers such as Fatma Betül Kaya, members of parliament and their family members has brought relations between the government and capital, as well as networks of economic power, under scrutiny.




The fraud unfolded in plain sight despite warnings from some economists and even direct applications to the Financial Crimes Investigation Board (MASAK) and the Capital Markets Board (SPK), including those made by former MASAK Deputy Chair Dr Ramazan Başak. The delayed investigation and failure to activate regulatory mechanisms have shifted attention beyond the companies involved to the system established by the AKP government, a government that has institutionalised fascism, suppressed the opposition through the judiciary, impoverished the public through its economic programmes, created a capitalist class from its supporters and reshaped oversight mechanisms around its own allies and policies.

content:
On the 28th anniversary of the international conspiracy carried out against Abdullah Öcalan on 9 October 1998, the Istanbul Platform of Democratic Institutions will hold an action at Saraçhane Square, located in the Fatih district.




The action will be held under the slogan “Freedom for Mr. Öcalan for Peace and a Democratic Society” on Friday 9th, at 6:00 p.m.

title: Two separate armed attacks in Aleppo: 2 people killed
content:
Two people were killed in two separate armed attacks that took place in different parts of Aleppo.




On Kelas Street in Aleppo’s Sulaymaniyah (Silêmanî) neighborhood, a person on a motorcycle opened fire on a shop owner. The seriously wounded business owner died at the hospital where he was taken. The identity of the attacker and the motive for the attack have not yet been determined.




In Aleppo’s Nêreb neighborhood, a young man was killed when unidentified armed individuals opened fire on the vehicle he was traveling in.




According to data from the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR), 408 murder cases have been recorded across Syria since the beginning of 2026. A total of 448 people have lost their lives in these incidents.

title: Fundamental ideological consciousness
content:
The most fundamental characteristic of today’s world system is that it is hostile to nature and women. These represent the greatest deviation from nature and from social life. Women object to this; they rebel and struggle. But what about nature? Who will stand up for nature? Undoubtedly, nature also has a form of objection and rebellion. This rebellion can reach such a point that the links in nature’s evolutionary chain are broken. When several of the evolutionary links that created humanity are broken, human life itself may disappear; indeed, many species may become extinct. Scientists are already discussing the consequences that the destruction of nature will bring to the world. It is said that the consequences will be extremely grave. If those who say these things are dismissed as pessimistic prophets of doom, what they predict may actually come to pass.




Seeing the harm that human beings have inflicted on nature, one could argue that the greatest deviation nature has experienced is the emergence of this human being. The fact that a part of nature evolved into this state and became nature’s greatest enemy naturally leads one to such an assessment. In the holy scriptures, God’s wrath is presented as a response to the deterioration of social life. The wrath brought about by the deterioration taking place in nature could completely destroy humanity.

title: Black Sea musicians call on artists to promote peace
content:
Black Sea musicians Ismail Hakkı Demircioğlu and Fuat Saka spoke to ANF about the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




Fuat Saka said there was nothing wrong with wanting peace or standing up for it: “It is called ‘peace’ for a reason. If peace is going to bring tranquillity to everyone, then that is how it should be. Peace is welcome, more than welcome. It is not something to fear, but something to embrace.”




Saka stressed that everyone living in these lands was part of the same fraternity, saying that great suffering had been endured in the past but that it was now time to put an end to it. He called for stronger steps towards building a democratic society and urged political actors to take responsibility.




Saka said: “I believe those who seek to govern this country need to approach this issue with greater sensitivity, just as they should with every other issue. I hope the days when friendship and fraternity are strengthened in these lands, when we can stand shoulder to shoulder, are not far away. Politicians have a major role to play here. The responsibility lies first with them, and then with all of us.”




Saka said one of the most fundamental functions of art was to break down prejudices. He stressed that art could bring people together and that this power would emerge as long as the intention behind it was positive.




Saka said artists had a responsibility

title: DEM Party: Events of October 6–8 must be fully investigated
content:
The Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) commemorated those who lost their lives during the protests of October 6–8, 2014, on the twelfth anniversary of the events and called for a full investigation into what happened. The party also demanded the immediate release of the politicians convicted in the Kobanê case.




The protests erupted in October 2014 during the attack on Kobanê by the terrorist organization Islamic State (ISIS). People took to the streets in numerous cities across the country in solidarity with the resistance of Kobanê’s population against ISIS and to protest against the Turkish government’s support for the jihadist group. The demonstrations and the violent events that followed resulted in numerous deaths.




According to various human rights organizations, 54 people were killed during the protests and violent clashes involving demonstrators, police, the military and organizations affiliated with ISIS, including 47 HDP members. “We respectfully commemorate our citizens who lost their lives during the protests of October 6–8,” the DEM Party stated. Even twelve years later, demands for a comprehensive investigation into the events remain unanswered, it added.




Instead of investigating the circumstances surrounding the events, the truth was obscured and proceedings that the DEM Party describes as the “Kobanê conspiracy trial” were brought again

title: YRK announces the death of guerrilla fighter Çekdar Paytext
content:
The Eastern Kurdistan Defense Units (YRK) announced the death of their fighter Çekdar Paytext, who lost his life in an accident in the Pêncewîn region of Southern Kurdistan (Northern Iraq) on September 2, 2026. In a statement released by its Press and Communications Center, the YRK extended their condolences to the Akan family and the people of Kurdistan and commended his life and path within the movement.




Çekdar Paytext’s birth name was Barış Akan. He was born into a patriotic family in the province of Amed (Diyarbakır) in Northern Kurdistan and grew up in an environment closely connected to the Kurdish freedom movement. His older brother, Nizam Akan, who used the nom de guerre Çekdar, had lost his life in 1994. When Çekdar Paytext joined the guerrilla ranks in 2023, he adopted his brother’s name in his memory.




The YRK paid tribute to him as a committed fighter whose life, it said, was marked by a deep bond with his comrades, his homeland and the philosophy of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan. Quoting his own writings, the YRK cited a passage reflecting his understanding of guerrilla life: “What matters is the organization. All comrades are prepared to give their lives for one another.”

title: Iraqi Prime Minister: Agreement reached on the withdrawal of Turkish troops
content:
Iraqi media have reported details of a meeting between Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Zeydi and tribal leaders.




According to the reports, the Iraqi Prime Minister said that funds recovered through corruption investigations would be transferred to the “Development Fund.” He emphasized that the rule of law and Iraq’s independence in decision-making would be safeguarded.




Zeydi reportedly praised the tribes for supporting the government and drawing attention to the country’s most sensitive issues. He announced that five armed groups were prepared to hand over their weapons, describing the move as a practical step.




Addressing the presence of the Turkish military on Iraqi territory, the Iraqi Prime Minister reportedly said that talks had been held with Turkish officials on a number of issues and that an agreement had been reached on the withdrawal of Turkish forces from Iraqi territory.

title: Bakırhan calls for work to begin under Öcalan’s coordination
content:
DEM Party co-chair Tuncer Bakırhan has called for concrete steps in the peace and democratic society process as the new parliamentary year begins. The Council for Disarmament and Strategic Coordination must begin its work under the coordination of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan. At the same time, he said, necessary conditions must be created for Öcalan to work freely, hold talks and communicate.




Bakırhan made the remarks at the DEM Party’s first parliamentary group meeting of the new legislative year. He devoted a substantial part of his speech to the peace process and the political and legal steps he believes must now be taken. “One concrete action is better than a thousand words,” Bakırhan said. Mutual trust, he added, can only be established if the developments so far are now followed by practical steps.




‘Disarmament requires a legal counterpart’




Bakırhan described the peace process as a scale with two sides. Disarmament, he said, must be matched by legal safeguards. “If the laying down of arms has been placed on one side of the scale, the law must be placed on the other. Because disarmament is a matter that requires a legal counterpart,” the Kurdish politician said. title: 10-week ‘Women, Justice and Memory Vigil’ against femicides launched in Amed
content:
The Amed (tr: Diyarbakır) Network for Combating Violence announced launched a “Women, Justice and Memory Vigil” against femicides and suspicious deaths of women.




The vigil began outside the Diyarbakır Courthouse today and will continue at the same location every Tuesday for 10 weeks.




Participants carried a banner reading “Women Hold a Vigil for Justice and Memory,” along with photographs of women who had been killed. Representatives of numerous political parties and civil society organizations attended the vigil on its first week.




Reading out the press statement, lawyer Cansel Talay said they had come together because they refused to forget or remain silent in a country where women are killed by men and where their deaths are left unresolved by being labeled “suicide,” “accident” or “suspicious.”







‘Femicide is a war directed against the truth and existence of women’

title: CDK-F launches France-wide campaign against drugs and criminal networks
content:
The Democratic Kurdish Council in France (CDK-F) has announced a nationwide community campaign aimed at protecting young people from drugs, violence and criminal networks. The campaign will include prevention and awareness-raising initiatives, support for families and young people, and greater efforts to connect young people with sports, cultural, social and educational activities. “Drugs and the recruitment of young people into criminal structures are not individual problems,” the CDK-F stated. “They affect the future of young people as well as their families and social coexistence in local communities.”




The CDK-F underlined that the sale of drugs to young people, their exploitation for criminal activities and the portrayal of violence as an expression of strength must not be tolerated. “Structures that profit from drug trafficking, threats, violence and the exploitation of young people must not be accepted within society. Gang crime is neither freedom nor success,” it stated.




The campaign will not be limited to condemning drug trafficking and criminal networks. Its main focus will be on prevention, awareness-raising and creating alternatives for young people. Information events for young people and families are planned in various French cities. title: Senior ISIS member arrested following attack in Hawija
content:
Following an attack on an Iraqi Federal Police base in Hawija (Hawîce), near Kirkuk, a senior member of the jihadist group Islamic State (ISIS) has been arrested. Two police officers were killed and several others injured in Monday’s attack.




The arrest took place on Tuesday morning during an operation by Iraqi intelligence services in Hawija district. A source in the Iraqi army told Roj News that the arrest was the result of intensive investigations and intelligence work. The detainee was described as a known ISIS official in the region.




His identity and precise position within ISIS were not initially disclosed. Further details are expected to be released once the ongoing investigation has been completed.

title: Two young Kurdish women athletes arrested by Iranian forces in Saqqez
content:
Iranian forces have arrested two young Kurdish women athletes, Rojan Ebrahimi and Aida Ghaderi, in Saqqez, Kurdistan Province, in recent days.




The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has reported that Ghaderi, a swimming coach, was arrested on 4 October after forces from the Ministry of Intelligence raided her family home in Saqqez without presenting a warrant.




Ebrahimi, an MMA athlete from Saqqez, was arrested a day earlier, on 3 October, after Ministry of Intelligence forces raided her family home.




Both arrests were carried out without warrants.




Any charges against the two women, as well as their current whereabouts and status, remain unknown.

author: Unknown
title: Two Iraqi police officers killed in ISIS attack
content:
ISIS militants attacked a position belonging to the Iraqi Federal Police forces in the Hawija district of Kirkuk.




Clashes reportedly broke out between ISIS militants and Iraqi federal police officers during the attack. Two police officers were killed, and several others were wounded in the clashes.




It was also reported that thermal cameras belonging to the police were destroyed by the militants. Following the attack, the Federal Police launched an investigation to locate the ISIS militants who attacked their position.

author: Unknown
title: Protest outside Sincan Prison over delayed releases of women
content:
A statement was made outside Sincan Women’s Closed Prison under the leadership of the Federation of Legal Solidarity Associations for Prisoners’ Families (TUHAD-FED) over the blocking of women prisoners’ releases.




The protest was attended by members of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), lawyers from the Lawyers for Freedom Association (ÖHD) and many others. Participants unfurled a banner reading: “We are holding a vigil against the blocking of political prisoners’ releases.”




TUHAD-FED Ankara Representative Sihan Kaya said the releases of many women prisoners had been postponed on various grounds since the establishment of the Prison Administration and Observation Boards in 2021.




Kaya said the releases of at least eight women prisoners at Sincan Women’s Closed Prison had been blocked. She said Nedime Yaklav’s release had been postponed seven times; those of Hicran Binici, Nuriye Adet and Devrim Adet five times; Zeliha Ustabaş four times; Melike Göksü, Emine Abiş and Fatma Aslan three times; and Pınar Tikit twice.




‘A second mechanism of punishment’




Kaya said the women included prisoners who were ill and others who had been imprisoned for 30 years, and condemned the postponement of their releases on subjective grounds such as “good conduct”, “remorse” and “compliance with rules”.




Kaya said the Prison Administration and Observation Boards

author: Unknown
title: Kurdish women’s movement delegation visits COPINH in Honduras
content:
A delegation representing the Kurdistan women’s liberation movement visited COPINH in Honduras, in Mesoamerica. COPINH (Civic Council of Popular and Indigenous Organizations of Honduras) is an organization dedicated to struggle and resistance, composed primarily of self-administered indigenous communities.




The Lenca people are one of the indigenous peoples of Central America, primarily distributed in southwestern Honduras, though their territories extend as far as San Salvador. To this day, many communities continue to resist in the mountains of that area, basing their survival on agriculture and livestock farming, carried out without industrial methods and in harmony with nature. On the slopes and among the trees, they grow corn and coffee, with corn being the staple food for these peoples. Following the Spanish occupation, they resisted fighting the colonization with a war led by the legendary Lempira. Despite this, they were subjected to forced conversion to Christianity; however, this failed to erase ancient traditions that still persist today, such as the “compostura” (a ritual of thanksgiving to Mother Earth for her bounty) or the spiritual connection to rivers, the earth, and fire. The spiritual dimension permeates every aspect of life, including political work: every assembly and every important gathering begins with the construction of an altar, on which—in additio

author: Unknown
title: Iran executes two more people over anti-government protests
content:
Iran’s judiciary announced that two people accused of involvement in the killing of four police officers during anti-government protests earlier this year had been executed.




According to Mizan, the judiciary’s official news outlet, Alireza Sepahi and Alireza Reisi were executed by hanging on Monday morning after the Supreme Court upheld their death sentences. Authorities did not disclose when the two men were arrested or when their trials took place.




Iran’s judiciary accused the two men of involvement in the killing of four police officers in the central city of Isfahan. The court also sentenced them to death on charges of membership of an armed group and threatening national security.




The protests began in Tehran in December over economic grievances and quickly spread to many parts of the country, developing into demonstrations directly opposing the government. The protests intensified particularly on 8 and 9 January, with serious clashes and loss of life reported across the country.




Iranian authorities claimed that more than 3,000 people were killed in the unrest, including hundreds of security personnel. The Tehran government has described the violence as “acts of terrorism” directed by the United States and Israel.




Human rights organisations outside Iran, however, have reported much higher death tolls and said security forces deliberately opened fire on

author: Unknown
title: Çelik: Peace requires a democratic state
content:
Debate over a new period aimed at resolving the Kurdish question continues in Turkey. The process, which followed statements by Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahçeli in October 2024 and began with the Call for Peace and Democratic Society issued by Kurdish People’s Leader Abdullah Öcalan on 27 February 2025, has remained on the public agenda for nearly two years.




Different sections of society have expressed a range of views on the process and the resolution of the Kurdish question, while expectations for peace have also continued to be debated over the past two years.




Reis Çelik, director of Let There Be Light (Işıklar Sönmesin), one of the first films to address the resolution of the Kurdish question in Turkey, spoke to ANF about the current state of cinema in Turkey and his views on the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




As a socialist, I am more inclined to tell the stories of what society experiences




Çelik said art was a field that gave voice to what remained unsaid and documented every aspect of life through different forms: “The primary function of art is to say what is left unsaid, to do what cannot otherwise be done, and to document every aspect of life through different means. Music does this, painting does this, sculpture does this, and literature does this. Cinema shows this courage more than any of them.




I am a storyteller. I

author: Unknown
title: Kobanê students react to the Ministry of Higher Education’s decision
content:
Kobanê students gathered in front of Kobanê University to protest the Syrian Ministry of Higher Education’s decision to close the faculties and academies and turn them into part of Aleppo University, demanding that their right to study at Kobanê University be upheld.




The students made several demands of the Kobanê University administration and called for their demands to be taken into consideration and followed up.




The students listed their demands as follows:




1. The preservation of all existing faculties, institutes, and departments




2. Guaranteeing Kobanê students’ right to receive their education in the city where they live




3. Preserving and continuing the experience of education in Kurdish




4. Guaranteeing students’ education and preventing them from suffering academic losses




5. Ensuring the full participation of students in decisions to be made concerning the future of the university




6. Preserving the name “Kobanê University”




7. Preserving the distinct character of Kobanê University throughout the process of organization and integration.




The statement concluded with the following: “As Kobanê students, we are not asking for special privileges. We simply want our rights to receive an education at the university and to equal opportunities to be protected, as well as the city’s access to university education and professional training oppor

author: Unknown
title: London Conference's conclusions: Peace must be guaranteed by rule of law and democratic institutions
content:
Following the Peace and Democratic Integration Conference, held in London on September 29–30, the Centre for Kurdish Affairs published its conclusions from the conference discussions, along with recommendations for the period ahead.




During the two-day conference, representatives of Kurdish political and civil society organizations, as well as figures involved in peace processes in different parts of the world, academics, politicians, and experts came together. They discussed a wide range of topics, from the democratic resolution of the Kurdish issue in Turkey to international experiences of peacebuilding; from legal guarantees and local democracy to the role of women, as well as developments in Syria and the wider region.




The Centre for Kurdish Affairs stressed that "this communiqué presents the Centre’s analysis of the conference discussions. The views, interpretations and conclusions contained herein should not be understood as a collective statement on behalf of every speaker, participant or supporting institution."




The text said: "The Centre for Kurdish Affairs convened a two-day international conference in London, bringing together peace practitioners, academics, political representatives, policymakers and civil society representatives to examine comparative experiences of conflict resolution, peacebuilding, constitutional accommodation, power-sharing and self-

author: Unknown
title: Director Ismail Güneş: Peace should be at the heart of cinema and art - Part Two
content:
Director Ismail Güneş spoke to ANF not only about his own cinema, but also about the current state of political cinema in Turkey and the role of art in the peace process.




Part one of this interview can be read 

here

. 




Ismail Güneş' latest movie, 

One of the Unplastered Houses, 

focuses on the story of a father and mother who, because they are poor, do not want their son to remain in conflict zones. He said: “I made this film not to repeat the artificial rhetoric of heroism produced by those in power or clichéd political slogans, but to tell the raw and naked reality of people waging their own quiet struggle for existence far from front lines and macro politics, in a stagnant town in Anatolia—in other words, the invisible philosophical tragedy of the ‘unplastered houses.’ Because while the themes of homeland and life are abstract concepts on ideological platforms, inside those homes in the grip of poverty they turn into a ruthless ontological contradiction between a child’s life and the family’s bread.




The mother figure before us is the purest manifestation on earth of universal compassion and the instinct to ‘keep alive’; while the desperate father figure, who wants his son to remain in the military and complete his service so that the money he earns there can sustain the family, is a disturbing mirror of how the capitalist system and deprivation subject human

author: Unknown
title: South Kurdistan after the Coalition: Kurdish national unity is crucial
content:
The mission of the International Coalition against ISIS in Iraq officially ended on 30 September after 12 years. The date marked not only the end of a military mission, but also the conclusion of the US military presence that had continued since the 2003 invasion and of the air defence system from which South Kurdistan (Bashur) had indirectly benefited. The withdrawal, announced by Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Zeydi, was welcomed as a victory in Baghdad and among Iran-aligned Shia groups, while it has been met with concern in Southern Kurdistan and among Sunni communities.




South Kurdistan, which has been targeted by more than a thousand drone and ballistic missile attacks since the US-Israel-Iran war began on 28 February, is entering a new period without air defences. Peshmerga forces have been unified on paper but remain affiliated with the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) on the ground. The Coalition’s financial support for the Peshmerga has also ended. Twenty-three months after the elections, a government has still not been formed in the Kurdistan Region.




The weakness of a common political will has now been compounded by the reality of a Kurdistan Region increasingly exposed to attacks.




23 years from invasion to withdrawal




US forces entered Iraq in 2003 to overthrow Saddam Hussein’s regime. US troop numbers peaked at 170,000

author: Unknown
title: Journalist Hemrînî: Baghdad seeks a model for solution in Shengal
content:
The withdrawal of US and International Coalition forces from Iraq, Baghdad’s efforts to bring armed groups under state control and strengthen the central army are reshaping the country’s security architecture. As Iraq seeks a new security balance, Shengal, which developed its own defense and governance mechanisms in the wake of DAESH attacks, has emerged as one of the key issues in this transformation.




The status of Shengal, the security of the Yazidis and the future of their self-defence forces are closely tied not only to Baghdad’s evolving security policies but also to the balance of power among regional actors. Journalist Hîwa Hemrînî said the demands of the Yazidis went beyond administrative or political arrangements: “The Yazidis are demanding a system that will protect their existence and enable them to develop it.”




Hemrînî stressed that Shengal’s future must be addressed on the basis of a solution that guarantees the continued existence of the Yazidis. He spoke to ANF about the talks between Shengal and Baghdad, the demands of the Yazidis, negotiations between Ankara and Baghdad over Bashiqa, and Iraq’s evolving security architecture.




Recent talks between Shengal and Baghdad, particularly the 11 September meeting between Prime Minister Ali Zeydi, the YBŞ and Yazidi representatives, appear to mark a new phase for Shengal’s future. What concrete issues were ag

author: Unknown
title: JINNEWS: 27 women and 6 children were murdered in September
content:
According to the September report compiled by JINNEWS, at least 27 women and 6 children were murdered, while 10 women and 6 children died under suspicious circumstances.




Twelve of the women were murdered by their spouses, 3 by men they were in the process of divorcing, 4 by men they had divorced, 1 by a man they had reportedly previously been in a relationship with, 1 by a family member, 1 by her son-in-law, 1 by the man her sister was married to, and 1 by her tenant. The relationship between 3 of the women and the perpetrators has not been clarified.




The cities where the women were murdered were: “3 in Manisa, 2 in Amed (Diyarbakır), 2 in Antalya, 2 in Sakarya, 1 in Adana, 1 in Ankara, 1 in Çorum, 1 in Denizli, 1 in Antep (Dîlok), 1 in Batman (Êlih), 1 in Hatay, 1 in Isparta, 1 in Istanbul, 1 in Kocaeli, 1 in Konya, 1 in Kütahya, 1 in Maraş, 1 in Mersin, 1 in Muğla, 1 in Osmaniye, 1 in Tekirdağ, and 1 woman in Elazığ (Xarpêt).”

author: Unknown
title: Activist allowed final meeting with his mother has been executed in Iran
content:
In a statement posted on social media, Sepahi’s lawyer, Şehrzad Şehbazi, announced that her client had been executed and said, “I will not forget him.”




Sepahi was allowed to meet with his mother, Somaya Afşar, who is also imprisoned, for the last time at Dastgerd Prison on Sunday, October 4 — in other words, shortly before his execution.




Arrests and executions in the country are increasing in connection with the protests that took place at the beginning of the year.




According to the NGOs Iran Human Rights and Together Against the Death Penalty, Iran executed at least 1,639 people in 2025. This figure was described as the highest number recorded since 1989.




According to Amnesty International, Iran is the country with the second-highest number of executions, after China.

author: Unknown
title: Hıdır Öztürk demands investigation into the murder of his daughter Ayten in 1992
content:
Thirty-four years after the abduction, torture and killing of Ayten Öztürk, her father, Hıdır Öztürk, is calling for the case, which was closed due to the statute of limitations, to be reopened. Particularly at a time when peace and a resolution of the Kurdish question are being discussed, the state must investigate and clarify the crimes of the past, Öztürk said.




His daughter’s case is among the grave human rights violations of the 1990s in Northern Kurdistan, when people were abducted, forcibly disappeared and extrajudicially executed by state and paramilitary structures. According to the Human Rights Association (İHD), at least 1,388 people disappeared while in state custody between 1980 and 2001.




Ayten Öztürk’s eyes were gouged out




Ayten Öztürk was 27 years old and worked at a state-owned flour factory in the district of Mazgirt in Dersim (Tunceli) province. On the evening of July 27, 1992, witnesses saw four men drag her into a white Land Rover and abduct her after she left work. Twelve days later, on August 8, her body was found near Kartaltepe in Elazığ. She had been hastily buried, with one hand protruding from the ground.




Öztürk had been so severely tortured and mutilated that her family was able to identify her only by her clothing. Among other injuries, her eyes had been gouged out. Nevertheless, no comprehensive autopsy was carried out, the signs of

author: Unknown
title: Protest in Ranya Against environmental destruction and Turkish military presence
content:
Numerous people in Ranya protested against the destruction of Kurdistan’s natural environment and the continued Turkish military presence in Southern Kurdistan. The rally, held in front of the city’s People’s Garden, was organized by the Koşan Group under the slogan “Êdî bes e dagirkerî û xirabkirina jîngeha Kurdistanê” — “Enough with the occupation and destruction of Kurdistan’s environment.”




Speaking on behalf of the group, Şadiye Samed said that for years the Turkish state had militarily occupied large areas of Behdînan under the pretext of waging war against the guerrillas of the Kurdish freedom movement. In addition to the deaths of numerous civilians, she said, the war had caused severe damage to the environment, nature and infrastructure of Southern Kurdistan.




















With the peace and democratic society process launched in February 2025, there was no longer any justification for continuing the war and military occupation in Southern Kurdistan, the Koşan Group stated. Nevertheless, it said, the destruction of the natural environment and the Turkish military presence have continued. “Protecting the borders and forests of Southern Kurdistan is not merely an environmental issue. It is also part of protecting our land, our culture and our identity,” the statement said.




Criticism was also directed at the government of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI). I

author: Unknown
title: Iran steps up military presence in Eastern Kurdistan
content:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has deployed heavy military equipment in the Şaho Mountains near Rewanser in Eastern Kurdistan and closed parts of the region to civilians. At the same time, artillery fire is targeting mountain ridges under the pretext of a military exercise.




According to the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN), citing a resident of a village at the foot of the Şaho Mountains, the Revolutionary Guards have deployed a convoy carrying heavy military equipment to the region in recent days.




Residents were informed through village councils that certain areas of the Şaho Mountains are off-limits until October 7. According to a notice issued by the Şiwankar village council, the restrictions apply to the mountain ridges stretching from Bedrawa through Pir-Xidir to the Goliçî Pass. The area around Pir-Xidir, among others, is being subjected to artillery fire.




The Şaho Mountains and the adjacent Kosalan Mountains were officially designated as a protected area by Iran’s Supreme Environmental Council in 2009. Nevertheless, the Revolutionary Guards have been expanding their military infrastructure there for years. At the end of August, the Revolutionary Guards heavily shelled the ridges of the Şaho Mountains in the Kamyaran area with artillery. Footage published by the KHRN subsequently documented extensive fires across the mountainous area.

author: Unknown
title: ISIS member arrested in Sulaymaniyah
content:
Counter-terrorism units have arrested a wanted member of the “Islamic State” (ISIS) in Sulaymaniyah. The man is said to have moved to Sulaymaniyah following the military collapse of ISIS and continued his activities for the organization there.




According to the Kurdish Counter-Terrorism Group Lexoman-Parastin (CTG), the arrest followed an extended period of surveillance and the analysis of detailed intelligence. The detainee reportedly belonged to a unit designated by ISIS as the “210th Division.”




Following the collapse of the jihadist group, the man settled in Sulaymaniyah. According to the security forces, however, he remained active as an ISIS member within the province until he was tracked down and arrested by counter-terrorism units.




His father had also held senior positions within ISIS. He initially served as commander of a military unit in the so-called “North Baghdad Province” and was later appointed ISIS “governor” of Fallujah. He was killed in an airstrike in the Abu Ghraib district.




A brother of the detainee, who was also a member of ISIS, was killed in the an-Nibāʿī area northwest of Baghdad, according to the security forces. No further information was provided about the detainee’s identity or his specific activities for ISIS in Sulaymaniyah.

author: Unknown
title: Syrian Federation for Human Rights calls for constitutional right to mother-tongue education
content:
The Syrian Federation for Human Rights Organizations and Bodies has called for the linguistic and cultural rights of all communities in Syria to be guaranteed by law and the constitution. The right to education in one’s mother tongue, it said, must not depend on temporary political or administrative decisions.




In a statement issued by its Executive Council, the federation described linguistic and cultural diversity as an integral part of fundamental human rights. Language, it said, is directly linked to identity and culture, the right to education, and equal participation in social life. The rights of Kurds, Syriacs, Armenians, Circassians and other communities must therefore be protected, the federation underlined.




Mother-tongue education does not mean division




According to the federation, the recognition of different languages does not contradict either Syria’s unity or the status of Arabic as the official language. The existence of an official state language must not be used as a justification for excluding other languages from education, culture and social life, it said.




“Protecting and learning one’s mother tongue means neither division nor isolation. On the contrary, it can strengthen a sense of belonging, participation and equality when the shared rights of all citizens are respected. Multilingual education can help preserve cultural diversity, promote mu

author: Unknown
title: Baluken: Öcalan’s status is linked to the status of the Kurdish people
content:
Kurdish politician Idris Baluken has warned against viewing the peace and democratic society process solely through the lens of the current balance of power in Turkey. Speaking at an event in Besançon, France, he said the Kurdish question must be considered in the context of the restructuring of the Middle East and the shifting balance of power in the region.




Baluken referred to dialogue and negotiation efforts over the past decades and emphasized that the search for a political solution is by no means new: “The leadership of the Kurdish people and the Kurdish movement was already seeking an interlocutor 30 years ago in order to resolve this issue and intervene in the course of developments during this historic period,” the former HDP MP said, referring to Abdullah Öcalan.






















“The issue goes far beyond the current government”




Baluken described the mistrust toward the Turkish government and criticism of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, the AKP and the position of MHP Chair Devlet Bahçeli as largely justified. However, he said that focusing solely on these actors is not sufficient to assess the current developments.




“The issue goes far beyond Erdoğan, Bahçeli, the AKP or the MHP. It goes far beyond the current political government in Turkey.”




The decisive factor, he said, is the restructuring of the Middle East. “At a time when regional powers ar

author: Unknown
title: Explosive device planted by ISIS explodes in Mosul, killing two Iraqi soldiers
content:
Iraqi Ministry of Defense spokesperson Yahya Rasoul announced that an explosive device previously planted by ISIS members detonated during a search and security operation north of the Rawa Desert in Mosul.




The statement said that two soldiers were killed and two others wounded in the explosion.




The wounded soldiers were taken to hospital for treatment.

author: Unknown
title: A journey from YDG-H to Kurdistan’s mountains: Andok Cuma Zagros
content:
The Kurdish Freedom Movement has been a revolutionary movement that has witnessed some of the greatest acts of resistance in the history of revolutions around the world. One of the movement’s slogans, voiced by Abdullah Öcalan, “We started young, we will finish young,” has resonated throughout every stage of the Freedom Movement.




Each period in the history of the Freedom Movement needs to be examined and understood in its own context. One such period was that of the Patriotic Revolutionary Youth Movement (YDG-H), a revolutionary organisation established by Kurdish youth in the metropolitan areas of Turkey and Kurdistan in 2015.







 







The YDG-H period coincided with 2015, when what the movement described as genocidal attacks resumed in Kurdistan. YDG-H emerged during this period as Kurdish youth, particularly those living in Turkey’s major cities, reorganised themselves around a revolutionary organisation.




YDG-H was not merely an organisation engaged in street protests or armed clashes. It also represented a practical application of the strategy of self-defence, which Abdullah Öcalan had identified as an important component of his new paradigm.




YDG-H resistance led to the free mountains




Andok Cuma Zagros (Erhan Uzun) was born in Istanbul in 2001 after his family had been forced to migrate there because of state repression in Kurdistan in the 1990s. He w

author: Unknown
title: Fate of at least five Kurds unknown after enforced disappearance
content:
Four arrests reported in 2026 have renewed concern about enforced disappearances in Rojhelat. The fifth unresolved case is that of Idris Faghihi and dates back to 2021.




According to the latest published reports, the families of these five people still have no clear answers about their fate or whereabouts.




Rojhelat Info said that "Idris Faghihi, a member of the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), was wounded during a clash near Bukan on 24 July 2021 and later arrested by Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces." The Kurdistan Human Rights Network said that year it had found evidence that he was alive and being held at an IRGC intelligence detention centre in Urmia. The authorities have still not formally told his family where he is or what has happened to him.




The first case of enforced disappearances, reported in 2026, is that of Sara Rashidi Kachalanlou, from Maku. She was arrested by IRGC intelligence agents near Kermanshah on 11 January 2026. She was initially taken to the Nabi Akram detention centre, but her family has received no clear information about her since then.




The second and third case reported is that of Zahra Pir-Dehghan and Parvin Rasegh Ghezelbash, who were arrested by IRGC intelligence agents in Urmia on 25 and 28 June 2026, respectively. The East Kurdistan Free Woman Society (KJAR) says both women are its members. Their families still d

author: Unknown
title: Journalist Nagihan Akarsel commemorated at her graveside
content:
Nagihan Akarsel, a member of the Jineology Research Center and a journalist who was killed in an armed attack outside her home in Sulaymaniyah in the Kurdistan Region on October 4, 2022, was commemorated at her graveside in the village of Gölyazı in Konya’s Kulu district. The commemoration was attended by Akarsel’s mother and relatives, members of the Jineology Research Center, the Mesopotamia Women Journalists Association (MKG) and the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG), the Konya and Ankara provincial organizations of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), DEM Party Istanbul MP Özgül Saki, and many others.




The commemoration began with a short march from the home of Akarsel’s family to the cemetery, followed by a moment of silence at her graveside. Roses and daisies were placed on her grave, while participants chanted “Şehîd namirin” (Martyrs are immortal) and “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî (Woman, Life, Freedom).




Saki: An attack on the philosophy of ‘Jin, Jiyan, Azadî’




Speaking after the moment of silence, DEM Party MP Özgül Saki described the attack as an attack on the philosophy of ‘Jin, Jiyan, Azadî,’ and said:




“They wanted to prevent Nagihan from conveying the truth to us by blending emotion and thought in the light of science. That struggle was undoubtedly continuing. In her writings, she said: ‘I am speaking to you from a geography where resis

author: Unknown
title: Lawyer Demir: The Hacı Lokman Birlik case is a litmus test for the peace process
content:
Eleven years after the killing of Hacı Lokman Birlik in Şırnak and the subsequent desecration of his body, the police officers responsible have still not been held criminally accountable. Following a ruling by Turkey’s Constitutional Court, the public prosecutor’s office is now set to reinvestigate the case. The family’s lawyer, Ramazan Demir, calls for investigations into all officers involved—from those who fired the shots to those in the chain of command. At the same time, he views the case as a litmus test for the ongoing peace and democratic society process.




27-year-old actor Hacı Lokman Birlik, also known by his Kurdish name Siyabend, was killed on October 3, 2015, during military operations in Şırnak. The city was under curfew and besieged by police and military forces. Police officers subsequently tied his body to an armored vehicle and dragged it through the streets. Footage of the incident was circulated by members of the police themselves.




The autopsy report documented 28 gunshot wounds, 17 of which were classified as fatal. Witnesses reported that Birlik had been sitting by the roadside when shots were fired at him from a passing vehicle. The shooting allegedly continued even after he had stopped moving. Despite the footage, the circumstances of his death, and the family’s years-long demands for justice, no effective criminal investigation was carried out.

author: Unknown
title: TEV-DEM condemns racist provocation in Hesekê
content:
Following a demonstration featuring anti-Kurdish demands in Hesekê, the Democratic Society Movement (TEV-DEM) warned against attempts to fuel ethnic tensions in the multi-ethnic city. At Friday’s rally in the predominantly Arab neighborhood of Xiwêran (Ghweiran), around 200 people called, among other things, for Kurds to be removed from institutions in Hesekê province.




During the demonstration, in which a particularly large number of children and young people participated, slogans were also chanted against Kurdish national symbols and flags. Kurdish flags were also reportedly burned following Friday prayers. In a statement on Sunday, TEV-DEM described the action as a racist provocation by a limited group and explicitly rejected attempts to portray it as reflecting the views or demands of the Arab population.




“Limited to a particular group”




According to TEV-DEM, the slogans voiced during the demonstration were aimed at inciting racism against the Kurdish population and other sections of society. The position expressed there was limited to a particular group, TEV-DEM stated. “Some of the rhetoric directly targeted the legitimate national and political rights of the Kurds. At the same time, rhetoric was used that fueled social discord and thereby served the enemies of Syria.”




TEV-DEM emphasized that the anti-Kurdish demands must not be attributed to the Arab popula

author: Unknown
title: Journalist Ferda Çetin spoke about Peace and Democratic Society Process in Giessen
content:
A public meeting was held in Giessen as part of the Peace and Democratic Integration Conference. The meeting was attended by journalist and politician Ferda Çetin, who discussed with participants the current stage of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the steps taken so far, and developments expected in the coming period.




In his remarks, Çetin said the Call for Peace and a Democratic Society issued by Kurdish people's leader Abdullah Öcalan on February 27 had opened the door to a new political period. He said the call had two central dimensions: bringing wars and conflicts to an end through dialogue and negotiations, and building a democratic society.




Çetin emphasized that lasting peace could only be achieved if people were actively involved in the process and had a meaningful role in shaping it. He also underlined the importance of broad social participation in the construction of a democratic society.




‘Baseless claims are being systematically circulated’




Participants at the meeting raised concerns about the spread of what they described as baseless claims on social media platforms including Facebook, YouTube and TikTok. They said misleading narratives targeting Abdullah Öcalan, the Freedom Movement and the peace process were being deliberately and systematically circulated with the aim of undermining the process.




Following Çetin’s presentation, the

author: Unknown
title: PYD: Cutting Kurdish language classes restricts the right to education
content:
The Democratic Union Party (PYD) has criticized the decision by the Damascus interim government to reduce Kurdish-language classes to three lessons per week, saying the move restricts the Kurdish people’s right to education in their mother tongue.




Party members Ahmed Suleiman and Beritan Najim read the statement in both Arabic and Kurdish outside the party’s office in Derbesiyê.




The statement rejected the decision by the Education Ministry of the interim government to reduce Kurdish-language classes to three lessons per week, arguing that the measure was incompatible with the requirements of Syria’s linguistic and cultural diversity.




The PYD called for the decision to reduce Kurdish-language classes to be reversed and for an education system to be implemented that guarantees students the right to learn their mother tongue without restrictions or discrimination.




The party also called on democratic forces, civil society organizations and human rights groups to support these demands.

author: Unknown
title: İmralı Delegation meets with Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz
content:
Pervin Buldan and Mithat Sancar, members of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) İmralı Delegation, met with Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz on Saturday.




The meeting, which lasted nearly one hour, reportedly addressed the two meetings held by the Monitoring and Evaluation Board, as well as the functioning of the four subcommittees established by the board.




During the meeting, the DEM Party İmralı Delegation also received information about the board’s activities and conveyed its views and proposals regarding the process to Yılmaz.

title: DFG publishes September report on rights violations against journalists
content:
The Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG) released its “September Report on Rights Violations Against Journalists.” The report stated that, in September, access restrictions were at the forefront in terms of press and freedom of expression.




The report emphasized that access to social media accounts had been blocked and stated: “According to the September data, access to 3,492 digital media content was blocked on the internet and digital media sphere. In addition, access to 15 news reports was blocked, while 4 websites were shut down. In September, the accounts or websites of media outlets such as JINNEWS, Mezopotamya Agency, Evrensel, Kısa Dalga and T24 faced access restrictions and platform interventions. In addition, the personal X accounts of numerous journalists were made invisible in Turkey on grounds such as ‘the protection of national security and public order.’”




The DFG report also included the following points.




“In September, 15 journalists were detained, and 8 journalists were arrested. The homes of 4 journalists were raided, 3 journalists were threatened, journalists were prevented from covering the news in 5 incidents, and 2 journalists were subjected to ill-treatment. title: Geothermal plants and rising costs hit fig producers
content:
Fig producers in Yaykın neighbourhood in the Karacasu district of Aydın are struggling with high input costs and falling crop prices. Gülhanım Tarhan, one of the producers who spoke to ANKA News Agency, said they sorted their figs according to quality, yet the average selling price still failed to reach even 100 Turkish Lira (TL, around 1.81 euros) per kilogram. Tarhan said they were making a loss this season on figs they had sold for between 225 and 250 lira per kilogram last year, adding that their income no longer covered production costs.




Average selling price falls to 67–70 TL




Another fig producer, Yeliz Tüzyılmaz, provided details of this year’s market prices. First-grade figs are sold for around 120 TL per kilogram, second-grade figs for 60–70 TL, and third-grade figs, known among producers as “baby” figs, for around 50 TL.




Tüzyılmaz said that once all grades were taken into account, the average income per kilogram had fallen to between 67 and 70 TL. Last year, she said, first-grade figs sold for 210 TL per kilogram and second-grade figs for between 120 and 130 TL.




Twenty kilos of figs do not cover a day’s wage




Tüzyılmaz said producers were being squeezed by rising fertiliser, diesel and labor costs, while Tariş had still not announced a base price despite the season nearing its end. She said this had deepened uncertainty in the market.

title: Director Ismail Güneş: Peace should be at the heart of cinema and art - Part One
content:
As the Peace and Democratic Society Process enters its second year, debates surrounding the process in Turkey continue across different social and cultural spheres. Artists share their views and criticisms of the process with the public through their statements and works.




Director Ismail Güneş, who brought the torture experienced in Turkey following the 12 September 1980 military coup to the screen with his movie 

Where the Rose Ends,

One of the Unplastered Houses

. Director Güneş spoke to ANF not only about his own cinema, but also about the current state of political cinema in Turkey and the role of art in the peace process.




Discussing the socialization of violence in his movies, Güneş said that violence emerges at the point where an individual loses the ability to establish a civilized and philosophical bond with “the other,” and continued: “Because violence is a primitive form of ‘imposing truth’ that begins where an individual loses the ability to establish a civilized and philosophical bond with the other, emerging at the moment when words run out. title: KCK commemorates Mam Jalal Talabani
content:
The Kurdistan Communities Union (KCK) commemorated Jalal Talabani, founder of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the first Kurdish president of Iraq, on the ninth anniversary of his death. In its statement, the KCK particularly highlighted Talabani’s role in the Kurdish freedom struggle, his efforts toward national unity, and his commitment to a political solution to the Kurdish question.




The KCK statement on Saturday reads as follows:




“Today marks the ninth anniversary of the death of President Mam (Uncle) Jalal Talabani, founder of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan and the first Kurdish president of the Federal Republic of Iraq. As an intellectual, revolutionary, Peshmerga, commander and accomplished Kurdish politician, President Mam Jalal Talabani shaped more than 50 years of the history of the freedom struggle of Kurdistan and the Kurdish people. Throughout numerous phases of the national and political struggle, he achieved significant gains for the Kurdish people.




Mam Jalal’s work and struggle for the freedom of Kurdistan and the Kurdish people were not limited to Southern Kurdistan. Whenever necessary, he supported and participated in the armed struggle in other parts of Kurdistan. Whenever required, he assumed a leading role in politics and diplomacy in pursuit of a solution and peace.

title: DFG commemorates Nagihan Akarsel on the fourth anniversary of her killing
content:
In a written statement, the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG) commemorated Nagihan Akarsel, a journalist and member of the Jineology Research Center who was killed on 4 October 2022, and called for those responsible to be identified and brought to justice.




“This year, as her colleagues and those who have followed in her footsteps, we once again call for the real perpetrators to be exposed and prosecuted,” the statement said.




“On the fourth anniversary of the killing of Nagihan Akarsel, one of the pioneers of the Free Press, we remember her with respect, love, and an enduring sense of longing,” the DFG said, adding: “Nagihan Akarsel once said 'I am an adventurer; I do not settle in one place.'




The struggle for freedom that she began within herself has today become a path for millions of women. Women, journalists who have followed in her footsteps, and the students she taught are keeping Nagihan Akarsel’s dreams alive through the struggle for women’s freedom. Nagihan Akarsel’s pen continues to write at every level of the Free Media. We once again reaffirm our commitment to preserving the legacy she left us and keeping her dreams alive.”




Nagihan Akarsel

title: The social meaning of peace: Kurdish seasonal agricultural workers
content:
The problem of seasonal agricultural labor cannot be understood separately from the region’s economic structure. Kurdish cities have fertile plains, abundant water resources, and a young population. Yet instead of developing this potential locally, the region has become part of a system that forces people to leave their homes in search of work.




Every year, pickup trucks and minibuses leave the plains of Mardin (Mêrdîn), Batman (Êlîh),  Diyarbakır (Amed), Urfa (Riha), Siirt (Sêrt), Şırnak (Şirnex), Van (Wan), and Muş (Mûş). Carrying hundreds, sometimes thousands, of families, they embark on long journeys, from the citrus groves of Çukurova to the hazelnut fields of the Black Sea, from the potato fields of Konya to the cotton fields and vineyards of the Aegean. These families spend much of the year far from home.




Seasonal labor is not simply a matter of “fate” or “natural poverty.” It is part of a system produced by the war in Kurdistan. Villages emptied and burned by soldiers during the 1990s, restrictions on pastures and highland grazing areas, and agricultural lands placed under embargo cut thousands of families off from their land and livestock. Even according to official figures, thousands of settlements were forcibly evacuated. Farmers dispossessed of their land were pushed into working-class neighborhoods in the cities and transformed into a reserve of cheap labor

title: Prof. Doğu Ergil: A search for a new order has begun in Turkey
content:
Recent developments in the relationship between the economy and politics in Turkey have sparked debate over whether the country is entering a new political era. Alongside the fund investigation and the reopening or renewed discussion of certain cases that previously generated public controversy, debates over legal arrangements concerning the resolution of the Kurdish question are also being viewed as possible signs of change in the structure of the state and politics.




Political scientist Prof. Dr. Doğu Ergil spoke to ANF about what these developments mean in terms of the relationship between the state, politics and capital.




‘The beginning of a transformation’




Stating that the developments in Turkey mark the beginning of a transformation, Ergil pointed out that the current system of governance is no longer capable of sustaining the country:




“It may be overly optimistic, but it is certainly the beginning of a transformation. Why am I certain? First, because the methods being employed in Turkey, the system of administration, the understanding of law and the concept of citizenship can no longer sustain the country. Crises are erupting in every area, and these crises show us that the existing mode of governance and the methods being used are no longer adequate and are no longer functioning.

title: Uca: Kurdish and Yazidi demands must remain on Germany’s agenda
content:
Kurdish politician Feleknas Uca said the rise of the Alternative for Germany (AfD), the spread of anti-immigrant rhetoric and growing military spending were threatening social peace in Germany. She stressed the need for a strong left-wing alternative to right-wing populist policies that blamed immigrants for social problems.




Feleknaz Uca spoke to ANF about recent political developments in Germany, the demands of the Kurdish and Yazidi communities, the future of Shengal, developments in Rojava and efforts to achieve peace in Turkey.




What do you think about the latest election results and the rise of the AfD? In particular, what impact are calls for “remigration” and attempts to blame immigrants for the country’s problems having on society?




I find the results of the latest state elections and the high level of support that the AfD has reached across Germany deeply concerning. As someone with a migrant background myself, I am particularly troubled, and at times even frightened, by some of the AfD’s rhetoric and positions. I find it dangerous when people are collectively portrayed as a “problem” simply because of their origin, religion or migrant background, and when migration is used as a tool for an exclusionary election campaign.

title: Ill prisoners in Van unable to access treatment
content:
According to a report published by the Human Rights Association (IHD), there are at least 1,400 ill prisoners in prisons across Kurdistan and Turkey. Of these, 335 are seriously ill prisoners. Despite calls and applications for their release, sick prisoners are not being released, while the conditions under which they receive treatment are becoming increasingly difficult.




For ill prisoners, hospital examinations, access to the infirmary, and obtaining medication have turned into processes that can take days. Decisions issued by the Forensic Medicine Institute (ATK) are also making prisoners’ living conditions even more difficult.




Van (Wan) is one of the cities where this situation is particularly prevalent. There are 30 seriously ill prisoners in the city’s prisons. Requests for transfers and releases made on behalf of the prisoners have gone unanswered, and prisoners are not being released even when hospital medical boards issue reports stating that they “cannot remain in prison.”




The families of seriously ill prisoners in Van’s prisons, including Necdet Koç, Botan Karsu, and Burhan Adsız, are demanding that their relatives be given access to medical treatment and provided with adequate healthcare conditions.

title: Turkish companies accelerate tree cutting in the Behdînan region
content:
In recent days, Turkish companies have intensified tree cutting in the Behdînan region, encompassing Zaxo, Duhok, Berwarî Bala and Amediyê. Increasing their logging activities ahead of winter, the Turkish companies are transporting the trees across the border in trucks under military supervision. Footage shows dozens of trucks carrying felled trees from rural areas. Some of the trucks are accompanied by Turkish armored vehicles.




Over the past 10 days, felled trees have been transported by more than 250 trucks in the Berwarî Bala area of Amediyê district in Duhok.




Residents who filmed the footage protested the tree cutting, saying: “What you see here are felled trees. These trucks belong to the Turks. They are transporting trees cut down in Kurdistan. At the security checkpoint, our vehicles were stopped to facilitate the passage of the trucks loaded with trees.”




















According to information provided to Rojnews by local sources, some of the areas and villages where tree cutting has intensified include Mîska, Qumri, Hirûrê, Kêste, Tirwaniş and Nizdûrê in Berwarî Bala. The sources said that the destruction of trees in the region has accelerated particularly with the approach of winter.

content:
The conference organized by the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) in Brussels to discuss Kurdish representation at the United Nations (UN) and the demand for international status continues with presentations by experts in international law and human rights.




Barry A. Fisher, an international law expert, delivered the first presentation at a panel discussion that also featured Prof. Miloon Kothari and former Iraqi Human Rights Minister Bakhtiyar Amin. Fisher, who has been involved in constitution and legislation drafting as well as legal reform efforts in various countries, offered assessments on the international status of the Kurds, their representation at the UN, and regional developments.




Fisher: It is now time to rectify the injustice experienced by the Kurds




In his presentation titled “For the Rebirth of the Kurdish Nation,” Barry A. Fisher said that recognition of the Kurds at the UN and obtaining observer status were among the central objectives of the international campaign. Fisher addressed a wide range of issues, from Turkey’s military presence in Syria and Iraq and regional alliances to Kurdish international representation and diaspora efforts.

title: Final declaration at KNK conference: Committee to be established for Kurdish representation at UN
content:
The final declaration of the Conference on the Representation of the Kurdish Nation at the United Nations, hosted by the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) in Brussels, has been released.




The declaration calls for the Kurds to be recognized as a nation at the UN and represented as observers in UN-affiliated institutions. It also states that a long-term effort should be undertaken to secure representation for the Kurds at the United Nations.







 







The final declaration reads as follows:

title: 46 countries call for executions in Iran to be halted
content:
In a report published on 1 October 2026, the Iran Human Rights Organization reported that 46 countries had called for a halt to the rising number of executions in the Islamic Republic of Iran.




According to the report, a joint statement presented by the representative of Liechtenstein at the 63rd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council on 30 September 2026, was signed by 46 countries.




The statement said that at least 31 protesters had been executed since the crackdown on protests in December 2025 began. It also noted that dozens of people, including women and children, were at risk of execution.




Citing findings by UN experts, the signatory countries emphasized that the death penalty in Iran was being used to instill fear, suppress dissent, and restrict the freedoms of peaceful expression and assembly.




The joint statement also raised concerns about secret trials, violations of fair trial guarantees, torture and ill-treatment, enforced disappearances, and forced confessions.




The 46 countries called on the Iranian authorities to immediately end the use of the death penalty.

title: Workers dismissed from Amed City Hospital construction site launch strike
content:
At the construction site of the City Hospital, currently under construction in the Peyas (Kayapınar) district of Amed, 90 members of the Construction, Road and Highway Workers’ Union employed by the main contractor and subcontractor were dismissed.




Workers who launched a strike outside the hospital construction site in protest against the dismissals received visits of support from the Amed Labor and Democracy Platform and representatives of political parties. During a statement outside the site, a banner reading “The world will belong to labor” was displayed, and protesters chanted slogans including “Gürbağ, don’t be mistaken, don’t push our patience to the limit.”




Speaking at the gathering, Sabahat Sever, co-chair of the Amed No. 2 Branch of the Genel-Iş Union, affiliated with DISK, said they stood in solidarity with construction workers who had joined a union and were fighting for their rights by exercising their constitutional rights.




Sever stated that the rights violations at the construction site were inseparable from the working conditions faced by workers across the country. She said workers were struggling for humane working conditions and wages that would allow them to make a living.

title: First Kurdish Film Festival kicks off in Freiburg
content:
The First Kurdish Film Festival in Freiburg, has begun at Kommunales Kino. The festival is organized by the Avesta Cultural Association, established through the joint initiative of Kurdish cinema organizations in Freiburg.




Members of the Freiburg Film Commune Organizing Committee, Newroz Sönmez and Mustafa Özel, delivered the festival’s opening speeches. They were followed by a performance by Hozan Axîn.




On the first day of the festival, “Zare,” a 1926 Armenian-language silent drama written and directed by Hamo Beknazaryan, was screened. The film, produced in the Armenian Soviet Socialist Republic, was presented on screen accompanied by a live musical performance.




The program also featured a short film by a Kurdish director born in Kirkuk who lives in Norway. The film, which tells the story of three young people living in a refugee camp in northern Norway, was screened on the festival’s opening day.







 







16 films to be screened




The three-day festival, taking place from October 2 to 4, will feature a total of 16 films: four feature films, four documentaries and eight short films.




On the second day of the festival, the documentary “Vartinis,” directed by Mehmet Ömer Biçer, will be screened at Kommunales Kino to mark the anniversary of the Vartinis Massacre.

title: Göksu: Lasting peace requires stronger democratisation
content:
Musician Yasemin Göksu told ANF that lasting peace could only be achieved through democratisation and said, “Replacing violence with dialogue and weapons with politics offers an invaluable opportunity for society.”




Göksu said music was one of the most powerful carriers of memory and that an environment of lasting peace would also contribute to the freedom of the arts. She also said: “Once lasting peace is established, artists will be able to create more freely and people will have greater access to one another’s cultures.”




How can artists contribute to building peace and making it part of society during this period? What role can music play in ensuring that peace resonates not only at the negotiating table but also in everyday life, in people’s minds and consciences?




I do not see peace as an issue that should be discussed only at the negotiating table by political actors. The real test of peace, and of the parties involved, takes place in everyday life. How we see one another, how much we listen to and truly hear each other’s stories, and how well we manage to live alongside one another with our differences are all vitally important.

content:

Turkey is one of the world’s five fragile economies




Temelli addressed the recent rise in fuel prices, the fund crisis and deepening poverty in Turkey, saying that the country’s economy remained structurally fragile: “Turkey’s economy is fundamentally fragile. It is one of the five fragile economies in the world, and this fragility simply does not go away. There are many reasons for this. There are structural problems as well as administrative and institutional ones. Of course, the current political situation also has a very serious impact. As a result, this fragile economy constantly generates crises. Because of this persistent mentality of plunder, it repeatedly produces cases of profiteering and corruption.




A very significant part of Turkey’s economy is already informal, and within that informal economy there is what we call the black economy as well as the grey economy. title: Journalist Derya Okatan remanded in custody
content:
Derya Okatan, a journalist and member of the Disciplinary Board of the Press-Iş union of the Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions of Turkey (DISK), was detained at her home in Ankara and taken to Istanbul Çağlayan Courthouse. Okatan was referred to a judge with a request for her arrest without even having her statement taken by the prosecutor. The court subsequently ordered Derya Okatan’s detention pending trial.




The Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG) reacted to Derya Okatan’s arrest. The DFG said: “We stand with Derya Okatan against the criminalization of journalistic activities and attempts to silence journalists through pressure and arrests, and we demand her immediate release. Journalism is not a crime.”

title: Women to begin “memory vigil”: No murdered woman should be forgotten!
content:
The Amed Network Against Violence is launching a “Women’s Justice and Memory Vigil” in response to the recent increase in violence against women, suspicious deaths of women and femicides.




For 10 weeks, women will hold a vigil in front of the Amed Courthouse every Tuesday at 12:30 p.m., where they will read the stories of murdered women and voice their demands for justice. The first vigil will take place on 6 October.




Lawyer Aycan Diril, a member of the Amed Women’s Commission of the Lawyers for Freedom Association (ÖHD), which is part of the network, said that what is happening has gone beyond femicides and become a form of femicide targeting women’s bodies, truths and existence.







 







“Judicial practice has become a male-dominated practice”




Speaking about the purpose and process of the vigil, Aycan Diril said that the killings taking place are not merely numbers and that they aim to create a collective memory in response.




Diril said that data collected by women’s organizations shows an increase in femicides and suspicious deaths of women, adding that the absence of official data is also a significant problem. title: KNK conference begins: Kurds seek representation and status at the UN
content:
The Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) hosts a conference in Brussels with the aim of securing Kurdish representation at the United Nations (UN) and gaining international status, has begun. Attended by representatives of political parties and organizations from the four parts of Kurdistan and various countries around the world, as well as academics and experts in international law, the conference will discuss diplomatic efforts aimed at ensuring that 60 million Kurds are represented internationally with their own identity and political will.




The conference, held at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), is attended by American legal expert Barry Fisher, academic Miloon Kothari, who has worked within the United Nations, and his wife, as well as former Icelandic Foreign Minister Ögmundur Jónasson, and Coni Ledesma, who works in the field of international law.




The conference began with the singing of the Kurdish anthem “Ey Reqîb” and a one-minute silence. This was followed by the election of the conference presidium. Fehmi Vergili, Nilüfer Koç and Wirya Qaradaxi were elected to the presidium.






















Nilüfer Koç: Why don’t Kurds speak in their own name?

title: Xebat Andok: The process needs to become more inclusive of society
content:
KCK Executive Council member Xebat Andok gave an in-depth interview to Stêrk TV.




The first part of the interview can be read 

here

. 




The Peace and Democratic Society Process has been ongoing for two years. But when we look at the Turkish side – specifically the role that the media is playing – even their rhetoric hasn’t changed. Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan is being directly targeted. At the same time, they are not granting him any means to defend himself. Is their still an opposition to the Peace and Democratic Society Process?




Yes, there are certain circles, both inside and outside the country, that oppose the process. One has to look at the Turkish state’s media and their rhetoric. Then again, state officials have made various statements from time to time. They said that they would change the narrative of their media. But to this day, we haven’t really seen much of that. They act opportunistically from time to time. Sometimes people wonder if they’ll make some changes, but then they revert to their default settings. The reason for this isn’t that journalists perceive these issues correctly or speak about them in that way. No, that’s not the source of the problem. Essentially, everyone knows that journalism in Turkey is dependent on the Turkish state in every respect. It is primarily the state itself that coordinates them and sets their daily agenda.

title: Aram Tigran commemorated at Amed Book Fair
content:
The 10th Amed Book Fair, held at the Mesopotamia International Fair and Congress Center, continued on its seventh day. ‘I am devoted to the Kurdish language and Kurdish art’
